section: Romans 9:11–12 — Election, Foreknowledge, and the Twins Esau and Jacob
text: Romans 9:11–12 — Election, Foreknowledge, and the Twins Esau and Jacob

section: Romans 9:11–12 — Election, Foreknowledge, and the Twins Esau and Jacob
text: Romans 9:11–12 “though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad — in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls — she was told, 'The older will serve the younger.'” (ESV)

section: Romans 9:11–12 — Election, Foreknowledge, and the Twins Esau and Jacob
text: Corrected translation: for though the twins, Esau and Jacob, had not yet been born, and though they had not yet accomplished anything good or evil, in order that the predetermined plan of God — the divine decrees — might remain in status quo in relationship to election, not from works but from him who elects — it was said to her, Rebecca, quoting Genesis 25:23, the older Esau shall be subservient to the younger Jacob.

section: Romans 9:11–12 — Election, Foreknowledge, and the Twins Esau and Jacob
text: Romans 9:11–12 concludes the exegesis of the divine decree clause begun in verse 11 and introduces the direct quotation from Genesis 25:23 spoken to Rebecca while the twins were still in the womb. The passage draws together the doctrines of omniscience, election, foreknowledge, and predestination, and applies them to the historical contrast between Jacob and Esau as representative figures of Israel and Edom. The controlling thesis is that all divine blessing is imputed from the justice of God to the indwelling righteousness of God apart from human merit.

section: I. Concluding Exegesis of Romans 9:11 — Not of Works, But of Him Who Elects
text: I. Concluding Exegesis of Romans 9:11 — Not of Works, But of Him Who Elects

section: I. Concluding Exegesis of Romans 9:11 — Not of Works, But of Him Who Elects
text: The final clause of verse 11 supplies the doctrinal ground for everything preceding it. The verse has established that the divine decrees antedated the birth, the actions, and the moral standing of the twins. The concluding clause now states the positive and negative sides of the same principle.

section: The Negative: οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων
text: The Negative: οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων

section: The Negative: οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων
text: The clause opens with the objective negative adverb οὐ (ou), denying the reality of an alleged fact. Combined with the prepositional phrase ἐκ (ek) plus the ablative plural of ἔργον (ergon, work, deed), the construction reads οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων — not from works. The plural is significant: it comprehends every category of human performance. The ablative of source indicates the origin of the false concept that election intends to exclude — namely, that human works of any kind are the basis of divine blessing.

section: The Negative: οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων
text: Election, foreknowledge, and predestination are entirely the work of God. They are not cooperative ventures. No system of human merit — morality, religious observance, personality, social action, liturgical practice, or any other form of volitional performance — can enter the plan of God as a basis for blessing. The ablative case seals this: works are the excluded source, not merely an insufficient supplement.

section: The Positive: ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος
text: The Positive: ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος

section: The Positive: ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος
text: The contrasting phrase is ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος — from him who calls or, in the theological context, from him who elects. The definite article τοῦ (tou) functions as a personal pronoun, referring to God the Father. The present active participle of καλέω (kaleō, to call, to elect) is circumstantial. The historical present tense views the past function of God in omniscience — feeding facts only into the computer of divine decrees — with the vividness of a present occurrence. The active voice indicates that God the Father produces the action in eternity past.

section: The Positive: ἐκ τοῦ καλοῦντος
text: The verb kaleo in the doctrine of election carries the force of divine selection on the basis of foreknown faith. It does not connote coercion but rather the recognition and formal incorporation into the divine plan of every individual whose free-will decision to believe in Christ was known to omniscience in eternity past.

section: II. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:11
text: II. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:11

section: II. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:11
text: 1. Omniscience does not tamper with free will. The omniscience of God knows the function of man's free will completely — every thought, every decision, every action — but does not interfere with that free will. Only the fact of each volitional choice is fed into the computer of divine decrees. There is no manipulation, no coercion, and no predetermination of the will itself.

section: II. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:11
text: 2. Election is the free and unconditional grace of God. It is not conditioned on foreseen merit, foreseen works, or foreseen moral quality. It is conditioned solely on the foreknown fact of faith in Christ.

section: II. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:11
text: 3. No human works can intrude into election, foreknowledge, or predestination. Human ability, talent, morality, personality, or any meritorious function is excluded from the divine plan of blessing by the very structure of election.

section: II. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:11
text: 4. Faith in Christ is the total absence of human merit. Faith is non-meritorious perception — a legitimate exercise of free will that makes no contribution of its own to the result. Because faith is non-meritorious, it does not violate the principle of self-determination; it is, in fact, a pure expression of it. Faith is the grace response of the human will, not a work.

section: II. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:11
text: 5. This verse denies superlapsarianism. The supralapsarian position, which makes God the author of sin by arranging the decree of election prior to and as the cause of the Fall, impugns the character of God and denies man's volitional responsibility in the angelic conflict. The passage places the ground of election not in God's sovereign causation of human choices but in God's omniscient recognition of them.

section: II. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:11
text: 6. The casting away of racial Jews is attributable to personal volitional rejection of Christ. Romans 10–11 will make explicit what is implicit here: individual Jews who reject Christ as Savior bear personal responsibility for that rejection. The principle of volitional accountability is embedded in the structure of election itself.

section: II. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:11
text: 7. Omniscience feeds only facts into the computer of divine decrees. In some cases the fact is unbelief — a person rejects Christ from their own free will. In other cases the fact is faith. The printout for each category differs accordingly. Election and predestination are printouts that describe the plan of God for believers only.

section: II. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:11
text: 8. Election protects the believer from the intrusion of self. The purpose of election is to exclude any human contribution to the plan of God so that all blessing is attributable to God alone. The believer cannot improve upon the plan by witnessing for blessing, giving for blessing, praying for blessing, or any other form of performance-oriented piety. The justice of God imputes blessing to divine righteousness alone — the equivalent perfection that is the only legitimate target for divine blessing.

section: III. Exegesis of Romans 9:12a — It Was Said to Her
text: III. Exegesis of Romans 9:12a — It Was Said to Her

section: III. Exegesis of Romans 9:12a — It Was Said to Her
text: Verse 12 moves from the doctrinal ground clause of verse 11 to the direct scriptural citation that proves it — the word spoken to Rebecca in Genesis 25:23 while the twins were still in utero.

section: ἐρρέθη αὐτῇ — It Was Said to Her
text: ἐρρέθη αὐτῇ — It Was Said to Her

section: ἐρρέθη αὐτῇ — It Was Said to Her
text: The verb form ἐρρέθη (errethē) is the aorist passive indicative from ῥέω (rheō). This root became obsolete and was functionally replaced by the aorist passive of λέγω (legō). The aorist tense is constative, viewing the action in its entirety — the single, momentous announcement God made to a pregnant woman before her children were born. The passive voice indicates that Rebecca receives the content of the divine communication. The indicative mood is declarative, introducing the citation of Genesis 25:23.

section: ἐρρέθη αὐτῇ — It Was Said to Her
text: The indirect object αὐτῇ (autē) is the dative singular of the intensive pronoun αὐτός (autos). Greek has no third-person personal pronoun distinct from the intensive; autos serves that function here. The dative is a dative of advantage: it was to Rebecca's advantage to know these things, and she acted upon this knowledge throughout her life in favor of her younger son.

section: ὅτι as Quotation Marker
text: ὅτι as Quotation Marker

section: ὅτι as Quotation Marker
text: The conjunction ὅτι (hoti) introduces the direct quotation. After verbs of saying or speaking, hoti functions as a recitative conjunction — the equivalent of opening quotation marks in modern punctuation. What follows is the content of the divine declaration to Rebecca.

section: The Quotation from Genesis 25:23
text: The Quotation from Genesis 25:23

section: The Quotation from Genesis 25:23
text: The full text of God's word to Rebecca, rendered from the Hebrew of Genesis 25:23, reads as follows: And the LORD said to her, Two nations are in your womb; consequently, two peoples shall be separated from your body. Furthermore, one people shall be stronger than the other. And — here is the clause Paul cites — the older shall serve the younger.

section: The Quotation from Genesis 25:23
text: The observation from this passage regarding the status of life before birth is exegetically significant: the statement is directed to a pregnant woman whose children have not yet been born. The text of Genesis does not attribute personhood to the embryos or fetuses in the womb. They do not become distinct human persons until they emerge from the womb and life is imputed by God. The prophecy concerns what they will become and what they will do, not what they already are in the womb. This is consistent with the biblical pattern of divine life-imputation at birth.

section: The Quotation from Genesis 25:23
text: The two peoples prophesied are Israel, descended from Jacob, and Edom, descended from Esau. The statement that one people will be stronger than the other tracks the historical relationship between Israel and Edom across the centuries — a relationship in which Israel repeatedly dominated Edom, culminating in the complete historical disappearance of the Edomite people by the time Paul wrote.

section: ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάσσονι — The Older Shall Be Subservient to the Younger
text: ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάσσονι — The Older Shall Be Subservient to the Younger

section: ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάσσονι — The Older Shall Be Subservient to the Younger
text: The key clause of the quotation employs μείζων (meizōn), the comparative of μέγας (megas, great). In this context it carries the sense of older — a reference to Esau as the firstborn twin. The future active indicative of δουλεύω (douleuō) means to be a slave, but in this context the sense is broader: to be inferior, to be subservient. Esau did not literally serve Jacob as a domestic slave. The meaning is that Jacob would consistently dominate — in the matters of spiritual heritage, divine election, covenant promises, and the trajectory of history. The dative object is ἐλάσσονι (elassoni), the comparative of small, meaning younger — a reference to Jacob.

section: ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάσσονι — The Older Shall Be Subservient to the Younger
text: Primogeniture — the right of the firstborn to the preeminent position of authority and inheritance — is here set aside by divine decree. The setting aside of primogeniture is not unprecedented in Israel's history: Isaac superseded Ishmael, Jacob superseded Esau, Ephraim superseded Manasseh. In each case, the divine choice is not determined by birth order but by the sovereign purpose of God operating through the foreknown decisions of free human will.

section: ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάσσονι — The Older Shall Be Subservient to the Younger
text: The corrected translation of verse 12: It was said to her, Rebecca — quoting Genesis 25:23 — the older Esau shall be subservient to the younger Jacob.

section: IV. Jacob and Esau as Historical Illustrations
text: IV. Jacob and Esau as Historical Illustrations

section: IV. Jacob and Esau as Historical Illustrations
text: The contrast between Jacob and Esau in the narrative of Genesis is not a contrast between a morally superior person and a morally inferior one. Both twins shared the same old sin nature, inherited through the same genetic line, and both manifested it — in different modes and in different directions. The distinction that matters for Paul's argument in Romans 9 is not moral quality but volitional orientation toward the grace of God.

section: IV. Jacob and Esau as Historical Illustrations
text: Esau was a man of the field, a hunter whose identity was organized around physical performance and the demonstration of prowess. His father Isaac developed a preference for him partly on the basis of shared interest. Yet Esau's characteristic pattern was to assign low value to spiritual realities: he sold his birthright for a single meal, and when he later sought to reclaim what he had despised, he found no opportunity to reverse the course his volition had set. His weeping over the lost blessing (Genesis 27:38; Hebrews 12:17) was the expression of regret without repentance — a desire for the consequences of faith without the substance of it.

section: IV. Jacob and Esau as Historical Illustrations
text: Jacob, whatever his moral defects, consistently valued the spiritual heritage. His methods were at times dishonest, and the narrative does not commend his deceptions. But the question Paul is pressing is not: who was the better man? The question is: who made the salvation adjustment to the justice of God through faith in Christ? Jacob did. Esau did not. That single volitional difference — known to omniscience in eternity past and fed into the computer of divine decrees — is the entire basis for the distinction Paul is drawing.

section: IV. Jacob and Esau as Historical Illustrations
text: The lesson from Esau's life applies beyond the specific historical figure. The pattern of spending one's life attempting to prove superiority through external performance — physical, professional, social — rather than orienting to the reality that life is determined by the content of the soul, is a universal temptation. The Esau pattern is one of inflexibility toward essential things (doctrine, faith, the grace of God) combined with stubborn insistence on proving worth through non-essential performance. The Jacob pattern, despite all its moral complications, is one of recognizing that the spiritual heritage is the thing worth having and that it comes by faith, not by achievement.

section: IV. Jacob and Esau as Historical Illustrations
text: Authority orientation is a related theme embedded in the contrast. Esau's descendants, the Edomites, exhibited at the national level the same inability to defer to a structure larger than themselves. They were formidable individual fighters but incapable of the sustained collective submission to authority that makes military victory possible. The principle of freedom through military victory requires that a people recognize and function within a chain of command. Edom could not sustain it, and as a result could be defeated in detail. The progeny of Esau have disappeared from history. The progeny of Jacob remain in every generation of human history, a demonstration of the faithfulness of God's unconditional covenants.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 1. The unconditional gracious promises to Abraham could only be fulfilled by regeneration, not natural generation. Neither Ishmael nor Esau qualified for the Abrahamic covenant promises because they did not parlay human life into eternal life through faith in Christ. Biological descent from Abraham produces no spiritual standing before God.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 2. Foreknowledge recognized what omniscience had fed into the computer of divine decrees. The foreknowledge of God made nothing certain; it acknowledged what was already certain — the free-will choices of each individual as known to omniscience. The statement of foreknowledge does not cause the outcome; it reflects it.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 3. Election, foreknowledge, and predestination apply to believers only. The unbeliever is not predestined to hell. He goes to hell from his own volition, by his own repeated rejection of the grace of God. Election, foreknowledge, and predestination are printouts from the divine decrees describing God's plan for those who believe in Christ.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 4. Since Esau would be an unbeliever, he was not included in divine election. He could not be the recipient of the grace promises to Abraham. To receive those promises, he would need two things: the imputation of divine righteousness and eternal life — both of which are imputed at the moment of faith in Christ.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 5. Only the spiritual seed of Abraham can be included in the unconditional promises of the Abrahamic covenant. Born-again Jews — those who have made the salvation adjustment to the justice of God through faith in Christ — are the heirs of the covenant. Racial descent is a necessary but not sufficient condition for covenant participation.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 6. The fundamental difference between the twins was attitude toward Christ, not birth order. Primogeniture was set aside not because God arbitrarily preferred one over the other, but because the foreknown faith of Jacob and the foreknown unbelief of Esau determined different printouts from the divine decrees.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 7. Jacob was not a morally superior person. Human morality had nothing to do with the distinction. The sole operative factor is expressed in the phrase from verse 11: not from works, but from him who elects. Jacob's election rested on his faith, not his character.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 8. Esau and Ishmael were not rejected because of parentage or sinfulness. They were excluded from covenant blessing because from their own free will they rejected Christ as Savior. Responsibility rests entirely with the individual's volitional choice.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 9. Paul's burden for the Jews is grounded in this passage. The Jews of Paul's generation possess the genetic heritage of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But genetic heritage confers no spiritual standing. Only those Jews who are born again — who have made the salvation adjustment — are heirs of the spiritual promises. The national rejection of Christ as Savior, known to God in eternity past, accounts for the casting away that Paul will address in Romans 10–11.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 10. The divine heritage of Israel is spiritual. No one functions as a true heir of the Abrahamic covenant without regeneration. The imputation of divine righteousness at salvation is the prerequisite for any subsequent imputation of blessing from the justice of God.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 11. The historical fate of Edom confirms the prophecy of Genesis 25:23. At the time Paul wrote, the Edomites had completely disappeared as a distinct people. Defeated repeatedly in the periods of David and Solomon, absorbed and superseded by the Nabatean Arabs, and finally eliminated as a distinct ethnic entity, the progeny of Esau had fulfilled the prophecy — not as servants in a household but as the subservient and ultimately extinct strand of history. The progeny of Jacob, by contrast, persist in every generation, preserved by the faithfulness of God's unconditional covenants.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 12. God did not predestine sin and is not the author of sin. Through redemption, God has overruled sin to His own glory and to the personal salvation of every believer. Both Jacob and Esau were sinners. Only one of them opted for God's solution through faith in Christ.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 13. Election does not eliminate human freedom. The fact that Jacob was elected, foreknown, and predestined does not make him a passive object of divine determination. It means that every person who believes in Christ is in the plan of God — elected, foreknown, and predestined — and that being in the plan of God excludes no legitimate human function while excluding all illegitimate claims to merit-based blessing.

section: V. Doctrinal Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 14. Jacob's superseding of Esau was a result of his salvation adjustment to the justice of God. The fact that Jacob from his own free will believed in Christ was known to God in eternity past. God always knew which way the free will of each twin would move on the decisive question: What do you think of Christ? The answer to that question is the organizing principle of all divine blessing, covenant participation, and the plan of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-One
text: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-One

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-One
text: 1. Election is the divine side of grace. Ephesians 2:8–9 states the human side: salvation is by grace through faith and not of works. Romans 9:11 states the divine side: the predetermined plan of God remains in status quo in relationship to election — not from works, but from him who elects. Both statements are two faces of the same principle. The grace of God excludes human merit from every point in the process.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-One
text: 2. The justice of God is the exclusive channel of divine blessing. All blessing flows from the justice of God to the divine righteousness imputed to the believer at salvation. No human performance — however commanded by Scripture in other contexts — can function as the basis for receiving that blessing. Tithing, prayer, witnessing, moral reform, and religious observance may each be legitimate in their proper context, but none of them is the mechanism by which divine blessing is released.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-One
text: 3. Omniscience and free will are not in conflict. The omniscience of God knows every decision the free will of every person will ever make. That knowledge does not cause those decisions, coerce them, or override them. God fed only facts into the computer of divine decrees. The printout of election is, therefore, not a violation of human freedom but a recognition of it — and a protection of the believer from any system that would make human performance the basis of standing before God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-One
text: 4. The spiritual seed of Abraham, not the natural seed, inherits the covenant promises. This is Paul's central argument in Romans 9–11. The promises to Abraham were never intended to be fulfilled by biological descent alone. They are fulfilled in and through faith in Christ — the same faith Abraham himself exercised. The temporary setting aside of Israel as a client nation (Romans 10–11; AD 70) does not annul the unconditional covenants; it demonstrates that their fulfillment awaits the regeneration of the nation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-One
text: 5. Orientation to reality — the soul, not the body — determines the course of a life. The contrast between Jacob and Esau illustrates the principle that life is determined by what is in the soul — by thought, by doctrine, by the decisions of the right lobe — and not by physical performance, social status, or demonstrated talent. Doctrine is a thought, not a muscle. The Jacobs of history — those who value and pursue the spiritual heritage — will consistently supersede those who invest their energies in proving superiority through external means.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-One
text: 6. The persistence of the Jewish people is a demonstration of the faithfulness of God. The Edomites have disappeared. The Jews remain. The two peoples prophesied in Genesis 25:23 have followed exactly the trajectories that the word of God announced before either of them had drawn a first breath. This is not coincidence; it is the faithfulness of the God whose omniscience fed only facts into the computer of divine decrees and whose justice has been maintaining those decrees in status quo ever since.

section: Glossary
text: The divine recognition of what omniscience has already fed into the computer of divine decrees. Foreknowledge makes nothing certain; it acknowledges what is already certain by virtue of omniscience knowing every free-will decision of every human being in eternity past.

section: Glossary

section: Glossary
text: The attribute of God by which He knows simultaneously and completely all actual and all possible events, decisions, and thoughts — past, present, and future. Only actual facts (not possibilities) are fed into the computer of divine decrees. Omniscience is the epistemological foundation for the entire system of election, foreknowledge, and predestination.

section: Glossary
text: One of the verbs used in the doctrine of election. In Romans 9:11 the present active participle is used circumstantially, describing God the Father as the one who elects. The historical present tense views the past function of God in eternity past with the vividness of a present occurrence.

section: Glossary

text: The moment of faith in Christ, at which the justice of God imputes divine righteousness and eternal life to the believer. Instantaneous and once for all. The salvation adjustment is the prerequisite for all subsequent divine blessing, since the justice of God can only impute blessing to its own equivalent — the divine righteousness now resident in the believer.

text: The unconditional covenant made between God and Abraham (Genesis 12, 15, 17), promising land, seed, and universal blessing. Its promises are inherited by the spiritual seed of Abraham — those who, like Abraham, believe God — not by natural descent alone.
Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Two

section: Romans 9:12 — Divine Decrees, Omniscience, and the Sovereignty of God
text: Romans 9:12 — Divine Decrees, Omniscience, and the Sovereignty of God

section: Romans 9:12 — Divine Decrees, Omniscience, and the Sovereignty of God
text: Romans 9:12 “she was told, 'The older will serve the younger.'” (ESV)

section: Romans 9:12 — Divine Decrees, Omniscience, and the Sovereignty of God
text: Corrected translation: It was said to her — Rebecca — 'The older, Esau, shall be subservient to the younger, Jacob.'

section: Romans 9:12 — Divine Decrees, Omniscience, and the Sovereignty of God
text: This chapter continues the verse-by-verse exposition of Romans 9, still working through verse 12. The announcement made to pregnant Rebecca — that the older twin would be subservient to the younger — opens the fundamental theological question of how God can make such a declaration prior to birth. The answer lies in the doctrine of divine decrees. Before the text can address why God loved Jacob and hated Esau, or why God hardened Pharaoh's heart, the foundational mechanics of omniscience, the computer of divine decrees, and the printout categories for believers must be established. That is the task of this chapter.

section: I. Romans 9:12 — The Declaration to Rebecca
text: I. Romans 9:12 — The Declaration to Rebecca

section: I. Romans 9:12 — The Declaration to Rebecca
text: The corrected translation of verse 12 reads: it was said to her — Rebecca — quoting from Genesis 25:23, the older, Esau, shall be subservient to the younger, Jacob. This declaration was made before either child had been born, before either had performed any act of obedience or disobedience. The announcement therefore cannot rest on foreseen human merit. It rests on the eternal counsel of God as expressed in the divine decrees.

section: The Pattern of Negative Volition in Israel
text: The Pattern of Negative Volition in Israel

section: The Pattern of Negative Volition in Israel
text: The Lord Jesus Christ addresses the same pattern of negative volition in Matthew 23:37, speaking to Jerusalem: 'O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to her — that is, sent with doctrine. How often I would have gathered your children together, the way a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing.' Luke 13:34 covers the same incident and closes with the even stronger expression of negative volition: you would not have it.

section: The Pattern of Negative Volition in Israel
text: The pattern is constant. Man always receives what he truly asks for, whether as an individual or as a national entity. When a nation experiences historical catastrophe, the catastrophe reflects the accumulated free-will choices of its citizens. Jesus Christ controls history. No historical outcome is arbitrary.

section: Eight Orienting Principles from Romans 9:12
text: Eight Orienting Principles from Romans 9:12

section: Eight Orienting Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 1. Jews following the line of Esau are characterized by the same negative volition described in Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34 — a persistent refusal of divine instruction.

section: Eight Orienting Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 2. Man always receives exactly what he asks for. This is true of individuals and of nations. No exceptions exist.

section: Eight Orienting Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 3. Perfect God is the source of divine good but is never responsible for sin, human good, or evil.

section: Eight Orienting Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 4. Sin, human good, and evil originate from the free will of man — self-determination motivated by the old sin nature.

section: Eight Orienting Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 5. Because the omniscience of God knew how the free will of man would operate in every situation, He fed those facts into the computer of divine decrees. Omniscience knows actuality and probability, but only actuality is entered into the decrees.

section: Eight Orienting Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 6. God is responsible for election and ordination; man is responsible for his own condemnation.

section: Eight Orienting Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 7. To God belongs the glory of the salvation of the elect; to mankind belongs the responsibility for the ruin of the old sin nature.

section: Eight Orienting Principles from Romans 9:12
text: 8. Man's responsibility meets God's glory in the doctrine of divine decrees. The computer of divine decrees prints out for believers: election, foreknowledge, predestination. It prints out for unbelievers: reprobation, condemnation, retribution.

section: II. The Doctrine of Divine Decrees — Definition and Description
text: II. The Doctrine of Divine Decrees — Definition and Description

section: II. The Doctrine of Divine Decrees — Definition and Description
text: With the orienting principles established, the text drives into the doctrine of divine decrees. This doctrine is the necessary foundation for understanding not only Romans 9:12 but also the passages immediately following — why God loved Jacob and hated Esau, and why God hardened Pharaoh's heart.

section: Point 1 — Definition
text: Point 1 — Definition

section: Point 1 — Definition
text: The decree of God is His eternal, holy, wise, and sovereign purpose — comprehending at once, simultaneously, all things that ever were or will be, in their causes, courses, conditions, successions, and relations, and determining their certain future.

section: Point 1 — Definition
text: The definition expresses both the nature and the source of the decrees. The source is the omniscience of God. The scope is total: every thought, every decision, every action of every person across all of human history and angelic history.

section: Point 2 — The Several Contents of One Eternal Purpose
text: Point 2 — The Several Contents of One Eternal Purpose

section: Point 2 — The Several Contents of One Eternal Purpose
text: The several contents of this one eternal purpose are, because of the limitations of human mentality, necessarily conceived of by us in partial aspects and logical relations. We therefore style them 'decrees,' plural. In reality the decree is singular and simultaneous. For teaching purposes, the logical order runs: omniscience first, decrees second, election and foreknowledge and predestination third. We examine each in turn.

section: Points 3–6 — The Scope and Nature of the Decrees
text: Points 3–6 — The Scope and Nature of the Decrees

section: Points 3–6 — The Scope and Nature of the Decrees
text: 3. The decrees of God are the eternal and immutable will of God regarding the future existence of events that will happen in time, and the precise order and manner of their occurrence. By the decrees, God has rendered certain all events of the universe — angelic history, human history, past, present, and future.

section: Points 3–6 — The Scope and Nature of the Decrees
text: 4. The decrees of God are the chosen and adopted plan of all God's works.

section: Points 3–6 — The Scope and Nature of the Decrees
text: 5. The decrees of God are His eternal purpose, according to the counsel of His own will, whereby for His own glory He has foreordained whatsoever comes to pass.

section: Points 3–6 — The Scope and Nature of the Decrees
text: 6. We exist for God's pleasure. God is not in existence for our pleasure.

section: Point 7 — The Computer Analogy
text: Point 7 — The Computer Analogy

section: Point 7 — The Computer Analogy
text: The decrees of God are pictured as a giant computer. The omniscience of God feeds the facts — thought, decision, action — into the computer of divine decrees simultaneously in eternity past. Three categories of time assist the finite mind in grasping this: alpha time (eternity past, in which God has always existed without beginning), history (the span of events from creation to the end of the millennium, including past, present, and future from the human perspective), and omega time (the eternal future). To God, everything that ever occurred in history was known before history began.

section: Point 7 — The Computer Analogy
text: God knew every thought you would ever think, every decision you would ever make, every action you would ever perform. He knew these things by name and in detail before Adam existed. He did not tamper with human free will to obtain this knowledge. The free will of every moral agent operates spontaneously within the framework of the decrees because the omniscience of God knew, with infinite precision, how every free agent would choose.

section: Points 8–9 — The Printout Categories
text: Points 8–9 — The Printout Categories

section: Points 8–9 — The Printout Categories
text: 8. The computer of divine decrees prints out facts about believers under three categories: election, foreknowledge, and predestination. It also prints out facts about unbelievers under the categories of reprobation, condemnation, and retribution.

section: Points 8–9 — The Printout Categories
text: 9. The decrees of God are the sum total of God's plan, designed in eternity past, relating to all events of every classification, collected into one single all-comprehensive whole through the omniscience of God. The omniscience of God is the key to understanding the divine decrees.

section: III. The Omniscience of God — Mechanics of the Decrees, Part 1
text: III. The Omniscience of God — Mechanics of the Decrees, Part 1

section: III. The Omniscience of God — Mechanics of the Decrees, Part 1
text: The doctrine of divine decrees is presented in three mechanical stages. The first is the omniscience of God, which supplies the input. The second is the decree itself. The third is the printout as it applies to believers. This section treats the first stage.

section: Points 1–6 — The Nature of Divine Omniscience
text: Points 1–6 — The Nature of Divine Omniscience

section: Points 1–6 — The Nature of Divine Omniscience
text: 1. God knows perfectly, eternally, and simultaneously all that is knowable, both actual and possible.

section: Points 1–6 — The Nature of Divine Omniscience
text: 2. Such perception and sagacity is totally compatible with His divine essence. God would not be God unless He knew the end from the beginning, knew it all simultaneously, and never was a time when He did not know it.

section: Points 1–6 — The Nature of Divine Omniscience
text: 3. God is eternal; His knowledge is eternal. God is sovereign; His knowledge is superior, not related to angelic or human limitation.

section: Points 1–6 — The Nature of Divine Omniscience
text: 4. The only link between God's superior knowledge and human inferior knowledge is Bible doctrine. Nothing is more important in life.

section: Points 1–6 — The Nature of Divine Omniscience
text: 5. Every minute detail of both angelic and human creation is completely and perfectly in His mind at all times.

section: Points 1–6 — The Nature of Divine Omniscience
text: 6. Omniscience perceives the free as free, the necessary as necessary, together with all their causes, conditions, and relations, as one indivisible system of things, every link of which is essential to the integrity of the whole. God will never tamper with the volition of the creature. Predestination does not mean that God has forced any moral agent into a course of action. The free will of every person operates genuinely and spontaneously within the framework that omniscience has always perfectly known.

section: Points 7–12 — Omniscience, Iffy History, and Foreknowledge
text: Points 7–12 — Omniscience, Iffy History, and Foreknowledge

section: Points 7–12 — Omniscience, Iffy History, and Foreknowledge
text: 7. Time has nothing to do with God's knowledge. The future is as perspicuous to God as the past. This should be a stabilizing comfort to the believer in adversity.

section: Points 7–12 — Omniscience, Iffy History, and Foreknowledge
text: 8. The omniscience of God also knows the alternatives to history — the probable as well as the actual. What would have happened if a different decision had been made at any given moment? We can only speculate. God knows precisely. This category — the knowledge of what could have happened but did not — is not entered into the computer of divine decrees. Only actuality is entered.

section: Points 7–12 — Omniscience, Iffy History, and Foreknowledge
text: 9. God knows all that would have been involved in every case where any person's decision might have been different from what it was.

section: Points 7–12 — Omniscience, Iffy History, and Foreknowledge
text: 10. There are three categories of divine knowledge. First, self-knowledge: God knows His own essence, the Trinity, and all things. Second, omniscience: God knows all of creation, angelic and human, actual and possible. Third, foreknowledge (prognōsis / πρόγνωσις): the knowledge of what is in the decrees as it relates to believers only. Foreknowledge is not omniscience. Foreknowledge is a printout limited to believers and limited to actuality.

section: Points 7–12 — Omniscience, Iffy History, and Foreknowledge
text: 11. The omniscience of God knows every thought, every act, every decision of history and how they relate — plus the alternatives, what would have been under every possible different decision.

section: Points 7–12 — Omniscience, Iffy History, and Foreknowledge
text: 12. Foreknowledge makes nothing certain. It merely acknowledges what is already certain — what is in the decrees regarding believers. Foreknowledge is a printout, not a cause.

section: Points 13–16 — The Three Printout Categories for Believers
text: Points 13–16 — The Three Printout Categories for Believers

section: Points 13–16 — The Three Printout Categories for Believers
text: 13. For believers, three categories of printout emerge from the computer of divine decrees: foreknowledge (prognōsis), election (eklogē / ἐκλογή), and predestination — also called predetermination or foreordination (proorismos / προορισμός).

section: Points 13–16 — The Three Printout Categories for Believers
text: 14. Foreknowledge means that nothing can be known until it is first decreed. Therefore God foreknows all events as certainly future because He has decreed them certainly future.

section: Points 13–16 — The Three Printout Categories for Believers
text: 15. The decrees of God relate equally to all future events of every kind — to the free actions of moral agents as well as the actions of necessary agents, to sin, evil, and human good as well as to honorable thoughts, decisions, and actions.

section: Points 13–16 — The Three Printout Categories for Believers
text: 16. Foreordination — synonymous with the decrees — alone establishes certainty. Foreordination is an act of the infinitely intelligent and wise God in determining the certain future of all events. The omniscience of God decreed everything simultaneously and not by stages, because it was all present to omniscience from eternity past.

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: Having established the omniscience of God as the first stage of mechanics, we move to the second stage: the decree itself.

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: 1. The omniscience of God fed only facts into the computer of divine decrees — thought, decision, action.

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: 2. This was accomplished in eternity past. The omniscience of God decreed everything simultaneously and not by stages. Every thought, every decision, every deed, every action is contained in the computer.

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: 3. The decrees have become the complete and consummated right of the sovereignty of God, determining the certain future of all things in human history.

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: 4. No event is directly effected or caused by the decrees.

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: 5. The decree itself provides in every case that the event shall be effected by causes acting in a manner consistent with the nature of the event in question. The believer is never deprived of free will.

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: 6. In the case of every free-will act of a moral agent, the decree itself provides at the same time: (a) that the agent shall be a free agent — volition, free will, self-determination; (b) that the antecedents and all antecedents of every act in question shall be what they shall be — the circumstances leading to any decision are themselves within the scope of the decrees; (c) that all present conditions of the act shall be what they are; (d) that the act shall be perfectly spontaneous and free on the part of the agent; (e) that it shall be certainly future.

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: 7. The decree vested solely with the will of God what His creation would be.

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: 8. Because God cannot contradict His own nature or being, the essence and attributes of God necessitated His willing the highest and best for mankind. God wills for each believer the highest and best. The possibility of attaining that highest and best remains genuine. But it requires the consistent intake of Bible doctrine over time — sustained orientation to the Protocol Plan of God.

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: 9. The decrees of God are His eternal and immutable will regarding the future existence of events that will happen in time, and the precise manner and order of their occurrence. All events are already certain in the divine decrees — already, as it were, on tape. The tape is still running from the human standpoint, but every frame of it was determined in eternity past. God does not change the outcome; He has always known the outcome. What appears to the human observer as open future is, from the vantage of divine omniscience, already accomplished certainty.

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: 10. The decrees express the eternal plan and will of God by which God has rendered certain all events of history, past, present, and future.

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: 11. The decrees are the eternal and simultaneous knowledge of the omniscience of God, expressing the sovereignty of God by which all things are brought into being and controlled, made subject to His divine pleasure, and resulting in His eternal glory.

section: IV. The Mechanics of the Decrees — Part 2: The Decree Itself
text: The third mechanic — the printout as it applies to believers, covering foreknowledge, election, and predestination in detail — will be taken up in the following chapter.

section: V. Application: Capacity for Life and Orientation to the Decrees
text: V. Application: Capacity for Life and Orientation to the Decrees

section: V. Application: Capacity for Life and Orientation to the Decrees
text: The practical implication of the doctrine of divine decrees is not fatalism but stability. Every difficulty, every privation, every historical disaster was known to God in eternity past. God knew the problem before it arose. He designed the solution before the creation of the world. The believer who has internalized Bible doctrine possesses the category of truth necessary to remain oriented when circumstances deteriorate.

section: V. Application: Capacity for Life and Orientation to the Decrees
text: Capacity for life — the capacity to receive and appreciate blessing — resides in the soul and is built through the consistent perception of Bible doctrine over time. It is not the quantity of possessions but the capacity of the soul that determines the quality of life. God can remove every material circumstance in an instant. What cannot be taken from the living believer is the doctrinal content of the soul. That content constitutes genuine wealth regardless of external conditions.

section: V. Application: Capacity for Life and Orientation to the Decrees
text: Complaining, panic, and theological crisis in adversity all reflect the same root deficiency: failure to understand that God knew the situation before it began and has already provided for it within the framework of the decrees. The believer with doctrine in the soul can say, with doctrinal precision, that the outcome is already certain in the decrees — and can function accordingly, not with passive resignation but with active, steady orientation to the Protocol Plan of God.

section: V. Application: Capacity for Life and Orientation to the Decrees
text: The mature believer's response to historical adversity is not the panic-prayer of unoriented faith but the stable application of a full structure of doctrinal categories. The doctrine of divine decrees is that structure in its most foundational form.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Two
text: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Two

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 1. The announcement to Rebecca in Romans 9:12 is grounded in the divine decrees. The declaration that the older twin would serve the younger was made before either child had performed any act. It rests not on foreseen human merit but on the eternal, simultaneous decree of the omniscient God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 2. The decree of God is His eternal, holy, wise, and sovereign purpose. It comprehends simultaneously all things that ever were or will be — their causes, courses, conditions, successions, and relations — and determines their certain future. This is a single, simultaneous act of the divine will, not a sequential series of divine responses to unfolding history.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 3. The omniscience of God is the key to understanding the divine decrees. God knows perfectly, eternally, and simultaneously all that is knowable — both actual and possible. He knows every thought, every decision, and every action of every person in history, and He has always known these things. There was never a moment when this knowledge was incomplete.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 4. Only actuality is entered into the computer of divine decrees. Omniscience knows both the actual and the probable — what did happen and what would have happened under alternative decisions. But only actuality is entered into the decrees. The probable constitutes the knowledge of what could have been, not what was foreordained.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 5. The decrees do not violate human free will. Omniscience perceives the free as free. In the case of every free-will act of a moral agent, the decree provides simultaneously that the agent shall be a free agent, that the circumstances surrounding the act shall be what they are, and that the act shall be perfectly spontaneous and free. Predestination is not coercion.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Two

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 6. Three categories of divine knowledge must be distinguished. Self-knowledge: God's eternal knowledge of His own essence and the Trinity. Omniscience: God's knowledge of all creation, actual and possible. Foreknowledge (prognosis): the printout from the decrees, limited to believers and to actuality only. Foreknowledge is not omniscience. It makes nothing certain; it merely acknowledges what is already certain in the decrees.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 7. The printout from the computer of divine decrees divides along two lines. For believers: foreknowledge, election, and predestination (foreordination). For unbelievers: reprobation, condemnation, and retribution. Election, foreknowledge, and predestination are never used of unbelievers.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Eighty-Two
text: 8. God wills the highest and best for each member of the human race. Because God cannot contradict His own nature, the essence and attributes of God necessitated His willing the highest and best for mankind. The attainment of that highest and best remains genuinely possible, but it requires the consistent intake of Bible doctrine and sustained orientation to the Protocol Plan of God.

What cannot be taken from the living believer is the doctrinal content of the soul. The believer who has internalized the doctrine of divine decrees can remain oriented in adversity, personal or historical, because that doctrine establishes that God has always known every problem and has already provided for it within the framework of the decrees.

The questions of why God loved Jacob and hated Esau (Romans 9:13) and why God hardened Pharaoh's heart (Romans 9:17–18) cannot be answered without a prior understanding of omniscience, the mechanics of the decrees, and the distinction between what omniscience knows and what is entered into the decrees as actual. The third mechanic — the printout categories of foreknowledge, election, and predestination — will be addressed in the following chapter.
