text: The provision by God of all that is necessary for the believer's physical existence and continued life on earth. Unconditional with respect to spiritual status — all believers receive it by virtue of possessing divine righteousness. The issue in logistical grace is always the integrity of God, not the merit of the recipient.

section: Glossary
text: GAP

section: Glossary
text: Grace Apparatus for Perception

section: Glossary
text: The Spirit-enabled process by which the believer receives, processes, and internalizes Bible doctrine. Requires the filling of the Holy Spirit, a prepared communicator, and positive volition on the part of the recipient. The daily function of GAP is the mechanism by which logistical grace is translated into the advance toward the maturity barrier.

section: Glossary
text: maturity barrier

section: Glossary
text: The threshold of spiritual maturity cracked through sustained intake and application of Bible doctrine over time. The believer who cracks the maturity barrier enters supergrace and becomes eligible for the six categories of special divine blessing. Abraham's circumcision is the pattern: a Gentile who advanced to the point of becoming the father of a new race.

section: Glossary
text: supergrace

section: Glossary
text: The stage of spiritual maturity beyond the maturity barrier, characterized by the imputation of six categories of special divine blessing to the righteousness of God in the mature believer. Distinguished from logistical grace in that the believer's spiritual status quo is the issue, not merely the possession of imputed righteousness.

section: Glossary
text: old sin nature (OSN)

section: Glossary
text: The sin capacity inherited at birth through the male genetic line. The source of self-righteousness, arrogance, and all forms of human good that compete with divine righteousness. The old sin nature is not eradicated at salvation but is countered by the filling of the Holy Spirit and the intake of doctrine.

section: Glossary
text: reversionism

section: Glossary
text: Retroactive spiritual regression — the process by which a believer abandons positive volition toward doctrine and returns to the thinking and values of the old sin nature. Reversionists still receive logistical grace support because the issue is the integrity of God, but they forfeit supergrace blessing and accumulate divine discipline, which in its terminal form is the sin unto death.

section: Romans 10:4 — Telos, Nomos, Dikaiosynē: Christ as the Termination of the Law with Reference to Righteousness
text: Romans 10:4 — Telos, Nomos, Dikaiosynē: Christ as the Termination of the Law with Reference to Righteousness

section: Romans 10:4 — Telos, Nomos, Dikaiosynē: Christ as the Termination of the Law with Reference to Righteousness
text: Romans 10:4 “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” (ESV)

section: Romans 10:4 — Telos, Nomos, Dikaiosynē: Christ as the Termination of the Law with Reference to Righteousness
text: Corrected translation: For Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness to each one because he believes.

section: Romans 10:4 — Telos, Nomos, Dikaiosynē: Christ as the Termination of the Law with Reference to Righteousness
text: Romans 10:4 concludes the doctrinal argument opened in verses 1–3, where Paul diagnosed Israel's failure: zeal for God without knowledge of doctrine, resulting in the pursuit of self-righteousness at the expense of God's imputed righteousness. Verse 4 now identifies the definitive theological reason for that failure and its resolution: the person and work of Christ terminates the law as a mechanism of righteousness, because at the moment of faith the believer receives the imputation of divine righteousness. This chapter provides the full grammatical, lexical, and doctrinal analysis of verse 4, together with its place in the plan of God.

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 10:4
text: I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 10:4

section: The Post-Positive Conjunction gar
text: The Post-Positive Conjunction gar

section: The Post-Positive Conjunction gar
text: The sentence opens in Greek with the post-positive conjunctive particle gar (γάρ), rendered in English at the head of the clause as for. As a post-positive conjunction, gar introduces the cause or reason for the preceding statement. Its function here is to ground verse 4 in the argument of verses 1–3: Israel's failure to submit to God's righteousness (v. 3) is explained by the fact that Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness.

section: The Subject: Christos
text: The Subject: Christos

section: The Subject: Christos
text: The subject is Christos (Χριστός), nominative singular, the fourth word in the Greek word order. The absence of the definite article before Christos is significant: it is qualitative, emphasizing the unique nature of the person rather than mere identification. The anarthrous construction underscores the hypostatic union — the Lord Jesus Christ is eternal God, co-equal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and simultaneously true humanity, the last Adam, impeccable, without an old sin nature, without the imputation of Adam's sin, and without personal sin.

section: The Predicate Nominative: Telos
text: The Predicate Nominative: Telos

section: The Predicate Nominative: Telos
text: The verb is supplied by legitimate ellipsis: the present active indicative of eimi (εἰμί), the verb of being, which governs two nominative-case nouns and so takes no expressed form. The predicate nominative is telos (τέλος), a neuter noun with the following semantic range in Koine Greek:

section: The Predicate Nominative: Telos
text: In Koine Greek, telos denotes: (1) termination, cessation, end; (2) objective or goal; (3) completion of a state — the final step or supreme stage. In classical Attic usage (notably Demosthenes) it could also carry the sense of obligation or achievement, but these connotations do not carry over into the Koine of the New Testament period. Accordingly, two primary translations are grammatically and lexically admissible in this verse: (a) objective / goal, and (b) termination / cessation.

section: The Predicate Nominative: Telos
text: Contextual considerations — particularly the supporting passages examined below (Romans 3:20, 28; Galatians 2:16; 3:24) — establish that the dominant meaning here is termination or cessation. Christ is the end, the cessation, the termination of the law.

section: The Object: Nomos and the Three Codices
text: The Object: Nomos and the Three Codices

section: The Object: Nomos and the Three Codices
text: The noun nomos (νόμος), used here without the definite article, refers to the Mosaic law. Paul elsewhere uses nomos for other portions of Scripture and occasionally for the entire Old Testament canon, but context here specifies the Mosaic law as the system Israel had been attempting to employ for salvation. The Mosaic law comprises three codices:

section: The Object: Nomos and the Three Codices
text: Codex 1 — The Decalogue. The Ten Commandments define freedom under divine establishment in negative terms (prohibitions), and in so doing they define sin. Hundreds of statements throughout Codex 1 and Codex 3 address hamartiology — mental attitude sins, sins of the tongue, and overt sins — bringing a consciousness of sin (Romans 3:20).

section: The Object: Nomos and the Three Codices
text: Codex 2 — The Levitical Ordinances. This codex presents a complete Christology and soteriology through typology: the tabernacle and its sacred furniture, the Levitical priesthood and its modus operandi, and the entire sacrificial system all point forward to the Lord Jesus Christ as the only Savior. It is Codex 2 that was fulfilled by the first advent.

section: The Object: Nomos and the Three Codices
text: Codex 3 — The Laws of Divine Establishment. These govern national life: legitimate government and its limitations, a proportional income tax (ten percent across the board, applicable to believers and unbelievers alike), military function and the draft, dietary regulations, criminal jurisprudence including the requirement of legitimate witnesses and the exclusion of hearsay, and the full range of social relationships.

section: The Object: Nomos and the Three Codices
text: In this verse, Paul focuses specifically on the law as it bears on righteousness and salvation. Codex 1 and Codex 3 demonstrate that man is a sinner who needs a Savior. Codex 2 reveals that Christ is the only Savior. Keeping any of these codices as a mechanism of salvation produces only self-righteousness; understanding Codex 2 and believing in Christ produces the imputation of divine righteousness.

section: The Prepositional Phrase: eis dikaiosynēn
text: The Prepositional Phrase: eis dikaiosynēn

section: The Prepositional Phrase: eis dikaiosynēn
text: The prepositional phrase is eis dikaiosynēn (εἰς δικαιοσύνην). The preposition eis with the accusative expresses reference or respect: with reference to righteousness. The noun dikaiosynē (δικαιοσύνη) is accusative singular. Paul's specification of this prepositional phrase is deliberate: Christ is the termination of the law not in every conceivable sense, but specifically with reference to righteousness — that is, with respect to the question of how a person obtains standing before God. The phrase eliminates the law as a means of producing righteousness acceptable to God.

section: The Dative Participle: to pisteuonti
text: The Dative Participle: to pisteuonti

section: The Dative Participle: to pisteuonti
text: The concluding clause employs the articular present active participle from pisteuō (πιστεύω), dative singular. The dative is a dative of advantage and indirect object from the adjective pas (πᾶς), used as a substantive in the singular: to each one. The definite article functions as a personal pronoun. The present tense is aoristic — punctiliar action at the moment of gospel hearing. The active voice indicates that the individual, at the point of hearing the gospel, produces the action: he believes. The participle is causal.

section: The Dative Participle: to pisteuonti
text: Corrected translation of the full verse: For Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness to each one because he believes.

section: II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages
text: II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages

section: II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages
text: Several passages confirm that telos here carries the meaning of termination or cessation and illumine the doctrinal content of verse 4.

section: II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages
text: Romans 3:20 “For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin.” (ESV)

section: II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages
text: Corrected translation: Therefore by the works of the law no human being shall be justified in his presence; for through the law is the consciousness of sin.

section: II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages
text: Romans 3:28 “For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.” (ESV)

section: II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages
text: Corrected translation: We conclude then that man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law.

section: II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages
text: Galatians 2:16 “Yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.” (ESV)

section: II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages
text: Corrected translation: Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Christ Jesus in order that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the law, for by the works of the law no human being will be justified.

section: II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages
text: Galatians 3:24 “So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith.” (ESV)

section: II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages
text: Corrected translation: Therefore the law has become a pedagogue to lead us to Christ that we might be justified by means of faith.

section: II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages
text: The word rendered guardian or schoolmaster is paidagōgos (παιδαγωγός), the Greek term for a slave who served as a bodyguard-escort for children, accompanying them to and from school to prevent kidnapping or harm. The paidagōgos was not a teacher but a conductor leading the child to the teacher. The Mosaic law functioned in an analogous way: Codex 1 exposed sin and the need for a Savior; Codex 2 revealed Christ as that Savior. The law conducted Israel toward Christ.

section: II. Exegetical Background: Supporting Passages
text: Matthew 5:17 — 'Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them' — is not directly pertinent to verse 4. The phrase 'the Law and the Prophets' designates the entire Old Testament canon (the Pentateuch and the Prophetical writings), not the Mosaic law specifically as a mechanism of righteousness. The fulfillment spoken of in Matthew 5:17 is broader in scope than the termination of Codex 2 addressed in Romans 10:4.

section: III. Christ as Termination of the Law: Two Dimensions
text: III. Christ as Termination of the Law: Two Dimensions

section: A. Fulfillment of Codex 2 at the First Advent
text: A. Fulfillment of Codex 2 at the First Advent

section: A. Fulfillment of Codex 2 at the First Advent
text: The first dimension in which Christ is the termination of the law concerns the fulfillment of Codex 2. Every Levitical sacrifice, every holy day, every article of the tabernacle furniture, every procedural function of the Levitical priesthood was a type pointing forward to the person and work of the Lord Jesus Christ. At the first advent, Christ received the imputation of every personal sin of the entire human race and was judged for them in His spiritual death on the cross. His physical death, burial, resurrection, and ascension completed this fulfillment. With the completion of the cross-work, every shadow in Codex 2 found its substance. There is nothing left to fulfill. Codex 2 is terminated.

section: A. Fulfillment of Codex 2 at the First Advent
text: Israel, however, was blind to the first advent. Rather than receiving the substance to which all the types pointed, Israel retained the shadows and pursued works-righteousness derived from keeping the law. Their self-righteousness stood in direct opposition to the imputed righteousness available through faith in the very Messiah their own law had been advertising.

section: B. Cessation of the Age of Israel and the Dispensational Transition
text: B. Cessation of the Age of Israel and the Dispensational Transition

section: B. Cessation of the Age of Israel and the Dispensational Transition
text: The second dimension is dispensational. When Christ ascended and was seated at the right hand of the Father, His session inaugurated a new royal category. The Lord Jesus Christ acquired a new title of royalty that required a royal family, and so the age of Israel was interrupted — not terminated permanently, but suspended. The Church Age is the period in which that royal family is being assembled. At salvation every believer in this dispensation receives thirty-six things simultaneously, one of which is the baptism of the Holy Spirit, which enters the believer into union with Christ seated at the right hand of the Father and constitutes him royal family of God.

section: B. Cessation of the Age of Israel and the Dispensational Transition
text: During the Church Age — the times of the Gentiles — no Jewish national entity functions as a client nation to God. Only Gentile nations can occupy that role in the present dispensation. When the royal family is complete it will be removed at the resurrection of the Church (the Rapture), the age of Israel will resume, the tribulation will run its course, and at the Second Advent Israel will be restored to client nation status and the four unconditional covenants to Israel will be fulfilled.

section: B. Cessation of the Age of Israel and the Dispensational Transition
text: In this dispensational sense, Christ is the cessation of the law: the law as the governing economy for God's client nation Israel has been suspended for the duration of the Church Age.

section: IV. Righteousness, Justification, and the Plan of God
text: IV. Righteousness, Justification, and the Plan of God

section: A. The Flow of Divine Blessing Through the Justice of God
text: A. The Flow of Divine Blessing Through the Justice of God

section: A. The Flow of Divine Blessing Through the Justice of God
text: All blessing from God to man flows through the justice of God, not directly through His love, sovereignty, or omnipotence. This is the central axis of the Epistle to the Romans. Divine justice must have a target — a home — into which it can impute blessing without compromising the holiness of God. The integrity of God consists of two attributes in union: righteousness and justice. What righteousness demands, justice executes. At the moment of faith in Christ, the justice of God imputes divine righteousness to the believer, establishing in the believer a permanent target for all subsequent divine blessing.

section: A. The Flow of Divine Blessing Through the Justice of God
text: This is why the imputation of divine righteousness is not merely a juridical formality but the structural foundation of the entire Christian life. Without it, God could not bless sinful man without self-contradiction. With it, every category of blessing — logistical grace provision and the special blessings of maturity — flows legitimately from the justice of God to His own righteousness resident in the believer. Not one category of divine blessing ever goes to human self-righteousness.

section: B. The Plan of God: Three Adjustment Points
text: B. The Plan of God: Three Adjustment Points

section: B. The Plan of God: Three Adjustment Points
text: The plan of God for every person can be charted across three reference points:

section: B. The Plan of God: Three Adjustment Points
text: Point X (Physical Birth): The plan of God begins not at the new birth but at physical birth. Human life is imputed to the soul immediately at birth — a real imputation, God personally bestowing life, implying that God has a plan for that individual from the first moment of existence. Simultaneously, Adam's original sin is imputed as a real imputation to its genetically-formed home: the old sin nature. This judicial imputation constitutes condemnation. No person is condemned on the basis of personal sins; condemnation rests on the imputation of Adam's sin. The significance is twofold: (1) condemnation must precede salvation, and therefore those who never reach the age of accountability — infants, those with severe cognitive disabilities — are automatically saved through the operation of divine justice; (2) the basis of condemnation is never personal sinful acts, a fact that eliminates arrogant testimonies grounded in false doctrine. When Scripture states 'all have sinned' (Romans 3:23, aorist tense), the reference is to the imputation of Adam's sin, not to accumulated personal transgressions. Condemnation at Point X creates the potential of salvation for the entire human race.

section: B. The Plan of God: Three Adjustment Points
text: Point Y (Salvation): The gospel — pertinent doctrine presenting redemption, reconciliation, and propitiation — constitutes the first hope: absolute confidence that faith in Christ produces eternal life. At the moment of faith, salvation adjustment to the justice of God occurs. This involves two judicial imputations: (1) all personal sins were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged there — they were reserved for the cross, not condemned at birth; (2) the righteousness of God is imputed to the believer, resulting in instant justification. This is the location in the plan of God addressed by Romans 10:4. Christ is the termination of the law with reference to this righteousness imputed at the moment of faith.

section: B. The Plan of God: Three Adjustment Points
text: Point Z (Spiritual Maturity): The imputation of divine righteousness at Point Y creates a second potential: the imputation of special blessing at maturity. Pertinent doctrine — the daily intake and perception of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception — constitutes the second hope: absolute confidence that sustained doctrine intake over time will crack the maturity barrier and bring the believer to supergrace, at which point the justice of God begins imputing special blessing in six categories to the righteousness of God resident in the believer. This constitutes maturity adjustment to the justice of God. The mature believer at Point Z then possesses the third potential: at the judgment seat of Christ following the Rapture, the imputation of eternal reward and blessing glorifies God permanently. This is the 'all things working together for good' of Romans 8:28 — the agathos, the intrinsic good of the eternal state.

section: C. Logistical Grace and Special Blessing
text: C. Logistical Grace and Special Blessing

section: C. Logistical Grace and Special Blessing
text: Prior to reaching the maturity barrier, all blessing is logistical grace: everything necessary for physical existence and the opportunity to advance spiritually — food, shelter, clothing, freedom, time, access to doctrine, someone to communicate it, transportation, environment. These provisions are imputed from the justice of God to the righteousness of God without any relationship to human merit. The believer does not earn or deserve logistical grace; it flows on the basis of divine integrity alone. This eliminates any system that teaches that giving money to a religious organization produces divine blessing. Tithing in the Old Testament was a ten-percent income tax on all inhabitants of Israel — believers and unbelievers alike — directed to the government treasury, not to a religious organization. It carried no spiritual connotation and was not a mechanism for obtaining divine blessing. Any system that conditions God's blessing on financial giving to a local institution has constructed a self-righteousness framework that competes with imputed divine righteousness, and where that competition exists, grace has been replaced by works.

section: C. Logistical Grace and Special Blessing
text: Special blessings beyond logistical grace — imputed at maturity in six categories — go equally and exclusively to the righteousness of God in the believer. Blessing by association (category three of special blessing) explains the prosperity sometimes observed among unbelievers who are closely associated with mature believers; this is a derivative, not a direct imputation.

section: V. Self-Righteousness Versus Imputed Righteousness
text: V. Self-Righteousness Versus Imputed Righteousness

section: V. Self-Righteousness Versus Imputed Righteousness
text: The entire argument of Romans 10:1–4 is the conflict between two systems of righteousness: (1) human self-righteousness generated by keeping the Mosaic law, and (2) divine righteousness imputed at the moment of faith in Christ. These two systems are mutually exclusive. They cannot coexist as complementary approaches to obtaining divine blessing. Either the believer accepts imputed divine righteousness as the sole basis of his standing before God, or he attempts to supplement or replace it with self-generated righteousness. The latter course is legalism, and legalism is defined in this passage as a failure to understand the implications of verse 4.

section: V. Self-Righteousness Versus Imputed Righteousness
text: The Jews Paul addresses here are a specific illustration of a broader pattern. Like the rich young ruler who came to our Lord asking what further deed was required for eternal life — and who acknowledged that he had kept the commandments — they had pursued moral achievement as the currency of salvation. The Lord's response in that encounter confirmed the outward observance while identifying the missing element: personal faith in the one standing before him. No amount of legal compliance can produce the righteousness God requires, because the righteousness God requires is His own — and it is given, not earned.

section: V. Self-Righteousness Versus Imputed Righteousness
text: After salvation the same dynamic applies. Believers who create internal systems of morality, rule-keeping, or religious performance as the basis of their spiritual standing before God have entered into reversionism. They lose momentum. They lose motivation. They substitute human achievement — whether on a witnessing program, a prayer schedule, a morality framework, or any other function — for the genuine advance that comes through the daily perception of doctrine. Their arrogance consists in the assumption that self-achievement can impress God. God is impressed only with His own integrity. His own righteousness is the target; nothing else qualifies.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five
text: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five
text: 1. Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness. The Greek telos (τέλος) in Romans 10:4 carries the meaning of cessation or termination in this context, confirmed by Romans 3:20, 28 and Galatians 2:16. Christ is the end of any law-based system for obtaining righteousness before God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five
text: 2. Faith in Christ is obedience to the righteousness of God. Romans 10:3 establishes the negative: Israel's failure to be obedient to the righteousness of God. Romans 10:4 supplies the positive: the one who believes in Christ has obeyed the righteousness of God, because believing is the non-meritorious means through which divine righteousness is received.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five
text: 3. The Jews sought to establish their own righteousness by keeping the law, but Christ is the termination of that system. For all who believe, Christ ends the pursuit of self-righteousness through law-keeping as a means of obtaining divine approval. The first advent fulfilled Codex 2 of the Mosaic law; there is no further typological function for the Levitical system to perform.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five
text: 4. Christ is the termination of any system of human self-righteousness with respect to righteousness before God. Faith in Christ results in the imputation of God's perfect righteousness. Once that imputation has occurred, no system of human self-righteousness can compete with it. Where the attempt to compete exists, the believer has abandoned grace orientation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five
text: 5. No system of human righteousness can compete with God's righteousness. Matthew 6:33 — 'Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness' — presupposes that the believer already possesses imputed divine righteousness as the basis of logistical grace provision. All the things that are 'added' flow to that righteousness, not to any human achievement.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five
text: 6. Israel failed as a client nation when it substituted self-righteousness for imputed righteousness. The blindness of Israel was the blindness of arrogance — the assumption that self-achievement could impress God. This substitution constituted a stumbling block in the previous dispensation and serves as a warning to Church Age believers against the same error.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five
text: 7. In the conflict between self-righteousness and divine imputed righteousness, there is no contest. Human arrogance alone concludes that righteousness derived from law-keeping could provide salvation or divine blessing. God's plan of grace not only excludes human self-righteousness but replaces it with His own perfect righteousness, against which no human alternative can compete.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five
text: 8. The imputation of divine righteousness at the moment of faith is the foundation and perpetual motivation for advancing to maturity. Because the individual believer receives the imputation of divine righteousness at salvation, this constitutes both instant justification and the permanent structural basis for momentum toward spiritual maturity through maximum doctrine resident in the soul.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five
text: 9. The conflict between self-righteousness and imputed righteousness is terminated at salvation when faith in Christ occurs — and must be kept there. The practical application of verse 4 is the refusal to construct any system of self-righteousness that competes with God's imputed righteousness after salvation. Legalism is the arrogance of ignorance: a failure to understand what happened at the moment of faith.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five
text: 10. Two systems of righteousness are mutually exclusive: self-righteousness and imputed divine righteousness. No believer can simultaneously build on both. Christian legalism is the arrogance of seeking to supplement imputed righteousness with self-generated works. Grace orientation is the humble recognition that the foundation is already laid by God and that the building material is the perception of doctrine, not moral performance.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five
text: 11. The power of thought exceeds the power of deed. Deeds have merit only as they express the thought that motivates them. Bible doctrine resident in the soul is the thought that motivates genuine compliance with the plan of God and produces authentic grace orientation to all of life.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Five
text: 12. Grace excludes any system of self-righteousness as the basis of merit or blessing from God. The only permissible foundation for the Christian life is imputed righteousness, and the only permissible building material is the daily perception of Bible doctrine. Every category of divine blessing — logistical grace and special blessing alike — flows from the justice of God to the righteousness of God resident in the believer, never to any form of human self-righteousness.

text: Masculine noun, Koine Greek. Used in the New Testament for the Mosaic law (most frequently), portions of the Old Testament canon, and occasionally the entire canon. In Romans 10:4, nomos refers specifically to the Mosaic law in its three codices: the Decalogue (Codex 1), the Levitical ordinances (Codex 2), and the laws of divine establishment (Codex 3).

At salvation, God's own perfect righteousness is imputed to the believer, establishing a permanent target in the believer into which the justice of God can impute all categories of divine blessing without compromising divine integrity.

section: Romans 10:4 — Self-Righteousness versus Imputed Divine Righteousness; The Termination of the Law; Four Principles
text: Romans 10:4 stands at the intersection of Israel's failure and the universal principle that all righteousness before God must be received, not achieved. The verse culminates Paul's analysis of Israel's zeal without doctrine (10:1–3) and introduces a four-part doctrinal development grounded in Old Testament documentation from Moses. This chapter completes the exegesis of verse 4 by drawing out the four principles embedded in the verse itself, each of which exposes a dimension of the conflict between human self-righteousness and the imputed divine righteousness that comes through faith in Christ.

section: I. First Principle: Faith in Christ Is Obedience to the Righteousness of God
text: I. First Principle: Faith in Christ Is Obedience to the Righteousness of God

section: I. First Principle: Faith in Christ Is Obedience to the Righteousness of God
text: The preceding verse (10:3) established that Israel, not knowing the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, failed to be obedient to the righteousness of God. Verse 4 supplies the explanation: obedience to the righteousness of God means faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. It is at the moment of that faith that the integrity of God becomes operative in relation to the believer's life.

section: I. First Principle: Faith in Christ Is Obedience to the Righteousness of God
text: The structure of divine integrity is central here. God possesses two attributes that together constitute His holiness: righteousness and justice. At salvation, the justice of God imputes perfect divine righteousness to the believer, establishing what may be called a home or target for all subsequent blessing. All blessing — whether logistical in the maintenance of daily life or special in the reward of spiritual maturity — flows from the justice of God to the righteousness of God resident in the believer. This pipeline is insulated by grace against any intrusion of human ability, merit, talent, or works.

section: I. First Principle: Faith in Christ Is Obedience to the Righteousness of God
text: Grace, properly defined, is the policy of the justice of God in imputing blessing to the righteousness of God resident in the believer. The Greek term charis (χάρις) carries this technical force throughout Paul's argument. Because no human effort can enter this pipeline, the integrity of God is never compromised. Justice cannot bless sinful man directly; it must bless divine righteousness already imputed to man.

section: I. First Principle: Faith in Christ Is Obedience to the Righteousness of God
text: The practical consequence is that every competing system — prayer treated as a merit mechanism, giving as a basis for blessing, witnessing as a claim on divine reward, moral achievement, self-sacrifice, or any form of religious performance — is excluded. These activities may be legitimate in their proper context, but they become distortions the moment they are set up as the ground of blessing from God. God does not bless on the basis of what any person does. He blesses on the basis of His own righteousness imputed to the believer and the justice that executes that imputation.

section: II. Second Principle: Imputed Righteousness as Justification and Motivation
text: II. Second Principle: Imputed Righteousness as Justification and Motivation

section: II. Second Principle: Imputed Righteousness as Justification and Motivation
text: The imputation of divine righteousness at the moment of faith in Christ accomplishes two things simultaneously: it constitutes instant justification, and it establishes perpetual motivation for the believer's advance to spiritual maturity. The mechanism is traced through the divine plan by means of three paired stages, each consisting of an imputation that creates potential, a doctrinal cognizance that converts potential into hope, and a grace execution that replaces hope with reality.

section: A. The Three-Stage Structure of the Divine Plan
text: A. The Three-Stage Structure of the Divine Plan

section: A. The Three-Stage Structure of the Divine Plan
text: The first stage encompasses the pre-salvation condition. At birth, every human being receives two imputations: human life to the soul, and Adam's original sin to the genetically transmitted sin capacity. The second imputation establishes the potential for salvation, since condemnation must precede the offer of deliverance. Gospel doctrine — covering Christ's substitutionary judgment, redemption, reconciliation, propitiation, and justification — converts that potential into hope, defined as absolute confidence about a future certainty. The first hope is the certainty that faith in Christ produces eternal life. This confidence, enabled by the common grace ministry of the Holy Spirit, is replaced by the reality of salvation at the moment of faith — the salvation adjustment to the justice of God through efficacious grace.

section: A. The Three-Stage Structure of the Divine Plan
text: The second stage is the believer's life in time. Two judicial imputations anchor this stage: all personal sins were imputed to Christ at the cross, providing the basis for His saving work; and divine righteousness is imputed to the believer at the moment of salvation. This second imputation establishes a new potential — the possibility of great blessing in time that glorifies God. Logistical grace is already a reality from salvation onward. As the believer functions daily in the grace apparatus for perception under the enabling ministry of the Holy Spirit, doctrine accumulates in the soul, and the second hope develops: absolute confidence that maximum doctrine resident in the soul will produce spiritual maturity. That hope is replaced by the reality of maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

section: A. The Three-Stage Structure of the Divine Plan
text: The third stage encompasses eternity. The imputation of eternal life at salvation, combined with the special blessing imputed to the mature believer in time, establishes a third potential: eternal reward and blessing at the judgment seat of Christ. The third hope is absolute confidence that at the resurrection and evaluation of Church Age believers, eternal reward will be imputed to those who have advanced to maturity. This final imputation glorifies God forever and constitutes the completion of the divine plan.

section: A. The Three-Stage Structure of the Divine Plan
text: Throughout all three stages, doctrine is the operative factor. Without knowledge of doctrine there is no motivation for the plan, no momentum within it, and no capacity to receive its blessings. The grace system of perception bypasses human intellectual capacity and establishes a Spirit-enabled system for the reception and internalization of divine truth.

section: III. Third Principle: Imputed Righteousness Replaces Self-Righteousness as the Foundation
text: III. Third Principle: Imputed Righteousness Replaces Self-Righteousness as the Foundation

section: III. Third Principle: Imputed Righteousness Replaces Self-Righteousness as the Foundation
text: Faith in Christ is the end of self-righteousness because it introduces a foundation that human righteousness cannot replicate. Every believer, at the moment of faith, receives the imputed righteousness of God as the permanent base on which the Christian life is constructed. The superstructure built on that foundation consists of Bible doctrine accumulated through the daily function of the grace apparatus for perception. When the superstructure reaches completion in the attainment of spiritual maturity, God imputes special blessing to the building — not because of anything the believer has done, but because the believer now has the capacity to receive blessing without being destroyed by it.

section: III. Third Principle: Imputed Righteousness Replaces Self-Righteousness as the Foundation
text: Blessing without capacity intensifies misery rather than producing happiness. Wealth imputed to a believer without the capacity for money produces new and more complex problems. Leadership responsibility given to a believer without the capacity for authority multiplies pressure. The right circumstance of life presented to a believer without the inner resources to sustain it becomes a burden. The solution is never to pursue the blessing; it is to pursue the doctrine that builds the capacity, and to allow the justice of God to execute the imputation at the appropriate time.

section: IV. Fourth Principle: The Antiquity of the Conflict and Its Old Testament Documentation
text: IV. Fourth Principle: The Antiquity of the Conflict and Its Old Testament Documentation

section: IV. Fourth Principle: The Antiquity of the Conflict and Its Old Testament Documentation
text: The conflict between self-righteousness and imputed divine righteousness is not a New Testament innovation. It is as old as the fall of man. The first act of human self-righteousness was the manufacture of garments from fig leaves in Genesis 3 — the assumption that a human solution to the problem of nakedness and guilt could constitute adjustment to God. Every subsequent generation has reproduced that assumption in new forms.

section: IV. Fourth Principle: The Antiquity of the Conflict and Its Old Testament Documentation
text: Paul does not construct his argument about self-righteousness from New Testament materials alone. He draws on Moses, who addressed this conflict at the inception of Israel's existence as a client nation. Two passages from the Mosaic corpus are brought forward in the verses immediately following, each serving a distinct doctrinal function.

section: A. Leviticus 18:5 — The Warning against Law-Righteousness (Romans 10:5)
text: A. Leviticus 18:5 — The Warning against Law-Righteousness (Romans 10:5)

section: A. Leviticus 18:5 — The Warning against Law-Righteousness (Romans 10:5)
text: The first Old Testament documentation, cited in Romans 10:5, comes from Leviticus 18:5. Paul uses this text as a warning against depending on righteousness through law-keeping. Moses himself, at the beginning of the dispensation of Israel as a client nation, placed this caveat in the record. The Mosaic law was never intended to function as a mechanism of salvation; its function within Codex 2 — the ordinances — was to reveal the person and work of Jesus Christ, demanding faith in Him as the only Savior.

section: B. Deuteronomy 30:11–14 — The Importance of Imputed Righteousness (Romans 10:6–8)
text: B. Deuteronomy 30:11–14 — The Importance of Imputed Righteousness (Romans 10:6–8)

section: B. Deuteronomy 30:11–14 — The Importance of Imputed Righteousness (Romans 10:6–8)
text: The second Old Testament documentation, drawn from Deuteronomy 30:11–14, appears in Romans 10:6–8. This passage emphasizes the importance of building on the foundation of imputed divine righteousness at the moment of faith in Christ. Together the two Mosaic citations frame the issue: the first warns against the error of law-righteousness; the second commends the reception of righteousness through faith.

section: C. Romans 10:9–10 — Salvation by Cause and Result in Any Dispensation
text: C. Romans 10:9–10 — Salvation by Cause and Result in Any Dispensation

section: C. Romans 10:9–10 — Salvation by Cause and Result in Any Dispensation
text: The conclusion of Paul's argument in Romans 10:9–10 will present the pattern of salvation in any dispensation on the basis of cause and result. These verses have been frequently misappropriated as a warrant for public confession as a condition of salvation; the exegesis will demonstrate that they present cause and effect — faith as the internal cause, confession as the external expression of an already-accomplished reality.

section: C. Romans 10:9–10 — Salvation by Cause and Result in Any Dispensation
text: The Mosaic law operated through three codices. Codex 1 comprised the Decalogue; Codex 2 comprised the ordinances, which foreshadowed and demanded faith in Jesus Christ as the God of Israel and only Savior; Codex 3 comprised the laws of divine establishment governing social order. The unbelieving Jew bypassed Codex 2, distorted Codex 1 into a pseudo-salvation system, and enlisted Codex 3 for moral self-justification. In the Church Age, the same rejection takes the form of accepting the alpha glory of the God of Israel while blotting out the omega glory — the incarnation, substitutionary death, and resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ.

section: C. Romans 10:9–10 — Salvation by Cause and Result in Any Dispensation
text: The Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4, Šəmaʿ Yisrāʾēl YHWH ʾĔlōhênû YHWH ʾEḥād (שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד), is correctly rendered: 'Jesus Christ is our God; Jesus Christ is unique.' The rejection of this identity — the refusal to recognize the Lord Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of Codex 2 — is the definitive act of unbelief in both dispensations.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six
text: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six
text: 1. Romans 10:4 defines obedience to the righteousness of God as faith in Christ alone: every other definition of religious obedience is exposed as a form of self-righteousness.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six
text: 2. The justice-to-righteousness pipeline is insulated by grace against all human intrusion: no work, talent, moral achievement, or religious performance can introduce blessing into a system designed to operate exclusively between the justice of God and the righteousness of God resident in the believer.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six
text: 3. The three-stage structure of the divine plan — salvation, maturity, and eternal reward — is entirely driven by doctrine: each stage consists of an imputation that creates potential, a doctrinal cognizance that produces hope, and a grace execution that replaces hope with reality.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six
text: 4. Self-righteousness and imputed divine righteousness are mutually exclusive systems: the believer must build exclusively on the foundation of imputed righteousness, using the building material of Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six
text: 5. Capacity must precede special blessing: blessing given without capacity intensifies misery; doctrine builds the capacity that makes it possible for justice to impute special blessing without harm.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six
text: 6. The power of thought exceeds the power of deed: Christianity is what the believer thinks; doctrine resident in the soul is the only resource that sustains the believer under pressure, at the approach of death, or in any condition of isolation from external support.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six
text: 7. The conflict between self-righteousness and imputed righteousness is as old as the fall: Moses addressed it at the inception of Israel's dispensation, and Paul draws on both Leviticus 18:5 and Deuteronomy 30:11–14 as canonical witnesses to the antiquity and universality of the principle.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six
text: 8. Codex 2 of the Mosaic law was designed to reveal Christ and demand faith in Him: the unbelieving Jew's bypass of Codex 2 is reproduced in the Church Age as the blotting out of the first advent — the rejection of the omega glory of the Lord Jesus Christ.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six
text: 9. Romans 10:9–10 will present salvation in any dispensation by cause and result: internal faith is the cause; external confession is the result, not an additional condition of salvation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Six
text: 10. The goal of Bible teaching is to make the believer spiritually self-sustaining: doctrine resident in the soul must function independently in every circumstance of life, because no external resource — human or institutional — can substitute for it when pressure reaches its maximum.

text: Romans 10:5 — Self-Righteousness and the Law: Moses, Paul, and the Codex of the Client Nation

section: Romans 10:5 — Self-Righteousness and the Law: Moses, Paul, and the Codex of the Client Nation
text: Romans 10:1–4 has established that Israel's zeal for God is not informed by doctrinal knowledge: the nation sought to establish its own righteousness by means of the law rather than submitting to the righteousness of God revealed in Christ. Romans 10:5 opens the Old Testament documentation of that failure. Paul quotes Leviticus 18:5, the writing of Moses. To interpret the quotation correctly, it is necessary to understand both what Moses was saying in Leviticus and what Paul is saying as he deploys that text in Romans — for they are not talking about the same subject.

section: I. The Integrity of God and the Prerequisite of Righteousness
text: I. The Integrity of God and the Prerequisite of Righteousness

section: I. The Integrity of God and the Prerequisite of Righteousness
text: Before examining the grammar and syntax of Romans 10:5, the foundational principle must be restated. Divine justice can only bless divine righteousness. The integrity of God is composed of His righteousness and His justice — the two are inseparable.

section: I. The Integrity of God and the Prerequisite of Righteousness
text: The older theological vocabulary for this compound is holiness. God is holy. There can be no compromise of attributes in the functioning of the divine essence. What the righteousness of God demands, the justice of God executes. Righteousness is the principle of divine integrity; justice is its function. God cannot accept anything less than perfect righteousness, and therefore He cannot bless anything less than perfect righteousness.

section: I. The Integrity of God and the Prerequisite of Righteousness
text: The practical consequence is direct: every system that attempts to receive divine blessing through talent, moral achievement, religious observance, sincerity, or sacrifice is operating outside the framework that God has established. Such systems produce only self-righteousness, which the justice of God is constitutionally unable to reward.

section: I. The Integrity of God and the Prerequisite of Righteousness
text: At the moment of faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, the believer receives the imputation of divine righteousness, with justification as the immediate result. Justification is God recognizing His own righteousness wherever it has been imputed. Justification precedes all subsequent blessings from the justice of God. Imputed righteousness and resultant justification constitute the prerequisite for all divine blessing — logistical grace now, and blessings exceeding all that we could ask or imagine in the progress toward maturity.

section: II. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 10:5
text: II. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 10:5

section: A. The Explanatory Conjunction
text: A. The Explanatory Conjunction

section: A. The Explanatory Conjunction
text: The verse opens with the post-positive conjunctive particle gar (γάρ), used here in its explanatory function: you see or for you see. It signals that what follows explains the assertion of verse 4 — that Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness.

section: B. Moses Writes — graphō
text: B. Moses Writes — graphō

section: B. Moses Writes — graphō
text: The verb is graphō (γράφω), to write. The tense is present — a historical present that views the past act of writing Leviticus with the vividness of a present occurrence. The active voice assigns the human authorship to Moses. The indicative mood is declarative, asserting the reality of the Old Testament canon as the source from which Paul quotes.

section: B. Moses Writes — graphō
text: The name Moses appears in Greek as Mōusēs (Μωϋσῆς), a transliteration of the Hebrew Mōšeh (מֹשֶׁה). The Greek form adds letters that do not appear in the three-consonant Hebrew root, a feature of Septuagintal transliteration conventions.

section: B. Moses Writes — graphō
text: Moses was not only a military, administrative, engineering, and musical genius; he was also a literary genius. His Hebrew prose and the Hebrew of Isaiah represent the two most highly developed styles in the entire Old Testament. Paul, himself a man of extraordinary intellectual reach, is here quoting from one of the great literary monuments of antiquity.

section: C. The hoti recitativum — Introducing Direct Discourse
text: C. The hoti recitativum — Introducing Direct Discourse

section: C. The hoti recitativum — Introducing Direct Discourse
text: Following graphō comes the conjunction hoti (ὅτι). Here it functions as the hoti recitativum — the Greek device for introducing direct quotation, equivalent to modern quotation marks. When used in this way it is not translated; it simply marks the opening of the cited text. The quotation from Leviticus 18:5 begins at this point.

section: D. The Double Article Construction — tēn dikaiosynēn tēn
text: D. The Double Article Construction — tēn dikaiosynēn tēn

section: D. The Double Article Construction — tēn dikaiosynēn tēn
text: Before the quotation itself, Paul frames its subject: he wrote about the righteousness which is by means of the law. The key phrase is tēn dikaiosynēn tēn (τὴν δικαιοσύνην τήν) — the noun dikaiosynē (δικαιοσύνη, righteousness) bracketed by two definite articles, both accusative feminine singular.

section: D. The Double Article Construction — tēn dikaiosynēn tēn
text: The first definite article carries a back-reference: it points to the human self-righteousness from keeping the law that Paul has been describing in verses 3 and 4. The second definite article functions as a relative pronoun. The full phrase therefore reads: about the righteousness which is. The prepositional phrase that completes it is ek nomou (ἐκ νόμου), the preposition ek (ἐκ) plus the ablative of means from nomos (νόμος, law): by means of the law. Corrected translation of the framing clause: You see, Moses wrote about the righteousness which is by means of the law.

section: E. The Quoted Text from Leviticus 18:5
text: E. The Quoted Text from Leviticus 18:5

section: E. The Quoted Text from Leviticus 18:5
text: After the hoti recitativum, the quotation proper begins. The Greek reads: ho poiēsas auta anthrōpos zēsetai en autois (ὁ ποιήσας αὐτὰ ἄνθρωπος ζήσεται ἐν αὐτοῖς) — the man who does them shall live by them. This closely follows the Hebrew of Leviticus 18:5, which reads: ʾăšer yaʿăśeh ʾōtām hāʾādām wāḥay bāhem — the relative particle ʾăšer, followed by the Qal perfect of ʿāśāh (עָשָׂה, to do), then the subject hāʾādām (הָאָדָם, the man), then the copulative wāw with the Qal perfect of ḥāyāh (חָיָה, shall live), and finally the preposition bāhem (בָּהֶם), by them. The Greek anthrōpos (ἄνθρωπος) is the exact equivalent of hāʾādām. Paul's translation is accurate.

section: III. What Moses Was Saying: The Context of Leviticus 18
text: III. What Moses Was Saying: The Context of Leviticus 18

section: III. What Moses Was Saying: The Context of Leviticus 18
text: Leviticus 18 opens with the Lord addressing Moses and directing him to speak to the people of Israel. The command is framed by two prohibitions: do not do what was done in Egypt, and do not do what is done in Canaan. Both prohibitions point to idolatry and its attendant sexual degeneration — the specific practices catalogued in the remainder of the chapter.

section: III. What Moses Was Saying: The Context of Leviticus 18
text: The speaker identifies Himself with the divine name — the tetragrammaton, Jehovah — which in its New Testament context is the pre-incarnate Lord Jesus Christ, the God of Israel. The authority behind the statutes and judgments of Leviticus 18 is divine.

section: III. What Moses Was Saying: The Context of Leviticus 18
text: The content of the chapter following verse 5 addresses incest, sexual relations between men, and sexual relations with animals. These are the degenerate expressions of idolatrous cultures. When a society maximizes sexual degeneration, it forfeits the conditions necessary for freedom. That connection — idolatry leading to degeneration, degeneration destroying freedom — is the framework within which Leviticus 18:5 stands.

section: III. What Moses Was Saying: The Context of Leviticus 18
text: Moses is not addressing salvation in Leviticus 18. He is addressing the obligations of the client nation Israel under Codex I and Codex III of the Mosaic Law. Codex I — the Decalogue — defines the moral foundation of freedom. Codex III — the laws of divine establishment — addresses the social, judicial, and military structures by which a client nation maintains that freedom. Codex I defines freedom in terms of morality; Codex III protects freedom through law enforcement, criminal justice, and national defense.

section: III. What Moses Was Saying: The Context of Leviticus 18
text: Codex II — the spiritual code, comprising the tabernacle, the Levitical offerings, the holy days, and the Levitical priesthood — is not referenced in Leviticus 18. Salvation and the post-salvation spiritual life are the province of Codex II alone. Moses is not writing about either topic here.

section: IV. What Paul Is Saying: The Function of the Quotation in Romans 10
text: IV. What Paul Is Saying: The Function of the Quotation in Romans 10

section: IV. What Paul Is Saying: The Function of the Quotation in Romans 10
text: The critical interpretive principle for this passage is this: Moses and Paul are not talking about the same subject. Moses, in Leviticus 18:5, is addressing the obligations of covenant Israel as a client nation under Codex I and Codex III — the conditions for national freedom and stability. Paul, in Romans 10:5, is addressing the Jewish error of appropriating those same obligations as a system of self-righteousness by which salvation is sought.

section: IV. What Paul Is Saying: The Function of the Quotation in Romans 10
text: Moses was correct. Obedience to Codex I and Codex III is the responsibility of every member of the client nation. The Ten Commandments are the foundation of civil freedom. The laws of divine establishment — including law enforcement, criminal penalties, and universal military service — are the infrastructure that protects that freedom against both internal crime and external aggression. These things are not bad; they are the divinely authorized mechanisms of national life.

section: IV. What Paul Is Saying: The Function of the Quotation in Romans 10
text: The error Paul is exposing is this: the Jewish generation of his own time had taken what Moses correctly described as the responsibilities of national citizenship and had distorted them into a works-righteousness system for obtaining salvation and divine blessing. The rich young ruler of the Gospels illustrates the pattern precisely — presenting his record of legal observance as the ground of his acceptance before God.

section: IV. What Paul Is Saying: The Function of the Quotation in Romans 10
text: Paul's genius is to take Moses — the common authority whom these Jews themselves accepted — and to show by the very context of the Mosaic text that keeping Codex I and Codex III was never intended as the mechanism of salvation. Codex II — the spiritual code, now fulfilled in Christ — is the only biblical description of how a human being is justified before God. Christ is the termination of the law with reference to righteousness for everyone who believes.

section: V. The Three Codices of the Mosaic Law
text: V. The Three Codices of the Mosaic Law

section: V. The Three Codices of the Mosaic Law
text: The Mosaic Law operates as an integrated system of three distinct codices, each with a different function and scope. Failure to distinguish them produces the kind of confusion that Paul is correcting in Romans 10.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Seven
text: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Seven

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Seven
text: 1. Divine justice can only bless divine righteousness. The integrity of God — composed of His righteousness and His justice — admits no exception. Righteousness is the principle; justice is the function. Every system that attempts to secure divine blessing through human achievement operates outside this framework and produces only self-righteousness, which the justice of God cannot reward.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Seven
text: 2. Imputed righteousness is the prerequisite for all divine blessing. At the moment of faith in Christ, divine righteousness is imputed to the believer and justification follows immediately. Justification precedes every subsequent blessing from the justice of God — logistical grace, spiritual growth, and the blessings of maturity beyond the maturity barrier.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Seven
text: 3. Romans 10:5 quotes Leviticus 18:5, but Moses and Paul are addressing different subjects. Moses, writing in Leviticus 18, addresses the obligations of client-nation Israel under Codex I (the Decalogue) and Codex III (the laws of divine establishment). Paul, quoting that same text in Romans 10, addresses the Jewish error of appropriating those obligations as a self-righteousness system for obtaining salvation. Interpreting the passage requires distinguishing what Moses intended from what Paul is arguing.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Seven
text: 4. The grammatical structure of Romans 10:5 reflects careful, precise composition. The explanatory particle gar introduces the doctrinal documentation. The historical present of graphō presents the writing of Leviticus as a living canonical authority. The hoti recitativum opens the direct quotation. The double-article construction tēn dikaiosynēn tēn — bracketing dikaiosynē with two definite articles — uses the first to back-reference the self-righteousness of verses 3–4 and the second as a relative pronoun introducing the clause.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Seven
text: 5. Paul's use of Moses as a witness against Jewish self-righteousness is an act of interpretive genius. Moses is the supreme authority for the very Jews Paul is addressing. By returning to Leviticus, Paul demonstrates from within their own tradition that Codex I and Codex III — obedience to which these Jews were treating as the ground of salvation — were never designed for that purpose. The Codex designed to address salvation is Codex II, now fulfilled in Christ. The law is good; it is only when the law is distorted into a way of salvation that everything goes wrong.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Seven
text: 6. Codex I and Codex III establish the conditions of national freedom, not the way of salvation. The Decalogue defines the moral basis of a free society. The laws of divine establishment protect that freedom through law enforcement, criminal justice, and national defense. These are necessary for any client nation to function. But observing them, however faithfully, does not justify anyone before God. Only Codex II — only Christ — provides salvation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Six Hundred Fifty-Seven
text: 7. The Hebrew of Leviticus 18:5 is accurately rendered in Paul's Greek quotation. The Hebrew subject hāʾādām (the man) is exactly equivalent to the Greek anthrōpos. The Qal perfect of ʿāśāh (to do) corresponds to the Greek aorist participle poiēsas. The Qal perfect of ḥāyāh (shall live) corresponds to zēsetai. The preposition bāhem (by them) corresponds to en autois. The quotation is grammatically faithful and theologically precise.

section: Romans 10:5 — Leviticus 18:5 and the Distinction Between Morality and Salvation
text: Romans 10:5 — Leviticus 18:5 and the Distinction Between Morality and Salvation

section: Romans 10:5 — Leviticus 18:5 and the Distinction Between Morality and Salvation
text: Romans 10:5 “For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them.” (ESV)

section: Romans 10:5 — Leviticus 18:5 and the Distinction Between Morality and Salvation
text: Corrected translation: You see, Moses wrote about the righteousness which is by means of the law: 'The man who does it shall live by it.'

section: Romans 10:5 — Leviticus 18:5 and the Distinction Between Morality and Salvation
text: We are continuing our verse-by-verse study of Romans 10, examining Paul's quotation of Leviticus 18:5 in Romans 10:5. The apostle cites Moses in order to draw a precise distinction between the righteousness that comes through the law — expressed as a lifestyle of establishment morality — and the righteousness of God received through faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. The passage has been consistently misread by those who collapse morality into the mechanism of salvation. Paul's purpose is to demonstrate that Israel's error was precisely this confusion, and that the resolution is found in Christ alone.

section: I. The Original Context: Leviticus 18:1–6
text: I. The Original Context: Leviticus 18:1–6

section: I. The Original Context: Leviticus 18:1–6
text: Before examining the Greek of Romans 10:5, it is necessary to establish what Moses was actually saying in Leviticus 18. The chapter opens with the Lord commanding Israel to separate itself from the sexual practices of Egypt and Canaan. The laws that follow in verses 6 and beyond address the prohibition of incest in its various forms, including relations between in-laws, as well as other categories of sexual degeneration. Sexual degeneration is identified in this passage as one of the visible indicators of national collapse — a failure to maintain the laws of divine establishment.

section: I. The Original Context: Leviticus 18:1–6
text: Leviticus 18:5 constitutes the central principle governing the chapter. The Hebrew reads:

section: I. The Original Context: Leviticus 18:1–6
text: The key phrase Paul quotes is ha-adam asher ya'aseh otam va-chai bahem — 'the man who does them shall also live by them.' Moses did not append ani Adonai ('I am Jehovah') to the portion Paul quotes; that closing formula belongs to the surrounding verses. The quotation itself is concerned with establishment lifestyle, not with the mechanism of salvation.

section: I. The Original Context: Leviticus 18:1–6
text: The Mosaic Law is divided into three codices: Codex 1, the freedom code (the Ten Commandments); Codex 2, the spiritual code (the ordinances, which present Old Testament soteriology through ritual and typology); and Codex 3, the establishment code (the judgments and statutes). Leviticus 18 belongs to Codex 3. Its subject is establishment morality as a requirement for life in the client nation, not the means by which a person is reconciled to God.

section: I. The Original Context: Leviticus 18:1–6
text: Salvation in both Testaments was always through faith in Christ as He is revealed in the theological vocabulary available at that time. Codex 2 — the ordinances — presented this reality through blood sacrifice and ritual. Israel scrupulously observed the ritual of Codex 2 while rejecting the reality to which it pointed: the person and work of the Lord Jesus Christ. Ritual without reality is religion. Ritual without reality is arrogance. And arrogance in religion produces a system of self-righteousness that, far from opening the gates of heaven, guarantees eternal condemnation.

section: II. Israel's Distortion of the Passage
text: II. Israel's Distortion of the Passage

section: II. Israel's Distortion of the Passage
text: The error Paul identifies is specific. Israel observed the establishment laws of Codex 1 and Codex 3, avoided the sexual degeneration prohibited in Leviticus 18, and concluded from this performance that their self-righteousness was sufficient grounds for salvation. They combined the freedom code and the establishment statutes into a system of works righteousness. In doing so, they placed their own righteousness in competition with the righteousness of God — which is no competition at all.

section: II. Israel's Distortion of the Passage
text: This is not an error unique to Israel. It is the characteristic error of all legalistic religion: the substitution of human performance for divine imputation. The classic Pauline statement of the principle is Ephesians 2:9 — 'not of works, lest any man should boast.' The word 'boast' identifies the arrogance that lies behind every system of works righteousness. Doing is a lifestyle. Believing in Christ is salvation. These two categories must never be confused.
