section: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: Three Stages, Three Imputations, and the Plan of God
text: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: Three Stages, Three Imputations, and the Plan of God

section: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: Three Stages, Three Imputations, and the Plan of God
text: Romans 12:12 “Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.” (ESV)

section: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: Three Stages, Three Imputations, and the Plan of God
text: Corrected translation: Be rejoicing with reference to the hope, enduring in pressure, persevering in prayer.

section: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: Three Stages, Three Imputations, and the Plan of God
text: Romans 12:12 stands at the operational center of the paraenetic section of Romans. The chapter has moved from the foundational doctrines of salvation and righteousness into their practical expression in the life of the mature believer. The single phrase under examination in this chapter — 'be rejoicing with reference to the hope' — opens into one of the most structured doctrinal presentations in the epistle: the three-stage equation of hope, grounded in the seven imputations that constitute the divine plan for every believer's life. The present chapter expounds the Doctrine of Hope in full, with attention to its etymological, theological, and structural dimensions.

section: I. The Three-Radical Equation: X + Y + Z = The Good
text: I. The Three-Radical Equation: X + Y + Z = The Good

section: I. The Three-Radical Equation: X + Y + Z = The Good
text: The phrase 'all things work together for good' (Romans 8:28) finds its structural explanation in an equation of three radicals — X, Y, and Z — each enclosing a pair of divine imputations, a resulting potential, pertinent doctrine, and a corresponding stage of hope. The sum of the three radicals is described by the Greek term

section: I. The Three-Radical Equation: X + Y + Z = The Good
text: The sum of the three radicals is designated by the Greek adjective agathos (αγαθός), the intrinsic good — the plan of God for the believer's life. The equation is not abstract; it is the skeletal outline of every divine imputation from physical birth through the judgment seat of Christ.

section: X Radical: Condemnation and the First Hope
text: X Radical: Condemnation and the First Hope

section: X Radical: Condemnation and the First Hope
text: The X radical opens at the moment of physical birth. Two imputations occur simultaneously: (1) the imputation of human life from God, and (2) the imputation of Adam's original sin from the justice of God. The result is total condemnation — spiritual death at the moment physical life begins. This is the lowest point any human being ever reaches. No accumulation of personal sins can deepen that condemnation, because the sentence of death was already executed at birth through the imputation of Adam's original sin.

section: X Radical: Condemnation and the First Hope
text: Total condemnation, however, is the precondition of salvation. God cannot save a person who is not condemned. The first potential therefore emerges directly from the imputation of Adam's sin: the potential of salvation. When pertinent doctrine — the accurate presentation of the gospel — is added, the potential becomes the first hope: confident anticipation that belief in Jesus Christ produces eternal life. This is the confidence that precedes and motivates the act of faith.

section: X Radical: Condemnation and the First Hope
text: The X radical closes at the moment of salvation. The first hope is set aside, not because it failed, but because the reality it anticipated has arrived. The believer has eternal life; hope one is replaced by fact.

section: Y Radical: Righteousness and the Second Hope
text: Y Radical: Righteousness and the Second Hope

section: Y Radical: Righteousness and the Second Hope
text: The Y radical begins at the moment of faith in Christ and contains the two judicial imputations that constitute salvation adjustment to the justice of God. Judicial imputation number one: all personal sins of every human being were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged there. Not a single personal sin — not even the first — was ever imputed to the sinner directly. The charge was transferred to the sinless substitute. Judicial imputation number two: the righteousness of God is imputed to the believer at the moment of faith. The believer receives

section: Y Radical: Righteousness and the Second Hope
text: The believer receives the dikaiosynē theou (δικαιοσύνη θεου), the righteousness of God, as a permanent judicial imputation. This is the sixth imputation's prerequisite: justice can only bless what righteousness approves, and righteousness approves only what equals itself.

section: Y Radical: Righteousness and the Second Hope
text: These two judicial imputations produce the second potential: the potentiality of blessing in time at the point of maturity and thereafter. When the believer learns the pertinent doctrine — the plan of God, the divine attributes, the divine decrees, the function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception — the second potential becomes the second hope: confident anticipation of the imputation of divine blessing at the maturity barrier. The believer advances from salvation toward maturity under this hope, sustained by consistent intake of Bible doctrine.

section: Y Radical: Righteousness and the Second Hope
text: The Y radical closes at the maturity barrier. The second hope is replaced by the reality of the sixth imputation — blessing in time begins. The believer is now in supergrace A.

section: Z Radical: Maturity, Suffering, and the Third Hope
text: Z Radical: Maturity, Suffering, and the Third Hope

section: Z Radical: Maturity, Suffering, and the Third Hope
text: The Z radical opens with two real imputations: (1) eternal life, imputed at salvation, which is now carried forward as a permanent possession, and (2) blessing in time, imputed at maturity as the sixth imputation. These two together establish the third potential: eternal blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ. When pertinent doctrine concerning the rapture, the judgment seat, and the eternal state is added — together with undeserved suffering, which maintains the mature believer's perspective during temporal prosperity — the third potential becomes the third hope: confident anticipation of the seventh imputation.

section: Z Radical: Maturity, Suffering, and the Third Hope
text: The seventh imputation occurs at the judgment seat of Christ, after the rapture of the church. Blessing and reward in eternity are imputed to the resurrection body. This is the hope under which the mature believer lives, and dies, and passes through the rapture if it occurs in his lifetime. It is the hope of Romans 12:12: 'Be rejoicing with reference to the hope.'

section: Z Radical: Maturity, Suffering, and the Third Hope
text: The Z radical does not close within the believer's lifetime. It closes at the judgment seat, and what follows is the reality of eternal blessing — the

section: Z Radical: Maturity, Suffering, and the Third Hope
text: The Z radical closes at the judgment seat, and what follows is the reality of eternal blessing — the agathos (αγαθός), the good — the complete execution of the plan of God.

section: II. The Doctrine of Hope
text: II. The Doctrine of Hope

section: Point 1 — Etymology and Definition
text: Point 1 — Etymology and Definition

section: Point 1 — Etymology and Definition
text: Hope, as a theological category, is not uncertainty. The common use of the word — 'I hope so,' meaning 'I think it might be true' — is the precise opposite of the biblical term. Hope in Scripture is

section: Point 1 — Etymology and Definition
text: Hope in Scripture is rendered from the Greek noun elpis (ἐλπίς) and the verb elpizō (ἐλπίζω). The consistent biblical meaning is confident anticipation or confident expectation of a future reality. Hope is not a wish; it is certainty directed toward what has not yet occurred. Once the anticipated reality arrives, hope is replaced by fact.

section: Point 2 — The Author of Hope
text: Point 2 — The Author of Hope

section: Point 2 — The Author of Hope
text: Two passages establish who originates each category of hope.

section: Point 2 — The Author of Hope
text: Titus 1:2 addresses the first hope: 'In the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before times eternal.' God the Father is the source of the first hope. His promise was lodged in eternity past, within the divine decrees, before history began. The omniscience of God encompassed every volitional decision every person would ever make — including every person who would believe in Christ — and the decrees were constructed accordingly. The first hope rests on the immutability of the promise of a God who cannot lie.

section: Point 2 — The Author of Hope
text: Colossians 1:27 addresses the second and third hopes: 'to whom God decreed to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.' God the Son — Christ indwelling the believer — is the source of the second and third hopes. The indwelling of Christ is the guarantee of the advance to maturity and of the eternal blessing that follows. The distinction between the second and third hopes is positional: the immature believer advancing toward maturity operates under the second hope; the mature believer who has cracked the maturity barrier operates under the third hope for the remainder of life.

section: Point 3 — Hope Anticipates the Function of the Integrity of God
text: Point 3 — Hope Anticipates the Function of the Integrity of God

section: Point 3 — Hope Anticipates the Function of the Integrity of God
text: Job 4:6 presents two rhetorical questions that encode this principle: 'Is not your awe of God your confidence? And is not your hope the integrity of your ways?' The first question establishes that confidence toward God rests on respect for divine authority — on knowledge of the divine attributes, the divine decrees, and the relationship between omniscience, foreknowledge, election, and predestination. Awe of God, informed by doctrine, produces confidence.

section: Point 3 — Hope Anticipates the Function of the Integrity of God
text: The second question introduces the royal family honor code. The integrity referred to is not morality in the ordinary sense. Morality is the standard required of the entire human race as a function of divine establishment. The Christian way of life operates on a different plane — not below morality, but categorically above it, in a manner that morality can neither produce nor approximate. This higher plane is integrity: the honor code of the royal family of God, grounded in the imputed righteousness of God rather than in human effort or behavioral compliance.

section: Point 3 — Hope Anticipates the Function of the Integrity of God
text: Psalm 71:5 extends the principle: 'For you are my hope, O Lord God, my confidence from my youth.' David, writing as a mature believer who had cracked the maturity barrier, identifies the Lord as both hope and confidence. The synonymous pairing is deliberate: hope is the forward-looking form of confidence, directed toward what has not yet been realized. The entire structure of the three-stage plan of God is captured in this identification of God as the source of hope at every stage.

section: Point 3 — Hope Anticipates the Function of the Integrity of God
text: Romans 4:17–18 provides the definitive historical illustration. Abraham at age one hundred was sexually incapacitated; Sarah at ninety-nine was long past the possibility of conception. Every natural condition contradicted the divine promise that Abraham would be 'a father of many nations' (Genesis 17:5). Yet the text states: 'who beyond hope believed in hope.' The phrase is precise. Beyond any natural or human ground for expectation, Abraham believed in the integrity of God — confident that the God who gave life to the sexually dead could restore every physical condition necessary to fulfill the promise. This is the third hope in operation: Abraham, standing as a mature believer past the maturity barrier, had total confidence that what God had imputed by promise would be executed by divine power.

section: Point 3 — Hope Anticipates the Function of the Integrity of God
text: Jeremiah 17:7 confirms the identification: 'Happy in essence is the man who puts his trust in the Lord, and whose hope is in the Lord.' Trust and hope are parallel but not identical. Trust is the confidence of the immature believer who does not yet see the mechanism of execution. Hope is the confidence of the mature believer who understands exactly what God will do and how. The difference between trust and hope maps directly onto the difference between the immature and the mature believer.

section: Point 3 — Hope Anticipates the Function of the Integrity of God
text: First Thessalonians 1:3 confirms the same pattern in the Thessalonian church: 'constantly bearing in mind your work of doctrine and labor of love and courage under pressure from hope in our Lord Jesus Christ in the presence of God the Father.' The Thessalonians were operating under the third hope — past the maturity barrier, enduring adversity with a confidence that derived not from circumstances but from the certainty of what the justice of God had committed to execute.

section: Point 4 — The Equation of Hope (Romans 15:13)
text: Point 4 — The Equation of Hope (Romans 15:13)

section: Point 4 — The Equation of Hope (Romans 15:13)
text: Romans 15:13 provides the summary statement: 'Now may the God of hope fill you with all happiness and prosperity in believing, in order that you may abound in hope by means of the Holy Spirit.' The passage identifies God as the source of hope and links three elements: happiness (the inner joy of the mature believer), prosperity (the imputation of blessing in time under six categories), and abounding in hope (the third hope, operating through the ministry of God the Holy Spirit, not through human works).

section: Point 4 — The Equation of Hope (Romans 15:13)
text: The structural principle behind this passage is the lesser-to-greater argument. If the justice of God provided the greater — the imputation of divine righteousness at salvation — it follows that the justice of God will provide the lesser: the imputation of blessing in time at maturity. And if the justice of God provided the greater at maturity — blessing in time — it follows that the justice of God will provide the lesser: blessing and reward in eternity at the judgment seat of Christ. The temporal blessings of the sixth imputation are the guarantee and the basis for confidence regarding the eternal blessings of the seventh.

section: Point 4 — The Equation of Hope (Romans 15:13)
text: Hebrews 11:1 functions as the epistemological statement: 'In fact, doctrine is the reality from which we receive the hope, the proof of matters not being seen.' This verse is not a definition of faith in the abstract; it is a structural statement about hope. The things not yet seen — the seventh imputation, the judgment seat, the eternal blessings — are rendered real and certain by doctrine resident in the soul. Hope is not the projection of desire onto an uncertain future; it is the confident forward extension of doctrinal certainty.

section: Point 5 — Imputation Is the Basis of Hope
text: Point 5 — Imputation Is the Basis of Hope

section: Point 5 — Imputation Is the Basis of Hope
text: The mechanics that make hope possible at each stage are the divine imputations. Seven imputations constitute the structural outline of the plan of God:

section: Point 5 — Imputation Is the Basis of Hope
text: Imputation 1: Human life, imputed at physical birth. Imputation 2: Adam's original sin, imputed simultaneously at birth, producing condemnation. Imputation 3 (Judicial): The personal sins of all humanity, imputed to Christ on the cross. Imputation 4 (Judicial): The righteousness of God, imputed to the believer at salvation. Imputation 5: Eternal life, imputed to the believer at salvation. Imputation 6: Blessing in time, imputed to the mature believer at the maturity barrier. Imputation 7: Blessing and reward in eternity, imputed at the judgment seat of Christ.

section: Point 5 — Imputation Is the Basis of Hope
text: The first two imputations produce condemnation and the first potential. The third and fourth produce salvation and the second potential. The fifth and sixth produce the third potential. Each pair of imputations, when combined with pertinent doctrine, generates a hope. Each hope is replaced by the reality of the next imputation. The equation balances because each side — imputations on one side, potentials and hopes on the other — corresponds exactly.

section: Point 6 — The Difference Between Potential and Hope Is Doctrine
text: Point 6 — The Difference Between Potential and Hope Is Doctrine

section: Point 6 — The Difference Between Potential and Hope Is Doctrine
text: A potential exists whether or not the believer is aware of it. Hope requires cognizance — specifically, cognizance of pertinent doctrine. The first potential becomes the first hope only when the gospel is accurately presented and understood. The second potential becomes the second hope only when the believer understands the plan of God: the nature of the divine attributes, the function of the decrees, the role of the Grace Apparatus for Perception, and the structure of the advance to maturity. The third potential becomes the third hope only when the believer understands the rapture, the judgment seat of Christ, and the relationship between temporal blessing and eternal reward.

section: Point 6 — The Difference Between Potential and Hope Is Doctrine
text: A potential that is unrecognized produces neither confidence nor advance. Doctrine is the bridge between what God has provided and what the believer can appropriate with confidence. This is why consistent, systematic intake of Bible doctrine is not one option among several — it is the only mechanism by which any potential becomes a functioning hope and any hope becomes an experienced reality.

section: Points 7–12 — Summary of the Structural Relationships
text: Points 7–12 — Summary of the Structural Relationships

section: Points 7–12 — Summary of the Structural Relationships
text: The following summary states the key structural principles of the Doctrine of Hope:

section: Points 7–12 — Summary of the Structural Relationships
text: 7. When the hope of salvation is replaced by the reality of salvation, the judicial imputation of divine righteousness becomes the basis for a new potential and a new hope: blessing and prosperity at maturity.

section: Points 7–12 — Summary of the Structural Relationships
text: 8. When the hope of blessing in time is replaced by the reality of blessing at maturity, two real imputations — eternal life and blessing in time — form the basis for the third potential and the third hope.

section: Points 7–12 — Summary of the Structural Relationships
text: 9. The third potential and the third hope constitute confident anticipation of blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ. This hope belongs to the mature believer — specifically to those who have reached supergrace A or beyond.

section: Points 7–12 — Summary of the Structural Relationships
text: 10. Each imputation replaces the preceding hope and provides the foundation for the next hope. This is why the equation contains six imputations across three radicals: the structure is not arbitrary but reflects the precise mechanics of the divine plan.

section: Points 7–12 — Summary of the Structural Relationships
text: 11. The imputation of blessing in time (sixth imputation) replaces the second hope and inaugurates the believer's life in supergrace.

section: Points 7–12 — Summary of the Structural Relationships
text: 12. The imputation of blessing in time also becomes the basis for the third hope through the lesser-to-greater argument: if God imputed the greater blessing in time, He will certainly impute the lesser blessing in eternity — at the judgment seat of Christ.

section: III. The Royal Family Honor Code: Initial Principles
text: III. The Royal Family Honor Code: Initial Principles

section: III. The Royal Family Honor Code: Initial Principles
text: The Doctrine of Hope intersects with the royal family honor code at the level of its third point: hope anticipates the integrity of God and the integrity of the royal family. Two foundational principles of that honor code surface in this chapter and will receive full treatment in the chapters covering Romans 13.

section: Privacy of the Royal Priesthood
text: Privacy of the Royal Priesthood

section: Privacy of the Royal Priesthood
text: The first principle is privacy. Every Church Age believer functions as a royal priest before God. The priesthood is individual and direct — there is no human intermediary. The believer's life is conducted before God, and the administration of that life, including its failures, belongs to that private relationship. Privacy is the structural foundation of freedom, and freedom is the environment in which doctrine can be assimilated without coercion or social pressure.

section: Privacy of the Royal Priesthood
text: The practical implication for corporate Bible study is direct: the content of Scripture addresses the believer's soul, not his public reputation. When a passage touches a pattern of sin, the response is internal and cognitive — objective reception of what the text teaches — not social or performative. Any environment that intrudes on that privacy undermines the inculcation of doctrine and thereby retards spiritual growth.

section: Blessing Through Doctrine, Not Works
text: Blessing Through Doctrine, Not Works

section: Blessing Through Doctrine, Not Works
text: The second principle is the categorical exclusion of works as the mechanism of blessing. The holiness of God — His integrity — is composed of righteousness and justice in encapsulation. The justice of God gives all blessing to the righteousness of God. Blessing flows from justice to righteousness — from one divine attribute to another — and the only point of contact between the believer and that transaction is the imputed righteousness received at salvation.

section: Blessing Through Doctrine, Not Works
text: No act of service, no pattern of moral behavior, no system of giving, no observance of religious taboos can initiate or augment the flow of blessing. These are not supplementary mechanisms; they are categorically excluded. The justice of God acts toward the righteousness of God, and what the righteousness of God demands, the justice of God executes. Doctrine resident in the soul is the only mechanism that advances the believer toward the point at which the sixth imputation begins.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Four
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Four

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Four
text: 1. Hope is confident anticipation, not uncertainty. The biblical term —

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Four
text: 1. Hope is confident anticipation, not uncertainty. The biblical term elpis (ἐλπίς) denotes certainty directed toward a future reality. Once the reality arrives, hope is replaced by fact. This distinction governs every use of the term in the three-stage equation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Four
text: 2. Three stages of hope structure the plan of God. Hope one: confident anticipation of salvation through faith in Christ. Hope two: confident anticipation of blessing in time at the maturity barrier. Hope three: confident anticipation of blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ. Each hope is replaced by reality as the believer advances through the divine plan.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Four
text: 3. God the Father is the author of the first hope; God the Son is the author of the second and third. Titus 1:2 grounds the first hope in the eternal promise of the Father. Colossians 1:27 grounds the second and third hopes in the indwelling of Christ, which is both the guarantee of advance to maturity and the pledge of eternal blessing.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Four
text: 4. Seven imputations are the mechanics of the plan of God. The first two produce condemnation and the potential of salvation. The third and fourth (judicial imputations) produce salvation adjustment and the potential of maturity blessing. The fifth and sixth produce the mature believer's life and the potential of eternal reward. The seventh is the eternal reward itself, imputed at the judgment seat of Christ.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Four
text: 5. Doctrine is the bridge between potential and hope. A potential that is unrecognized produces neither confidence nor advance. Cognizance of pertinent doctrine at each stage — the gospel, the plan of God, the rapture and judgment seat — is what converts potential into functioning hope and hope into experienced reality.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Four
text: 6. The lesser-to-greater argument guarantees the third hope. If the justice of God provided the greater blessing — imputed righteousness at salvation and blessing in time at maturity — it follows with logical necessity that the justice of God will provide the lesser: eternal blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ. The temporal blessings of supergrace are the basis of confidence regarding eternity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Four
text: 7. Undeserved suffering in the Z radical preserves the mature believer's eternal perspective. Prosperity in time, if not balanced by divinely appointed adversity, can redirect the mature believer's attention from eternity to the temporal. Undeserved suffering is not punitive; it is a grace provision that maintains the perspective necessary for the third hope to function as the organizing principle of the mature believer's life.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Four
text: 8. The integrity of God — not human effort — is both the source and the object of hope. Hope is not self-confidence, nor is it confidence in other persons. It is confidence in the divine attributes: the righteousness that demands, and the justice that executes. Abraham's hope beyond hope (Romans 4:18) illustrates the principle at its maximum: every natural ground for expectation had been removed, and confidence in the integrity of God remained absolute.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Four
text: 9. Privacy of the priesthood and the exclusion of works are the first two principles of the royal family honor code. Privacy provides the environment in which doctrine can be received without social pressure or performative coercion. The exclusion of works reflects the encapsulation of divine integrity: the justice of God gives all blessing to the righteousness of God, and no human act can alter or supplement that transaction.

Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Five

section: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: Points 6–8 — Confidence Based on Doctrine; The Three Hopes in the Equation
text: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: Points 6–8 — Confidence Based on Doctrine; The Three Hopes in the Equation

section: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: Points 6–8 — Confidence Based on Doctrine; The Three Hopes in the Equation
text: Romans 12:12 “Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.” (ESV)

section: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: Points 6–8 — Confidence Based on Doctrine; The Three Hopes in the Equation
text: Corrected translation: With reference to the hope, be rejoicing; with reference to tribulation, be enduring; with reference to prayer, be persistent.

section: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: Points 6–8 — Confidence Based on Doctrine; The Three Hopes in the Equation
text: Romans 12:12 presents three parallel imperatives governing the posture of the mature believer. This chapter resumes the exposition of the second phrase — 'with reference to the hope, be rejoicing' — and continues the systematic study of the doctrine of hope. The preceding chapter established the etymology and definition of hope, the two authors of hope, and the role of the integrity of God as the horizon toward which all hope is oriented. The present chapter takes up points six through eight: hope as confidence based on doctrine, the first hope in the equation of the plan of God, and the second hope in that equation.

section: I. Point 6 — Hope as Confidence Based on Doctrine
text: I. Point 6 — Hope as Confidence Based on Doctrine

section: I. Point 6 — Hope as Confidence Based on Doctrine
text: The sixth point in the doctrine of hope identifies the precise mechanism by which a believer moves from spiritual potential to genuine, operational confidence. The critical distinction is between potential and hope. A potential is a real possibility — it exists objectively in the structure of the divine plan — but it remains inert and functionally inaccessible apart from pertinent doctrine resident in the soul. Hope, by contrast, is absolute confidence. It is not guesswork, not desire, not optimism. It is the state in which the believer knows exactly where he stands in the plan of God and knows exactly what the plan of God will produce.

section: I. Point 6 — Hope as Confidence Based on Doctrine
text: The New Testament word for hope is elpis (ελπίς), which never carries the sense of uncertainty or conjecture. It always designates total confidence — confidence, however, that is grounded in knowledge. Without doctrine resident in the soul, a potential remains a potential. With doctrine, the potential becomes a hope — that is, an operational, motivating certainty about what God will do.

section: I. Point 6 — Hope as Confidence Based on Doctrine
text: This principle is the subject of Hebrews 11:1, literally rendered: 'In fact, doctrine is the reality from which we keep receiving the hope, the proof of matters not being seen.' Doctrine is the substance that converts potential into confidence. The entire eleventh chapter of Hebrews demonstrates this proposition through the lives of believers who acted on the basis of what they knew — not on the basis of what they could see, produce, or control.

section: I. Point 6 — Hope as Confidence Based on Doctrine
text: Hebrews 11:2 states that by means of doctrine resident in the soul, men of old gained divine approval — that is, they cracked the maturity barrier and received the sixth imputation of blessing from the justice of God. Verse 3 establishes that by means of doctrine, the believer understands the structure of the divine decrees and the unfolding of history. Verse 4 demonstrates that Abel offered a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain by means of doctrine. Verse 5 records that Enoch was transferred without experiencing death by means of doctrine. In each case the formula is identical: doctrine converts potential into confident expectation, and that expectation produces the course of action that leads to maturity and to imputed blessing.

section: I. Point 6 — Hope as Confidence Based on Doctrine
text: Hebrews 11:6 provides the climactic statement: without doctrine resident in the soul it is impossible to please God. The one who approaches God must be convinced — must have doctrinal certainty — that God possesses divine integrity and that He becomes the rewarder of those who diligently seek Him. The seeking is the daily intake of Bible doctrine through the grace apparatus for perception (GAP). The reward is the sixth imputation of blessing in time, followed by the seventh imputation of blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ.

section: I. Point 6 — Hope as Confidence Based on Doctrine
text: The structural principle that emerges from Hebrews 11 maps precisely onto the equation of the plan of God. That equation is expressed as X + Y + Z = the Good, where the Good is the absolute good of Romans 8:28 — the complete plan of God for the believer's life. Within each radical of the equation, the same pattern recurs: imputation establishes a potential; doctrine converts the potential into a hope; and the reality that follows replaces the hope with fulfilled blessing. Hope is always absorbed into the reality it anticipated.

section: I. Point 6 — Hope as Confidence Based on Doctrine
text: Romans 8:24 states the principle: 'Now when a hope is seen, it is no longer a hope. For who hopes for what he sees?' Elpis is the anticipation of what has not yet arrived. Once the imputation occurs, the hope has accomplished its purpose and the reality stands in its place. Motivation for the Christian way of life therefore derives not from activity, effort, or religious performance, but from doctrine resident in the soul — which is to say, from hope in the technical sense.

section: I. Point 6 — Hope as Confidence Based on Doctrine
text: All motivation for life resides in the soul. The motivation of the royal family of God for the execution of the protocol plan is doctrine resident in the right lobe — knowledge of where one stands in the plan, knowledge of what the plan will produce, and the operational confidence that the justice of God will deliver exactly what it has promised.

section: II. The Equation of the Plan of God: Three Hopes in Three Radicals
text: II. The Equation of the Plan of God: Three Hopes in Three Radicals

section: II. The Equation of the Plan of God: Three Hopes in Three Radicals
text: The plan of God in time is organized around six imputations and three radicals. Each radical contains two imputations, a resulting potential, pertinent doctrine that converts the potential into a hope, and a plus — a reality that replaces the hope and opens the next radical. The three hopes that emerge from this structure are the immediate referent of the command in Romans 12:12 to rejoice with reference to the hope.

section: A. The X Radical: Hope One — Salvation Adjustment
text: A. The X Radical: Hope One — Salvation Adjustment

section: A. The X Radical: Hope One — Salvation Adjustment
text: The X radical contains the first two imputations in the plan of God. The first is the imputation of human life to the human soul at physical birth — a real imputation in which human life, the factor, is matched to its divinely prepared home, the soul, on the basis of affinity. The second is the simultaneous imputation of Adam's original sin to the old sin nature, which is genetically transmitted through the male line and formed in the body during gestation. The result is that every member of the human race is born physically alive but spiritually dead — condemned by one man's sin before any personal sin has been committed.

section: A. The X Radical: Hope One — Salvation Adjustment
text: The justice of this arrangement is frequently misunderstood. Condemnation must precede justification in the structure of the divine plan, because the justice of God is the point of reference for all divine action. Furthermore, no personal sins are ever imputed to any member of the human race for condemnation. All personal sins — past, present, and future — were collected by God and imputed to Jesus Christ on the cross, where they were judged by the justice of God in a real judicial imputation. This means that the condemnation of the human race rests on Adam's original sin alone, and it means that Christ's substitutionary work was exhaustive: there is no sin of the human race that was not actually judged at Calvary.

section: A. The X Radical: Hope One — Salvation Adjustment
text: The combination of total condemnation and total provision at the cross establishes the first potential: salvation through faith in Jesus Christ. This potential exists for every member of the human race. The pertinent doctrine that converts this potential into hope one is the gospel. Gospel hearing, through whatever medium God provides — personal witness, an evangelist, a pastor, written Scripture — goes into the left lobe (the staging area of the soul). The Holy Spirit, acting in common grace as a surrogate human spirit for the unbeliever who lacks one, transfers that information into the right lobe where it becomes a cognitive reality. The unbeliever now has hope one: absolute confidence that the moment he believes in the Lord Jesus Christ, he possesses eternal life.

section: A. The X Radical: Hope One — Salvation Adjustment
text: Hope one is the point at which volition is engaged. With the information in the right lobe and the issue clearly defined — believe on the Son and have everlasting life; reject the Son and the wrath of God abides — the individual either responds with positive volition or exercises the freedom to reject. If positive, faith in Christ is expressed in the privacy of the soul, and in that moment the hope is replaced by the reality of eternal salvation. This is efficacious grace: the Holy Spirit makes the act of faith effectual for regeneration.

section: A. The X Radical: Hope One — Salvation Adjustment
text: What is not required for salvation is instructive. No public display is required. No ceremonial act — baptism, church membership, financial contribution, aisle-walking, hand-raising — has any place in the transaction. No renunciation of sins is required, because the renunciation of personal sin patterns is not within human capacity in any case, and because God does not invite the believer to assist in a work that is already complete. Salvation was accomplished at the cross. The Father planned it; the Son executed it; the Spirit reveals it. The only appropriate human response is non-meritorious faith directed toward the person of Christ.

section: A. The X Radical: Hope One — Salvation Adjustment
text: Hebrews 7:19 states the case precisely: 'The law made nothing perfect, but on the other hand there is the bringing in of a better hope, through which we draw near to God.' The Mosaic law has legitimate functions — it describes the nature of freedom, provides a framework for jurisprudence, and delineates the structure of a just society. But the one thing the law cannot accomplish is salvation. It cannot impute dikaiosynē (δικαιοσύνη). That belongs exclusively to the work of Christ, received through faith, which is hope one — the better hope through which the believer draws near to God.

section: A. The X Radical: Hope One — Salvation Adjustment
text: The first hope in the equation is also the hope of the Gentile world. Romans 15:12 anticipates the Davidic fulfillment: 'In His name the Gentiles will hope.' The Gentiles, upon hearing the gospel, have confident assurance that by simply believing in the Lord Jesus Christ they receive eternal life. This is the first stage of the plan of God, and when it becomes a reality through faith, the X radical closes and the Y radical opens.

section: B. The Y Radical: Hope Two — Maturity Adjustment
text: B. The Y Radical: Hope Two — Maturity Adjustment

section: B. The Y Radical: Hope Two — Maturity Adjustment
text: The Y radical contains judicial imputations three and four. The third judicial imputation is the imputation of all personal sins of the human race to Christ at the cross — 'Christ died for our sins.' The fourth judicial imputation is the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at the moment of salvation. This is the foundation of everything that follows in the believer's life, because it establishes the basis for a higher standard of operation and for the future imputation of divine blessing.

section: B. The Y Radical: Hope Two — Maturity Adjustment
text: The imputation of divine righteousness at salvation produces the second potential: the possibility that through the consistent daily intake of Bible doctrine the believer will crack the maturity barrier and receive great blessing as the sixth imputation from the justice of God. The mechanism of affinity operates here as it did in the X radical: the justice of God imputes blessing to the divine righteousness that is already resident in the believer. When the imputed righteousness reaches the level of maximum capacity through doctrinal saturation, the justice of God responds with the imputation of blessing.

section: B. The Y Radical: Hope Two — Maturity Adjustment
text: The pertinent doctrine that converts this second potential into hope two includes the major Church Age epistles — Romans, Hebrews, Ephesians, Philippians, and the corpus of doctrine that systematically informs the believer about where he is in the plan of God, what God has provided, and what the structure of divine blessing looks like. Any sustained and accurate presentation of Bible doctrine constitutes the pertinent doctrine of the Y radical.

section: B. The Y Radical: Hope Two — Maturity Adjustment
text: Hope two is therefore the operational confidence of every positive believer between salvation and the maturity barrier: absolute assurance that by continuing to take in doctrine consistently, the maturity barrier will be cracked and the justice of God will impute divine blessing. This is not aspiration; it is operational certainty derived from knowledge of the plan. The believer knows the structure of the imputations, knows that divine righteousness is already resident in his soul as the prepared receptor for blessing, and knows that the integrity of God will perform exactly what it has promised.

section: B. The Y Radical: Hope Two — Maturity Adjustment
text: The six categories of blessing that constitute the sixth imputation are: (1) spiritual blessings, (2) material blessings, (3) blessing by association, (4) historical impact, (5) undeserved suffering as a form of blessing that maintains eternal perspective, and (6) dying grace. Each of these is anticipated through hope two, and each is realized through imputation at the moment of maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

section: B. The Y Radical: Hope Two — Maturity Adjustment
text: Lamentations 3:21–25 provides the Scriptural anchor for this second hope. 'This I recall to mind, therefore I have hope.' The believer recalls pertinent doctrine and thereby has confident expectation. The passage continues: 'The Lord's mercies never cease' — logistical grace, the provision that sustains the believer through every stage between salvation and maturity — 'for His compassions never fail' — the forgiveness that is always available through rebound — 'they are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness.' God provides the believer with the time and the resources necessary to crack the maturity barrier one day at a time. Verse 24: 'The Lord is my portion, says my soul; therefore I will hope in Him.' Verse 25: 'The Lord is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul who seeks Him' — that is, to the believer who is positive toward Bible doctrine.

section: B. The Y Radical: Hope Two — Maturity Adjustment
text: The importance of logistical grace in this context must be noted. Between salvation and the maturity barrier, everything God provides for the believer — food, shelter, clothing, transportation, health, relationships — is logistical support rather than the covenant blessing of the sixth imputation. It is not a blessing in the technical sense of the plan of God; it is the provision that makes sustained doctrine intake possible. The believer may have abundant material comfort or very little during this period, but whatever he has is the logistical support of grace, calculated to sustain him until he cracks the maturity barrier and crosses into supergrace.

section: B. The Y Radical: Hope Two — Maturity Adjustment
text: When the maturity barrier is cracked, hope two is replaced by reality — the actual imputation of blessing to the divine righteousness resident in the believer's soul. The Y radical closes with the second plus: maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

section: III. The Integrity of God as the Source of All Contact
text: III. The Integrity of God as the Source of All Contact

section: III. The Integrity of God as the Source of All Contact
text: Throughout the exposition of both hopes, a structural principle recurs that is central to the theology of Romans: the justice of God is the point of reference for all divine action toward man. God's love, sovereignty, omnipotence, and omniscience do not directly dispense blessing. All blessing flows through the justice of God, which imputes to the divine righteousness resident in the believer. This is why adjustment to the justice of God is the organizing axis of the entire Epistle.

section: III. The Integrity of God as the Source of All Contact
text: The pipeline of blessing runs from the justice of God to the righteousness of God resident in the believer. Human works cannot intrude upon that pipeline. Legitimate commanded functions — exercise of spiritual gifts, prayer, witnessing — cannot intrude upon it either. The imputation is pure grace, executed by the justice of God on the basis of the believer's doctrinal capacity and nothing else. When that imputation occurs, God is glorified.

section: III. The Integrity of God as the Source of All Contact
text: The principle of the greater and the lesser — what the classical tradition calls the argument from the greater to the less — applies here with full force. Blessing in time is imputed to divine righteousness at the moment of maturity. Blessing and reward in eternity are imputed to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ. If the justice of God provides the greater blessing at maturity in time, it follows by the lesser that the justice of God will provide the blessing of eternity to the resurrection body. Blessing in time is parlayed into blessing in eternity. The sign that a believer will be rewarded at the judgment seat of Christ is that he has cracked the maturity barrier and received the sixth imputation. Zero in time is parlayed into zero in eternity; blessing in time is parlayed into blessing in eternity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Five
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Five

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Five
text: 1. Hope in the New Testament is never guesswork or desire. The Greek term ελπίς (elpis) designates absolute confidence — confidence grounded in knowledge of doctrine resident in the soul. When Scripture commands the believer to rejoice with reference to the hope, it commands rejoicing based on doctrinal certainty about what God will do.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Five
text: 2. The distinguishing factor between potential and hope is Bible doctrine. Every radical of the plan of God contains a potential established by divine imputation. That potential remains inert and experientially inaccessible until pertinent doctrine enters the right lobe of the soul through the grace apparatus for perception. Doctrine is the reality from which hope is continuously derived (Hebrews 11:1).

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Five
text: 3. The plan of God in time is organized around six imputations in three radicals. The X radical contains the imputation of human life and the imputation of Adam's original sin, establishing the first potential of salvation. The Y radical contains the judicial imputations of sins to Christ and righteousness to the believer, establishing the second potential of maturity blessing. The Z radical contains the imputation of eternal life and of blessing in time, establishing the third potential of reward at the judgment seat. Each potential becomes a hope through doctrine, and each hope is replaced by reality through imputation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Five
text: 4. Salvation is accomplished entirely by the work of God and received through non-meritorious faith. No personal sins of the human race were imputed to any member of that race for condemnation; condemnation rests on the imputation of Adam's original sin. All personal sins were collected and imputed to Christ at the cross. The justice of God judged them there. Nothing can be added to that work. Salvation is received by believing in Christ — in the privacy of the soul, without ceremony, without moral reformation, without public display.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Five
text: 5. Common grace is the ministry of the Holy Spirit that converts gospel potential into hope one. Because the unbeliever lacks a human spirit, he cannot process spiritual information. The Holy Spirit acts as a surrogate human spirit — common grace — making the gospel cognitively real in the right lobe of the unbeliever's soul. Once hope one is established, the issue of volition is engaged: positive volition expressed as faith in Christ is made effectual by efficacious grace, producing the reality of eternal salvation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Five
text: 6. Hope two is the operational confidence of every advancing believer between salvation and the maturity barrier. It rests on the imputation of divine righteousness at salvation, which establishes both the honor code of the royal family and the receptor base for future blessing. The believer who consistently takes in Bible doctrine has absolute assurance that the justice of God will impute blessing when doctrinal capacity reaches maturity. This confidence — not religious performance or Christian service activity — is the motivation for the execution of the protocol plan.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Five
text: 7. Logistical grace sustains the believer through every stage prior to the maturity barrier. Whatever God provides between salvation and cracking the maturity barrier — material comfort or hardship, health or adversity — is logistical support calculated to sustain the believer in the daily function of doctrine intake. It is not the covenant blessing of the sixth imputation. The blessing of the sixth imputation is reserved for the moment of maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Five
text: 8. Blessing in time is the basis and guarantee of blessing in eternity. The argument from the greater to the less applies: if the justice of God provides the greater blessing at the maturity barrier in time, the same justice will provide the lesser blessing of eternal reward at the judgment seat of Christ. Blessing is parlayed from time into eternity. The believer who accumulates zero in time through reversionism or neglect of doctrine will parlay zero into eternity; the believer who cracks the maturity barrier will parlay that blessing into eternal reward.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Five
text: 9. The justice of God is the exclusive point of reference for all divine blessing. God's love, sovereignty, and omnipotence do not directly dispense blessing to the believer. All blessing flows through the justice of God, which imputes to the divine righteousness resident in the soul on the basis of doctrinal capacity. Human merit, religious works, and Christian service activity cannot intrude on this pipeline. The adjustment to the justice of God — at salvation, through rebound, and at maturity — is the single mechanism through which all blessing is received.

section: Glossary
text: ελπίς elpis — hope, confident expectation

section: Glossary
text: The standard New Testament word for hope. Never denotes guesswork, uncertainty, or mere desire. Always designates absolute confidence grounded in knowledge — specifically, in doctrine resident in the soul. In the equation of the plan of God, elpis is the operative confidence that a divinely established potential will be fulfilled through imputation.

section: Glossary
text: dikaiosynē

section: Glossary
text: δικαιοσύνη dikaiosynē — righteousness

section: Glossary
text: In the context of the plan of God, the divine righteousness (plus R) imputed to the believer at the moment of salvation. This imputed righteousness serves as the receptor base for divine blessing: because of the principle of affinity, the justice of God can impute blessing directly to the divine righteousness resident in the believer. It is also the foundation of the royal family honor code and the basis for the command to love the brethren.

section: Glossary
text: Common Grace

section: Glossary
text: The ministry of the Holy Spirit by which the gospel is made cognitively real in the right lobe of the unbeliever's soul. Because the unbeliever lacks a human spirit, he cannot process spiritual information independently. The Holy Spirit acts as a surrogate human spirit during gospel presentation, enabling the unbeliever to understand the issue of faith in Christ. Common grace converts the first potential of salvation into hope one.

section: Glossary
text: Efficacious Grace

section: Glossary
text: The ministry of the Holy Spirit by which the act of faith in Christ is made effectual for regeneration. When the unbeliever responds to common grace with positive volition — believing in Christ — efficacious grace brings that faith to its intended result: eternal salvation. Hope one is replaced by the reality of justification.

section: Glossary
text: GAP

section: Glossary
text: Grace Apparatus for Perception

section: Glossary
text: The Spirit-enabled process by which Bible doctrine is received in the left lobe of the soul (the staging area), transferred by the Holy Spirit into the right lobe, and stored in the frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary storage, and norms-and-standards center. GAP is the mechanism by which doctrine converts a spiritual potential into an operational hope.

section: Glossary
text: Logistical Grace

section: Glossary
text: God's provision of everything necessary for the physical existence and sustained function of the believer between salvation and the maturity barrier. Logistical grace includes food, shelter, clothing, health, transportation, and all other resources required to sustain the believer in the daily intake of doctrine. It is distinct from the covenant blessing of the sixth imputation, which is reserved for the moment of maturity adjustment.

section: Glossary
text: Maturity Barrier

section: Glossary
text: The threshold of spiritual maturity that is cracked through sustained, consistent intake of Bible doctrine over time. Cracking the maturity barrier triggers the sixth imputation: the justice of God imputes divine blessing in six categories to the divine righteousness resident in the mature believer. It is the transition from logistical grace support into the supergrace stage of the plan of God.

section: Glossary
text: Supergrace / Ultra-Supergrace

section: Glossary
text: The stages of spiritual maturity following the cracking of the maturity barrier. Supergrace A designates the initial stage of maturity blessing; supergrace B a more advanced stage; ultra-supergrace the highest stage of spiritual maturity attainable in the Church Age. Each stage involves progressive reception of divine blessing through the continued imputation of the justice of God.

section: Glossary
text: Rebound

section: Glossary
text: The instantaneous restoration of fellowship with God accomplished by naming known sins to God the Father (1 John 1:9). Rebound is the repeated adjustment available to the believer whenever personal sin disrupts fellowship. It is distinct from salvation adjustment (which is once for all) and from maturity adjustment (which is progressive). The compassions of God that 'never fail' (Lamentations 3:22) provide the basis for rebound throughout the believer's advance toward maturity.
Chapter Three Hundred Sixty-Six

section: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: The Three Hopes in the Equation of the Good
text: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: The Three Hopes in the Equation of the Good

section: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: The Three Hopes in the Equation of the Good
text: Romans 12:12 “Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.” (ESV)

section: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: The Three Hopes in the Equation of the Good
text: Corrected translation: With reference to the hope, be rejoicing; with reference to tribulation, be patient; with reference to prayer, be persevering.

section: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: The Three Hopes in the Equation of the Good
text: Romans 12:12 stands within Paul's extended paraenesis on the transformed life of the believer who has been adjusted to the justice of God. This chapter continues the exposition of verse 12, focusing specifically on the phrase 'with reference to the hope, be rejoicing.' In order to exegete that phrase with precision, it is necessary to set forth the full doctrine of hope as it appears throughout the New Testament. The present chapter covers points seven through nine of that doctrine, treating the three hopes in the equation of the good — the equation X + Y + Z = the good (

section: Romans 12:12 — The Doctrine of Hope: The Three Hopes in the Equation of the Good
text: agathos) — as they relate to the three categories of divine imputation and the believer's confident anticipation of blessing at each stage of the Protocol Plan of God.

section: I. Review of the Equation of the Good
text: I. Review of the Equation of the Good

section: I. Review of the Equation of the Good
text: The equation of the good organizes the entire soteriological and sanctification program of the justice of God around three radicals: X, Y, and Z. Each radical contains a set of imputations, the pertinent doctrine required to convert potential into confident anticipation, and a point of reality at which hope is replaced by actual reception of the promised blessing.

section: I. Review of the Equation of the Good
text: X radical: Imputation of human life + imputation of Adam's original sin = the first potential (condemnation, requiring salvation) + pertinent doctrine (the gospel) = the first hope + the point of reality (faith in Christ).

section: I. Review of the Equation of the Good
text: Y radical: Judicial imputation 1 (all personal sins imputed to Christ on the cross) + judicial imputation 2 (divine righteousness imputed at salvation) = the second potential (blessing in time at the maturity barrier) + pertinent doctrine = the second hope + the point of reality (cracking the maturity barrier).

section: I. Review of the Equation of the Good
text: Z radical: Imputation of eternal life at salvation + imputation of blessing in time at maturity = the third potential (reward and blessing at the judgment seat of Christ) + pertinent doctrine + undeserved suffering = the third hope. X + Y + Z = agathos, the good — the seventh imputation, which glorifies God forever.

section: I. Review of the Equation of the Good
text: The fundamental principle operating throughout the equation is that the justice of God can only bless the righteousness of God. Divine justice is the origin of every blessing; divine righteousness, imputed to the believer at salvation, is the recipient of every blessing. Because the blessing flows from justice to righteousness — not from justice to any human merit, works, or morality — there is no compromise of the divine essence. This is grace in its highest conceptual form.

section: II. The Integrity of God and the Exclusion of Human Merit
text: II. The Integrity of God and the Exclusion of Human Merit

section: II. The Integrity of God and the Exclusion of Human Merit
text: The integrity of God is composed of two inseparable attributes: divine righteousness and divine justice. Righteousness is the principle of divine integrity; justice is the function of divine integrity. What righteousness demands, justice executes. Righteousness demands perfect righteousness; justice demands perfect justice. No attribute of the divine essence is ever compromised, which is the basis of God's immutability: God cannot be anything less than God.

section: II. The Integrity of God and the Exclusion of Human Merit
text: This structure has a decisive practical implication: no human activity of any kind — prayer, witnessing, missionary service, tithing, self-sacrifice, administration in a local church, or any other form of Christian service — constitutes a basis for receiving blessing from God. Blessing flows exclusively from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. Human works of any description are categorically excluded from the channel through which divine blessing travels.

section: II. The Integrity of God and the Exclusion of Human Merit
text: The believer's dual identity as royal priest and royal ambassador clarifies the issue further. As a royal ambassador, the believer gives blessing to others through the expression of spiritual gifts and the execution of commands related to the Great Commission. As a royal priest with maximum doctrine resident in the soul, the believer receives blessing. These two functions must not be confused. No amount of ambassadorial activity — however faithfully executed, however spiritually motivated — transfers into the priestly channel through which divine blessing is imparted. The source remains the justice of God; the recipient remains the righteousness of God; the prerequisite remains the cracking of the maturity barrier through sustained intake of Bible doctrine.

section: II. The Integrity of God and the Exclusion of Human Merit
text: This excludes as well the informal convention by which believers pronounce blessing on one another. No human being has the standing to call down divine blessing on another person by declaration. The pastor-teacher's function is to explain the mechanism by which God blesses — that is, to set forth the conditions under which the justice of God imputes blessing to the righteousness of God — not to pronounce that blessing by verbal formula.

section: III. Point Seven — The First Hope in the Equation (X Radical)
text: III. Point Seven — The First Hope in the Equation (X Radical)

section: III. Point Seven — The First Hope in the Equation (X Radical)
text: The first hope is the confident anticipation that precedes the moment of salvation. Every human being is born under the double imputation of human life and Adam's original sin. This creates the first potential: condemnation, and therefore the need for salvation. The pertinent doctrine is the gospel — the message that God the Son took all personal sins to the cross, that they were judged in him, and that eternal life is received by faith alone in Christ alone. The first hope is the non-meritorious confidence that when one believes in Christ, eternal life is received immediately and permanently. The point of reality — faith in Christ — replaces the anticipation with the fact, and the believer moves to the Y radical.

section: IV. Point Eight — The Second Hope in the Equation (Y Radical)
text: IV. Point Eight — The Second Hope in the Equation (Y Radical)

section: IV. Point Eight — The Second Hope in the Equation (Y Radical)
text: The second hope is the confident anticipation of blessing in time through cracking the maturity barrier. Two judicial imputations form the structural basis of this radical: first, the imputation of all personal sins to Christ on the cross at the moment of his substitutionary death; second, the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at the moment of salvation. Together these two imputations create the second potential: as long as the believer lives, there is the possibility of cracking the maturity barrier and receiving great blessing in time from the justice of God — the sixth imputation. With the intake of pertinent doctrine, that potential becomes the second hope: confident anticipation that continued doctrine intake will bring the believer to the maturity barrier and into the category of temporal blessing.

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: Lamentations 3:21–25 “But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness. 'The LORD is my portion,' says my soul, 'therefore I will hope in him.' The LORD is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him.” (ESV)

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: Corrected translation: This I recall to mind, therefore I have hope. The great grace functions never cease — that is logistical grace. His compassion never fails — the provision of logistical grace. They are new every morning. The LORD is my portion, says my soul, therefore I have hope in him. The LORD is good to those who trust in him, to the soul who seeks him — positive volition toward Bible doctrine, perpetuated.

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: The second hope in Lamentations 3 is the anticipation of great blessing in time after cracking the maturity barrier. The passage acknowledges logistical grace as the sustaining provision during the interval between salvation and maturity, while directing the soul's confident expectation toward the greater blessing that awaits at the point of maturity.

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: 2 Corinthians 10:15 “We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others, but our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged.” (ESV)

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: Corrected translation: Not boasting beyond our measure in other men's labors — that is, not receiving blessing by association with someone who has cracked the maturity barrier — but with the hope, that is, confident anticipation, that as your doctrine increases, we shall be within our sphere enlarged even more by you.

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: The second hope here is the confident anticipation that sustained doctrine intake will issue in the cracking of the maturity barrier and the receipt of great blessing as a real imputation from the justice of God.

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: Galatians 5:5 “For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness.” (ESV)

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: Corrected translation: For we through the Spirit by faith are waiting for the hope of righteousness.

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: The phrase 'hope of righteousness' expresses the second hope: the confident anticipation of the fulfillment of the purpose for which divine righteousness was imputed at salvation. Divine righteousness imputed at salvation is incomplete — that is, unfulfilled — until the justice of God can impute the six categories of temporal blessing to it. This fulfillment occurs when the believer cracks the maturity barrier through maximum doctrine resident in the soul. The principle is irreversible: the justice of God can only bless the righteousness of God. Nothing less than that righteousness — no human performance of any kind — qualifies as the recipient.

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: Romans 5:17 “For if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.” (ESV)

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: Corrected translation: For if by the transgression of the one, Adam's original sin, spiritual death ruled through that one — and it does — much more, they who receive in life this surplus from grace and the gift of righteousness shall reign through the one, Jesus Christ.

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: The surplus of grace received in life is the sixth imputation — the six categories of temporal blessing imputed to the believer at the point of maturity. The gift of righteousness is the prerequisite: the imputation of divine righteousness at salvation is the basis without which no surplus of grace could ever be received. Romans 5:17 contains both the second and the third hope: the surplus of grace in life corresponds to the second hope; the reign through Jesus Christ corresponds to the third hope. The lesser-to-greater argument underlies both: if the justice of God provides the greater at maturity — temporal blessing — it follows necessarily that the justice of God will provide the less in eternity — eternal blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ.

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: Matthew 6:33 “But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.” (ESV)

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: Corrected translation: But seek first the kingdom and his imputed righteousness, and all these things — X plus Y plus Z — shall be provided for you.

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: Romans 5:1 “Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” (ESV)

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: Corrected translation: Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace — prosperity — face to face with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.

section: Supporting Passages for the Second Hope
text: Justification — the judicial recognition of imputed divine righteousness — necessarily precedes all blessing from the justice of God. This is not a sequential accident but a structural necessity: there can be no imputation of blessing to anything less than the righteousness of God.

section: V. Point Nine — The Third Hope in the Equation (Z Radical)
text: V. Point Nine — The Third Hope in the Equation (Z Radical)

section: V. Point Nine — The Third Hope in the Equation (Z Radical)
text: The third hope is the confident anticipation of the mature believer regarding great blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ. Two imputations provide the basis: the imputation of eternal life at salvation, which assures the believer of existence in the presence of God forever; and the imputation of blessing in time at maturity, which functions as the guarantee of greater blessing in eternity. Together these equal the third potential: the prospect of receiving, at the judgment seat of Christ following the rapture, the seventh imputation — the full weight of eternal reward and blessing in the resurrection body. With the addition of pertinent doctrine and undeserved suffering — the latter necessary to maintain perspective during a period of temporal prosperity — the potential becomes the third hope.

section: V. Point Nine — The Third Hope in the Equation (Z Radical)
text: The third hope is the dominant hope of the mature believer. It is related specifically to what occurs in eternity: the seventh imputation, which is a real imputation. All real imputations have two factors in view here — blessing and reward in eternity, and the resurrection body — and there is antecedence or affinity between eternal blessing and the resurrection body as the recipient. The third hope is thus inseparable from the doctrine of bodily resurrection.

section: V. Point Nine — The Third Hope in the Equation (Z Radical)
text: The lesser-to-greater argument continues to apply. If the justice of God provides the greater at maturity — the sixth imputation, blessing in time — it follows necessarily that the justice of God will provide the less at the judgment seat of Christ — the seventh imputation, blessing in eternity. Time blessing and eternity blessing are related as the greater to the lesser in this argument, because time blessing requires the ongoing sustenance of the old sin nature and all the friction of human existence, whereas eternity blessing, received in a resurrection body free from the old sin nature, is unencumbered.

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope
text: Paul's statement before the Sanhedrin was accurate in the deepest theological sense. He was on trial for the third hope: his confident anticipation of the resurrection, which would be the vehicle for the imputation of eternal blessing at the judgment seat of Christ. The same statement recurs at Acts 24:15 and Acts 26:6.

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope
text: Ephesians 1:18–19 “Having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints, and what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might.” (ESV)

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope

The third hope — the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints — is the confident anticipation of eternal reward at the judgment seat of Christ. Once temporal blessing is received by the mature believer, it functions as the guarantee of greater eternal blessing: the sixth imputation is the earnest of the seventh.

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope
text: Philippians 1:20–21 “It is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be at all ashamed, but that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” (ESV)

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope
text: Christ is exalted by the believer's life when the justice of God imputes temporal blessing to the righteousness of God at the point of maturity. Christ is exalted by the believer's death when those temporal blessings are paralleled into eternal blessings imputed to the resurrection body at the judgment seat of Christ. The gain of dying, for the mature believer, is not the cessation of hardship but the transition into a state of greater and permanent blessing.

text: The blessed hope of Titus 2:13 is the third hope specifically: the mature believer's confident anticipation of great reward and blessing in eternity, tied to the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ. It is the mature believer who has this hope with confidence, because the sixth imputation already received in time is the guarantee and the pattern of the seventh imputation to be received in eternity.

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope
text: Hebrews 6:18–20 “So that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us. text: Corrected translation: In order that by two immutable things — God's oath and God's promise from the integrity of God — in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have strong encouragement, strong hope, who have fled for refuge in doctrine, for the purpose of attaining the hope set before us. section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope
text: The anchor metaphor from Hebrews 6 captures the function of the third hope with precision. In ancient navigation, an anchor secured the vessel against storm, current, and drift. The third hope functions as exactly such an anchor for the mature believer moving through the unpredictable seas of time: absolute security, located not in the circumstances of life but in the Holy of Holies in heaven, where the high priest after the order of Melchizedek has already entered as the forerunner. The third hope is not wishful thinking; it is theological certainty grounded in the integrity of God — his immutable oath and promise — and secured by the completed work of the great High Priest.

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope
text: 1 Peter 1:3 “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! According to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.” (ESV)

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope
text: Corrected translation: Blessed be the God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has caused us to be born again — the time of the imputation of divine righteousness — to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope
text: The living hope of 1 Peter 1:3 is the third hope. It is called living because it is grounded in the bodily resurrection of Christ: because Christ has a resurrection body, the believer has the certain prospect of receiving a resurrection body as well, which is the basis for the imputation of eternal blessing and reward. The resurrection of Christ is the guarantee of the believer's resurrection, and the believer's resurrection is the prerequisite for the seventh imputation.

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope
text: 1 Peter 1:13 “Therefore, preparing your minds for action, and being sober-minded, set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.” (ESV)

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope
text: The grace being brought at the revelation of Jesus Christ is the seventh imputation: great blessing imputed at the judgment seat of Christ following the rapture. For the mature believer who has already cracked the maturity barrier and received the sixth imputation in time, this grace is not hypothetical. It is the certain extension of a pattern already established by the justice of God.

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope
text: 1 Peter 1:21 “Who through him are believers in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope are in God.” (ESV)

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope

section: Supporting Passages for the Third Hope
