Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Three

section: Romans 13:1 — Laws of Divine Establishment: Divine Institutions Three and Four
text: Romans 13:1 — Laws of Divine Establishment: Divine Institutions Three and Four

section: Romans 13:1 — Laws of Divine Establishment: Divine Institutions Three and Four
text: Romans 13:1 “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God.” (ESV)

section: Romans 13:1 — Laws of Divine Establishment: Divine Institutions Three and Four
text: Corrected translation: Let every soul be in subordination to superior authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those which exist have been appointed by God.

section: Romans 13:1 — Laws of Divine Establishment: Divine Institutions Three and Four
text: Romans 13 is one of the most concentrated expressions of the laws of divine establishment in all of Scripture. Before the exegesis of the chapter itself can proceed, the theological framework that undergirds it must be established. This chapter continues a point-by-point study of the divine establishment laws that provide the context for Paul's instruction regarding civil authority. The present chapter covers divine institution number three (the family) and divine institution number four (the nation), both of which are essential to understanding why Paul commands subordination to governing authorities.

section: I. The Plan of God: Three Stages
text: I. The Plan of God: Three Stages

section: I. The Plan of God: Three Stages
text: The plan of God for the human race operates in three stages, each with its own confidence and hope that leads to action. These stages are represented schematically as X, Y, and Z.

section: Stage One: The X Radical — Physical Birth and the First Potential
text: Stage One: The X Radical — Physical Birth and the First Potential

section: Stage One: The X Radical — Physical Birth and the First Potential
text: The X radical encompasses the imputation of human life at the moment of birth combined with the imputation of Adam's original sin. These two simultaneous imputations produce the condition in which every human being enters the world: possessing true human life yet standing condemned. Human life is imputed by the justice of God to its divinely prepared home, the human soul. Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. This is the sole basis for the condemnation of the human race. Personal sins, by contrast, are never imputed to the individual for condemnation — they were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged there.

section: Stage One: The X Radical — Physical Birth and the First Potential
text: From this condition of condemnation the justice of God is able to provide great blessing. The first potential arising from the X radical is the potential of salvation. The first hope is the absolute assurance that the moment one believes in Jesus Christ, eternal life is received. Within the X radical the laws of divine establishment begin to operate, making possible the existence of human freedom within the framework of authority and under the protection of privacy. The first plus — the transition to Stage Two — is salvation adjustment to the justice of God through personal faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

section: Stage Two: The Y Radical — Judicial Imputation and the Second Potential
text: Stage Two: The Y Radical — Judicial Imputation and the Second Potential

section: Stage Two: The Y Radical — Judicial Imputation and the Second Potential
text: The Y radical contains two judicial imputations. First, the imputation of all personal sins to Jesus Christ on the cross — the saving work of Christ. Second, the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at the moment of salvation. The possession of God's righteousness creates the basis for the next stage: righteousness demands righteousness; justice demands justice; what righteousness demands, justice executes. The divine righteousness resident in the believer becomes the target for the imputation of divine blessing, which glorifies God forever.

section: Stage Two: The Y Radical — Judicial Imputation and the Second Potential
text: The second potential is the potential of the imputation of divine blessing in time as the means of glorifying the Lord Jesus Christ. The second hope is absolute confidence that when enough doctrine has been received to crack the maturity barrier, the sixth imputation of divine blessing — in six categories — will be received as the tactical victory in the angelic conflict. The second plus is maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Within the Y radical the operative standard rises from establishment law to the Royal Family Honor Code, which adds to but does not set aside establishment.

section: Stage Three: The Z Radical — Ultra-Supergrace and the Third Potential
text: Stage Three: The Z Radical — Ultra-Supergrace and the Third Potential

section: Stage Three: The Z Radical — Ultra-Supergrace and the Third Potential
text: The Z radical is the final stage of the Christian life on earth, the zone in which the mature believer operates. The imputation of eternal life and salvation combined with the imputation of blessings in time at the point of maturity produces the third potential: great blessing and reward in eternity. The third hope is absolute confidence of reward at the judgment seat of Christ. The third stage includes undeserved suffering designed to maintain eternal perspective.

section: Stage Three: The Z Radical — Ultra-Supergrace and the Third Potential
text: The formula X plus Y plus Z equals the plan of God — the good of Romans 8:28. All things work together for the purpose of the good because the plan proceeds in three ordered stages, each with its confidence, its hope, and its required action.

section: II. The Royal Family Honor Code
text: II. The Royal Family Honor Code

section: II. The Royal Family Honor Code
text: Once a person believes in the Lord Jesus Christ and enters the Y radical, the operative standard expands from establishment law alone to include the Royal Family Honor Code. The believer operates under two identities simultaneously.

section: II. The Royal Family Honor Code
text: First, as a royal ambassador, the believer represents the Lord Jesus Christ on the earth. Production — witnessing, giving, prayer, service under one's spiritual gift — flows from this identity. However, no production, no sacrifice, no function under a spiritual gift produces blessing from God. Blessing does not come through works, personality, morality, asceticism, or any form of self-sacrifice.

section: II. The Royal Family Honor Code
text: Second, as a royal priest, the believer approaches God directly. All blessing comes from doctrine resident in the soul, accumulated through the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). Doctrine provides capacity for blessing. When maximum doctrine has been received in the soul, blessing begins to flow in the six categories of the sixth imputation. The combination of establishment law and the Royal Family Honor Code produces the historical impact of freedom for any nation.

section: III. Divine Institution Three: The Family
text: III. Divine Institution Three: The Family

section: III. Divine Institution Three: The Family
text: The third divine institution is the family. Its function is to bridge the gap between the helplessness of physical birth and the responsibilities of adult life under the laws of establishment.

section: A. Physical Birth and the Dual Imputation
text: A. Physical Birth and the Dual Imputation

section: A. Physical Birth and the Dual Imputation
text: Physical birth and the simultaneous imputation of human life and Adam's original sin leaves the infant both helpless and condemned. Human life is not present in the womb; it is imputed by the justice of God at birth to the human soul. Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. All personal sins accumulate but are never imputed to the individual for condemnation — they were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged. This is why Christ is the issue in salvation and why the Scripture declares, 'Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and thou shalt be saved.'

section: B. Parental Authority as the Basis for Life Preparation
text: B. Parental Authority as the Basis for Life Preparation

section: B. Parental Authority as the Basis for Life Preparation
text: God has provided parents to protect, care for, nourish, provide for, train, and discipline children in order to prepare them for life. Parental authority is therefore the basis for preparing children for a normal life. Permissiveness destroys this preparation. Recognition of authority and orientation to the principles of life must be inculcated in the home; they cannot be deferred to any educational system. Parents hold the right and privilege of this inculcation.

section: C. The Content of Authority Training
text: C. The Content of Authority Training

section: C. The Content of Authority Training
text: The highest expression of parental love is discipline administered in order to instill character. Children must be trained to respect the privacy of others, to respect property, to respect the rights of others, and to understand and operate within the framework of freedom without abusing it. Authority training — distinct from and higher than mere behavioral conditioning — equips children with objectivity, respect for law and order, and a well-founded patriotism that includes willingness to defend national freedoms against external enemies.

section: C. The Content of Authority Training
text: In addition to establishment training, Christian parents bear a spiritual responsibility. They are to evangelize their children and provide pre-doctrinal training, as taught in Deuteronomy 6:6–9 and Deuteronomy 7–9. It is the responsibility of parents to instill respect for the Word of God and for the teaching authority of the pastor-teacher (Hebrews 13:7, 17). Whatever personal reservations a parent may hold about a given pastor, these are not to be communicated to children, who require an unobstructed orientation to authority in order to be functional in life.

section: IV. Divine Institution Four: The Nation
text: IV. Divine Institution Four: The Nation

section: IV. Divine Institution Four: The Nation
text: The fourth divine institution is the nation. It exists because, prior to the millennium, the entire human race cannot be brought under one rule without self-destruction. Internationalism in any form — civic, political, or religious — is therefore prohibited for this stage of history. Every human being possesses an old sin nature; the division of humanity into distinct national entities is the divine safeguard that perpetuates history until its logical conclusion.

section: A. The Origin of Nations
text: A. The Origin of Nations

section: A. The Origin of Nations
text: The divine judgment of the original internationalist project — the Tower of Babel recorded in Genesis 11 — divided the human race into distinct nations. The original definition of national entities was based on racial, geographical, and linguistic norms. The pertinent Scripture references authorizing nations while prohibiting international superstructures include Genesis 10:5, Deuteronomy 32:8, and Acts 17:26–28.

section: B. The Myth of Racial Purity
text: B. The Myth of Racial Purity

section: B. The Myth of Racial Purity
text: As history progressed, true racial distinctions were obliterated in the rise of civilization. Racial purity is a myth in any historically developed national entity. The populations of Western Europe illustrate this clearly: the English are a mixture of Teutonic, Celtic, Scandinavian, and other peoples; the French, whose very name derives from the Frankish Teutonic peoples, are largely of Teutonic origin despite cultural assumptions to the contrary; the Spanish show Celtic, Teutonic (Visigothic and Ostrogothic), and Iberian strands; the Italians reflect the passage of virtually every major civilization through the peninsula over two millennia. Racial ideology used as a basis for political power, as in the case of National Socialism in Germany, is a myth employed as political expediency.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Nations that follow the norms and standards of divine establishment exhibit the following characteristics. There is no such thing as a Christian nation — there are Christians within nations — but nations can align themselves with establishment norms and thereby function as client nations of God.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: First, interior protection of freedom through an honorable system of law enforcement and jurisprudence. The principle of law enforcement is essential to the preservation of individual freedom and privacy. A corrupt individual within a law enforcement institution does not invalidate the institution any more than a dishonest employee invalidates the corporation employing him. The response to corruption is prosecution and removal — not abolition of the institution.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: The inherited jurisprudential tradition of Western nations — drawing on principles from the Mosaic law, Roman law, and Anglo-Saxon common law — includes the prohibition of double jeopardy, the presumption of innocence, and the exclusion of hearsay testimony as the sole basis for conviction. These are not merely legal conventions but reflections of biblical standards of justice.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Second, exterior protection of freedom through an honorable military establishment. All freedom that any national entity has ever possessed was secured through military victory. The military functions as the exterior protection of national freedom in the same way that law enforcement functions as the interior protection. Both are among the oldest and most honorable of human institutions.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Third, a government of whatever constitutional form — monarchy, oligarchy, or republic — that protects the freedoms and rights of its citizens without abusing its power to destroy those freedoms. The United States was constituted as a republic, not a democracy. Democracy, which is governed by the opinion of the numerical majority, is incompatible with the standards of divine establishment. Christianity can function under virtually any form of government except pure democracy, because what the majority of people think at any given moment is of no consequence as a standard of truth or justice. Democracy is proximate to anarchy; no democracy in history has long survived without degenerating toward it.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Fourth, an economy based on free enterprise and capitalism. Under this standard, the investor and management hold the sole right to formulate business policy within a company or corporation. Neither central government, labor organizations, nor criminal enterprises have the right to superimpose policy on private business. Sound management invariably takes care of its own productive members; the imposition of external control destroys both productivity and the self-respect of those who participate in the system.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Fifth, a system of common law that prohibits criminal action and thereby protects the freedom, rights, life, and property of individuals. Critically, law must not be distorted into an instrument for solving social problems. Law is designed to restrain criminal action. Legislation that coerces private associations, invades individual rights, or redistributes personal property under the name of the common good exceeds the proper function of law and becomes an instrument of oppression.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Sixth, a common culture that reflects the spiritual life, morality, corporate spirit, nobility, integrity, and patriotism of the nation. A nation's culture is the outward expression of the interior values of its people.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Seventh, a government administration that exercises its power without abusing it to destroy freedom — a system of mutual authority that encourages freedom rather than restrains it, maintains an honorable military on a realistic basis, enforces law and order without the destruction of human freedom, and administers taxation, law enforcement, and jurisprudence within its proper scope.

section: V. Establishment and Evangelism
text: V. Establishment and Evangelism

section: V. Establishment and Evangelism
text: The laws of divine establishment are not ends in themselves. They are designed to protect human freedom for the purpose of genuine evangelism. Where positive volition toward the gospel exists in a population, establishment provides the framework within which that volition can be freely exercised. Where negative volition exists, establishment provides protection from coercion.

section: V. Establishment and Evangelism
text: The individual citizen must be free to accept or reject Christ as Savior without interference. Evangelism that uses public pressure — requiring people to raise their hands, walk forward in a crowd, or make a public declaration — violates both human privacy and the principle of non-meritorious faith. The merit in salvation lies entirely with the object, the Lord Jesus Christ, not with any action of the one believing. True faith is an act of the will in the privacy of the soul.

section: V. Establishment and Evangelism
text: The state must neither coerce acceptance of Christ nor punish rejection of Him. No church has the authority to persecute those who reject Christ as Savior. The state must never adopt an official religion supported by public taxation; all religious bodies must be free from taxation and free from state support equally. The separation of church and state is therefore not an anti-religious principle but a foundational establishment principle protecting the very freedom that makes genuine evangelism possible.

section: V. Establishment and Evangelism
text: The alternative is visible in the historical record of regions where a state church held coercive power. The dominance of a state church destroys religious freedom; the resulting resentment and reaction leave populations unable to conceptualize an alternative other than the opposite extreme. The doctrine of John 3:36 frames the issue with absolute clarity: 'He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life; he that believeth not the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God abideth on him.' The choice is binary and entirely private. Establishment exists to ensure that choice is genuinely free.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Three
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Three

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Three
text: 1. The plan of God operates in three sequential stages. Stage One (X radical) establishes the human condition at physical birth and the potential of salvation. Stage Two (Y radical) encompasses the judicial imputations of salvation and the believer's advance toward maturity. Stage Three (Z radical) is the supergrace life with its eternal rewards. Each stage carries its own hope — its own absolute confidence — that generates appropriate action.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Three
text: 2. All blessing from God flows from the justice of God to the righteousness of God. Justice and righteousness together constitute divine integrity. The justice of God is the pipeline through which all blessing is dispensed. No blessing comes through works, personality, morality, or sacrifice. Blessing comes through doctrine resident in the soul, which provides capacity for the divine blessing that justice imputes to righteousness.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Three
text: 3. The family is the third divine institution, designed to bridge helplessness at birth and responsibility in adult life. Parental authority is the essential mechanism of this bridge. Authority training — instilling respect for the privacy of others, for property, for law and order, and for legitimate government — must begin in the home. It cannot be deferred. Christian parents bear an additional responsibility to evangelize their children and to model respect for the teaching authority of the Word of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Three
text: 4. The nation is the fourth divine institution, designed to protect human freedom. The division of humanity into distinct national entities at Babel was a divine judgment against internationalism and a protective design for the perpetuation of history. Internationalism in any form — political, civic, or religious — is outside the authorization of divine establishment for this stage of history.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Three
text: 5. Racial ideology has no foundation in the historical record. As civilization developed, racial distinctions were obliterated through migration, conquest, and intermarriage. The populations of every historically developed nation are composites. Racial purity is a myth; its use as political ideology is a form of expediency that has no support from the Word of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Three
text: 6. Nations aligned with divine establishment exhibit seven identifiable characteristics. These are: interior protection of freedom through honorable law enforcement and jurisprudence; exterior protection through an honorable military; a government that protects rather than destroys freedom; a free-enterprise economy; a system of common law that restrains crime without exceeding its proper function; a national culture reflecting integrity and patriotism; and a government administration that exercises authority within its proper limits.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Three
text: 7. Law must not be weaponized as an instrument for solving social problems. The proper function of law is to restrain criminal action and protect the freedom, rights, life, and property of individuals. Legislation that invades private associations, coerces private economic decisions, or redistributes personal property under the claim of advancing the common good exceeds the proper scope of law and becomes a form of oppression.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Three
text: 8. Democracy is incompatible with the standards of divine establishment. A republic — a government of enumerated powers and constitutional limits — is compatible with Scripture. Democracy, governed by numerical majority opinion, is not. Majority opinion carries no authority as a standard of truth or justice. Every democracy in history has tended toward anarchy without the restraining structure of constitutional government.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Three
text: 9. The laws of divine establishment exist to protect the freedom that makes genuine evangelism possible. Where people are free — free to accept Christ, free to reject Him, free from coercion in either direction — the gospel can be heard and believed in the privacy of the soul. Evangelism that depends on public pressure or crowd psychology violates both human privacy and the principle of non-meritorious faith. The state must neither coerce religious belief nor punish religious choice. Separation of church and state is a biblical establishment principle, not an anti-religious one.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Three
text: 10. The separation of church and state protects the integrity of both institutions. A state religion always destroys human freedom. Where a church holds coercive state power, it destroys the very freedom of conscience that genuine faith requires. History demonstrates that populations long subjected to coercive state religion become unable to conceive of genuine religious freedom and are therefore susceptible to the opposite extreme. Establishment law, properly applied, prevents this outcome.

section: Glossary
text: The threshold of spiritual maturity reached through sustained intake of Bible doctrine over time. Cracking the maturity barrier triggers the sixth imputation — the imputation of divine blessing in six categories as the tactical victory in the angelic conflict.

text: A national entity that aligns itself with the norms and standards of divine establishment, thereby receiving divine blessing and serving as a base for evangelism and the communication of Bible doctrine. section: Glossary

section: Glossary
text: The higher standard of conduct operative in the Y and Z radicals of the plan of God. It adds to but does not set aside the laws of divine establishment. section: Glossary
text: Imputation

section: Glossary
text: The divine act of crediting something to someone's account. Seven key imputations structure the plan of God: (1) human life to the soul at birth; (2) Adam's original sin to the old sin nature; (3) personal sins to Christ on the cross; (4) divine righteousness to the believer at salvation; (5) eternal life to the believer at salvation; (6) divine blessing to the believer at maturity; (7) rewards and blessings at the judgment seat of Christ.

section: Glossary
text: Old sin nature (OSN)

section: Glossary
text: The sin capacity inherited at physical birth through the male genetic line. Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. Personal sins accumulate in the OSN but are not imputed to the individual for condemnation — they were judged in Christ on the cross.

section: Glossary
text: Salvation adjustment

section: Glossary
text: The instantaneous, once-for-all act by which a person is brought into right relationship with the justice of God through personal faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Non-meritorious: the merit resides entirely in the object of faith, not in the act of believing.

section: Glossary
text: Maturity adjustment

section: Glossary
text: The progressive advance of the believer toward spiritual maturity through the daily intake of Bible doctrine via GAP. section: Romans 13:1 — Laws of Divine Establishment: Divine Institutions Three and Four
text: Romans 13:1 — Laws of Divine Establishment: Divine Institutions Three and Four

section: Romans 13:1 — Laws of Divine Establishment: Divine Institutions Three and Four
text: Romans 13:1 “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God.” (ESV)

section: Romans 13:1 — Laws of Divine Establishment: Divine Institutions Three and Four
text: Corrected translation: Let every soul be in subordination to superior authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those which exist have been appointed by God.

section: Romans 13:1 — Laws of Divine Establishment: Divine Institutions Three and Four
text: Romans 13 is one of the most concentrated expressions of the laws of divine establishment in all of Scripture. Before the exegesis of the chapter itself can proceed, the theological framework that undergirds it must be established. This chapter continues a point-by-point study of the divine establishment laws that provide the context for Paul's instruction regarding civil authority. The present chapter covers divine institution number three (the family) and divine institution number four (the nation), both of which are essential to understanding why Paul commands subordination to governing authorities.

section: I. The Plan of God: Three Stages
text: I. The Plan of God: Three Stages

section: I. The Plan of God: Three Stages
text: The plan of God for the human race operates in three stages, each with its own confidence and hope that leads to action. These stages are represented schematically as X, Y, and Z.

section: Stage One: The X Radical — Physical Birth and the First Potential
text: Stage One: The X Radical — Physical Birth and the First Potential

section: Stage One: The X Radical — Physical Birth and the First Potential
text: The X radical encompasses the imputation of human life at the moment of birth combined with the imputation of Adam's original sin. These two simultaneous imputations produce the condition in which every human being enters the world: possessing true human life yet standing condemned. Human life is imputed by the justice of God to its divinely prepared home, the human soul. Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. This is the sole basis for the condemnation of the human race. Personal sins, by contrast, are never imputed to the individual for condemnation — they were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged there.

section: Stage One: The X Radical — Physical Birth and the First Potential
text: From this condition of condemnation the justice of God is able to provide great blessing. The first potential arising from the X radical is the potential of salvation. The first hope is the absolute assurance that the moment one believes in Jesus Christ, eternal life is received. Within the X radical the laws of divine establishment begin to operate, making possible the existence of human freedom within the framework of authority and under the protection of privacy. The first plus — the transition to Stage Two — is salvation adjustment to the justice of God through personal faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

section: Stage Two: The Y Radical — Judicial Imputation and the Second Potential
text: Stage Two: The Y Radical — Judicial Imputation and the Second Potential

section: Stage Two: The Y Radical — Judicial Imputation and the Second Potential
text: The Y radical contains two judicial imputations. First, the imputation of all personal sins to Jesus Christ on the cross — the saving work of Christ. Second, the imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at the moment of salvation. The possession of God's righteousness creates the basis for the next stage: righteousness demands righteousness; justice demands justice; what righteousness demands, justice executes. The divine righteousness resident in the believer becomes the target for the imputation of divine blessing, which glorifies God forever.

section: Stage Two: The Y Radical — Judicial Imputation and the Second Potential
text: The second potential is the potential of the imputation of divine blessing in time as the means of glorifying the Lord Jesus Christ. The second hope is absolute confidence that when enough doctrine has been received to crack the maturity barrier, the sixth imputation of divine blessing — in six categories — will be received as the tactical victory in the angelic conflict. The second plus is maturity adjustment to the justice of God. Within the Y radical the operative standard rises from establishment law to the Royal Family Honor Code, which adds to but does not set aside establishment.

section: Stage Three: The Z Radical — Ultra-Supergrace and the Third Potential
text: Stage Three: The Z Radical — Ultra-Supergrace and the Third Potential

section: Stage Three: The Z Radical — Ultra-Supergrace and the Third Potential
text: The Z radical is the final stage of the Christian life on earth, the zone in which the mature believer operates. The imputation of eternal life and salvation combined with the imputation of blessings in time at the point of maturity produces the third potential: great blessing and reward in eternity. The third hope is absolute confidence of reward at the judgment seat of Christ. The third stage includes undeserved suffering designed to maintain eternal perspective.

section: Stage Three: The Z Radical — Ultra-Supergrace and the Third Potential
text: The formula X plus Y plus Z equals the plan of God — the good of Romans 8:28. All things work together for the purpose of the good because the plan proceeds in three ordered stages, each with its confidence, its hope, and its required action.

section: II. The Royal Family Honor Code
text: II. The Royal Family Honor Code

section: II. The Royal Family Honor Code
text: Once a person believes in the Lord Jesus Christ and enters the Y radical, the operative standard expands from establishment law alone to include the Royal Family Honor Code. The believer operates under two identities simultaneously.

section: II. The Royal Family Honor Code
text: First, as a royal ambassador, the believer represents the Lord Jesus Christ on the earth. Production — witnessing, giving, prayer, service under one's spiritual gift — flows from this identity. However, no production, no sacrifice, no function under a spiritual gift produces blessing from God. Blessing does not come through works, personality, morality, asceticism, or any form of self-sacrifice.

section: II. The Royal Family Honor Code
text: Second, as a royal priest, the believer approaches God directly. All blessing comes from doctrine resident in the soul, accumulated through the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). Doctrine provides capacity for blessing. When maximum doctrine has been received in the soul, blessing begins to flow in the six categories of the sixth imputation. The combination of establishment law and the Royal Family Honor Code produces the historical impact of freedom for any nation.

section: III. Divine Institution Three: The Family
text: III. Divine Institution Three: The Family

section: III. Divine Institution Three: The Family
text: The third divine institution is the family. Its function is to bridge the gap between the helplessness of physical birth and the responsibilities of adult life under the laws of establishment.

section: A. Physical Birth and the Dual Imputation
text: A. Physical Birth and the Dual Imputation

section: A. Physical Birth and the Dual Imputation
text: Physical birth and the simultaneous imputation of human life and Adam's original sin leaves the infant both helpless and condemned. Human life is not present in the womb; it is imputed by the justice of God at birth to the human soul. Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. All personal sins accumulate but are never imputed to the individual for condemnation — they were imputed to Christ on the cross and judged. This is why Christ is the issue in salvation and why the Scripture declares, 'Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and thou shalt be saved.'

section: B. Parental Authority as the Basis for Life Preparation
text: B. Parental Authority as the Basis for Life Preparation

section: B. Parental Authority as the Basis for Life Preparation
text: God has provided parents to protect, care for, nourish, provide for, train, and discipline children in order to prepare them for life. Parental authority is therefore the basis for preparing children for a normal life. Permissiveness destroys this preparation. Recognition of authority and orientation to the principles of life must be inculcated in the home; they cannot be deferred to any educational system. Parents hold the right and privilege of this inculcation.

section: C. The Content of Authority Training
text: C. The Content of Authority Training

section: C. The Content of Authority Training
text: The highest expression of parental love is discipline administered in order to instill character. Children must be trained to respect the privacy of others, to respect property, to respect the rights of others, and to understand and operate within the framework of freedom without abusing it. Authority training — distinct from and higher than mere behavioral conditioning — equips children with objectivity, respect for law and order, and a well-founded patriotism that includes willingness to defend national freedoms against external enemies.

section: C. The Content of Authority Training
text: In addition to establishment training, Christian parents bear a spiritual responsibility. They are to evangelize their children and provide pre-doctrinal training, as taught in Deuteronomy 6:6–9 and Deuteronomy 7–9. It is the responsibility of parents to instill respect for the Word of God and for the teaching authority of the pastor-teacher (Hebrews 13:7, 17). Whatever personal reservations a parent may hold about a given pastor, these are not to be communicated to children, who require an unobstructed orientation to authority in order to be functional in life.

section: IV. Divine Institution Four: The Nation
text: IV. Divine Institution Four: The Nation

section: IV. Divine Institution Four: The Nation
text: The fourth divine institution is the nation. It exists because, prior to the millennium, the entire human race cannot be brought under one rule without self-destruction. Internationalism in any form — civic, political, or religious — is therefore prohibited for this stage of history. Every human being possesses an old sin nature; the division of humanity into distinct national entities is the divine safeguard that perpetuates history until its logical conclusion.

section: A. The Origin of Nations
text: A. The Origin of Nations

section: A. The Origin of Nations
text: The divine judgment of the original internationalist project — the Tower of Babel recorded in Genesis 11 — divided the human race into distinct nations. The original definition of national entities was based on racial, geographical, and linguistic norms. The pertinent Scripture references authorizing nations while prohibiting international superstructures include Genesis 10:5, Deuteronomy 32:8, and Acts 17:26–28.

section: B. The Myth of Racial Purity
text: B. The Myth of Racial Purity

section: B. The Myth of Racial Purity
text: As history progressed, true racial distinctions were obliterated in the rise of civilization. Racial purity is a myth in any historically developed national entity. The populations of Western Europe illustrate this clearly: the English are a mixture of Teutonic, Celtic, Scandinavian, and other peoples; the French, whose very name derives from the Frankish Teutonic peoples, are largely of Teutonic origin despite cultural assumptions to the contrary; the Spanish show Celtic, Teutonic (Visigothic and Ostrogothic), and Iberian strands; the Italians reflect the passage of virtually every major civilization through the peninsula over two millennia. Racial ideology used as a basis for political power, as in the case of National Socialism in Germany, is a myth employed as political expediency.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Nations that follow the norms and standards of divine establishment exhibit the following characteristics. There is no such thing as a Christian nation — there are Christians within nations — but nations can align themselves with establishment norms and thereby function as client nations of God.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: First, interior protection of freedom through an honorable system of law enforcement and jurisprudence. The principle of law enforcement is essential to the preservation of individual freedom and privacy. A corrupt individual within a law enforcement institution does not invalidate the institution any more than a dishonest employee invalidates the corporation employing him. The response to corruption is prosecution and removal — not abolition of the institution.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: The inherited jurisprudential tradition of Western nations — drawing on principles from the Mosaic law, Roman law, and Anglo-Saxon common law — includes the prohibition of double jeopardy, the presumption of innocence, and the exclusion of hearsay testimony as the sole basis for conviction. These are not merely legal conventions but reflections of biblical standards of justice.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Second, exterior protection of freedom through an honorable military establishment. All freedom that any national entity has ever possessed was secured through military victory. The military functions as the exterior protection of national freedom in the same way that law enforcement functions as the interior protection. Both are among the oldest and most honorable of human institutions.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Third, a government of whatever constitutional form — monarchy, oligarchy, or republic — that protects the freedoms and rights of its citizens without abusing its power to destroy those freedoms. The United States was constituted as a republic, not a democracy. Democracy, which is governed by the opinion of the numerical majority, is incompatible with the standards of divine establishment. Christianity can function under virtually any form of government except pure democracy, because what the majority of people think at any given moment is of no consequence as a standard of truth or justice. Democracy is proximate to anarchy; no democracy in history has long survived without degenerating toward it.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Fourth, an economy based on free enterprise and capitalism. Under this standard, the investor and management hold the sole right to formulate business policy within a company or corporation. Neither central government, labor organizations, nor criminal enterprises have the right to superimpose policy on private business. Sound management invariably takes care of its own productive members; the imposition of external control destroys both productivity and the self-respect of those who participate in the system.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Fifth, a system of common law that prohibits criminal action and thereby protects the freedom, rights, life, and property of individuals. Critically, law must not be distorted into an instrument for solving social problems. Law is designed to restrain criminal action. Legislation that coerces private associations, invades individual rights, or redistributes personal property under the name of the common good exceeds the proper function of law and becomes an instrument of oppression.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Sixth, a common culture that reflects the spiritual life, morality, corporate spirit, nobility, integrity, and patriotism of the nation. A nation's culture is the outward expression of the interior values of its people.

section: C. The Standard of a Nation Under Divine Establishment
text: Seventh, a government administration that exercises its power without abusing it to destroy freedom — a system of mutual authority that encourages freedom rather than restrains it, maintains an honorable military on a realistic basis, enforces law and order without the destruction of human freedom, and administers taxation, law enforcement, and jurisprudence within its proper scope.

text: The higher standard of conduct operative in the Y and Z radicals of the plan of God. It adds to but does not set aside the laws of divine establishment. The believer operates under two identities: royal ambassador (representing Christ in the world) and royal priest (approaching God directly through doctrine and prayer).

section: Glossary
text: Imputation

section: Glossary
text: The divine act of crediting something to someone's account. Seven key imputations structure the plan of God: (1) human life to the soul at birth; (2) Adam's original sin to the old sin nature; (3) personal sins to Christ on the cross; (4) divine righteousness to the believer at salvation; (5) eternal life to the believer at salvation; (6) divine blessing to the believer at maturity; (7) rewards and blessings at the judgment seat of Christ.

section: Glossary
text: Old sin nature (OSN)

section: Glossary
text: The sin capacity inherited at physical birth through the male genetic line. Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically formed old sin nature. Personal sins accumulate in the OSN but are not imputed to the individual for condemnation — they were judged in Christ on the cross.

section: Glossary
text: Salvation adjustment

section: Glossary
text: The instantaneous, once-for-all act by which a person is brought into right relationship with the justice of God through personal faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Non-meritorious: the merit resides entirely in the object of faith, not in the act of believing.

section: Glossary
text: Maturity adjustment

section: Glossary
text: The progressive advance of the believer toward spiritual maturity through the daily intake of Bible doctrine via GAP. Culminates in cracking the maturity barrier and receiving the sixth imputation of divine blessing. Represents the second major adjustment to the justice of God in the plan of God.

section: Romans 13:1 — Introduction Continued: Divine Establishment, Human Freedom, and the Decalogue

text: Romans 13:1 “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God.” (ESV)

section: Romans 13:1 — Introduction Continued: Divine Establishment, Human Freedom, and the Decalogue
text: Corrected translation: Every soul must subordinate himself to superior authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and the existing authorities have been established by God.

section: Romans 13:1 — Introduction Continued: Divine Establishment, Human Freedom, and the Decalogue
text: Chapter thirteen of Romans has not yet received its verse-by-verse exegesis. The preceding sessions have been devoted to introducing the chapter through a systematic exposition of the doctrine of divine establishment. The present chapter continues that introduction, treating establishment and human freedom (points eight through eleven) and the relationship of the Decalogue to the laws of divine establishment (point nine). These doctrinal foundations govern the proper understanding of the believer's obligation to governmental authority in Romans 13:1–7.

section: I. Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Point 8: Establishment and Human Freedom
text: I. Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Point 8: Establishment and Human Freedom

section: I. Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Point 8: Establishment and Human Freedom
text: Freedom is not a political abstraction but a theological reality grounded in the act of creation. When God prepared a human soul and imputed life to it, the capacity for freedom was simultaneously established. The soul's constituent functions — volition, mentality, emotion, conscience, and self-consciousness — are the faculties through which freedom is exercised. Freedom therefore exists as an extension of those functions.

section: I. Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Point 8: Establishment and Human Freedom
text: Freedom operates in two distinct areas. The first is an extension of the imputation of human life at birth, which is the domain of the laws of divine establishment and applies to all people regardless of spiritual status. The second is an extension of the imputation of God's righteousness at salvation, which belongs to the believer alone and is governed by the principles of Bible doctrine and the royal family honor code. The laws of divine establishment protect the first area; the principles of the honor code develop the second.

section: I. Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Point 8: Establishment and Human Freedom
text: Because man was created to resolve the angelic conflict, human freedom is an extension of that conflict into history. The laws of divine establishment are therefore designed to protect freedom so that evangelism and spiritual advance can occur in every generation. These laws protect the privacy, property, freedom, and individual volition of all people. The Decalogue — the Ten Commandments — is an integral part of this protective framework.

section: Biblical Witness to Human Freedom
text: Biblical Witness to Human Freedom

section: Biblical Witness to Human Freedom
text: Several key passages define the scope of freedom under divine establishment. Galatians 5:1 declares: "In the sphere of freedom Christ has freed us; stand firm therefore and stop being enmeshed by the yoke of slavery" — the slavery in view being not physical bondage but enslavement to legalism and to the evil system. John 8:32 anticipates the royal family honor code: knowledge of doctrine produces freedom. Romans 8:21 speaks of a future freedom, the freedom of glory belonging to the children of God. 2 Corinthians 3:17 locates spiritual freedom in the present ministry of the Holy Spirit: "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." Psalm 119:45 connects freedom to positive volition toward doctrine: "I will walk in freedom, for I seek Your doctrines" — the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) requires freedom in which to operate.

section: Establishment Freedom Distinguished from Spiritual Freedom
text: Establishment Freedom Distinguished from Spiritual Freedom

section: Establishment Freedom Distinguished from Spiritual Freedom
text: The spiritual freedom belonging to the believer must be carefully distinguished from establishment freedom, which is the heritage of all people within a national entity. Establishment freedom applies to believer and unbeliever alike. Its existence and perpetuation demand two things: respect for establishment authority, and a shared understanding of the legal and constitutional framework within which that authority operates. A national entity that fails to maintain this shared framework undermines the very freedom it was designed to protect.

section: Establishment Freedom Distinguished from Spiritual Freedom
text: The existence and perpetuation of freedom also demand self-discipline and self-sacrifice — not only when freedom is externally threatened, but when it is not internally understood. Military victory is one means by which national freedom and the laws of divine establishment are maintained. Under those laws, freedom demands responsibility from both believer and unbeliever alike. However, in Romans 13:1–7, the passage under examination, the responsibility for freedom under establishment principles is addressed specifically to the believer. The royal family honor code requires the Church Age believer to render to government the things that are government's and to God the things that are God's — including compliance with the nation's laws and, when necessary, its defense.

section: II. Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Point 9: Establishment and the Decalogue
text: II. Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Point 9: Establishment and the Decalogue

section: II. Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Point 9: Establishment and the Decalogue
text: The Decalogue, or Ten Commandments, is filed primarily in Exodus 20:1–17. In the Hebrew text these commandments are introduced by the imperfect tense used as an imperative — the force of a categorical prohibition or mandate. The Decalogue does not have as its primary subject the cataloguing of sins. Its subject is human freedom. It just so happens that certain sins constitute attacks upon freedom, and at those points the two subjects converge. Essentially the Ten Commandments define human freedom in terms of three relationships: attitude toward God, attitude toward people, and attitude toward property.

section: The First Commandment — Exodus 20:3
text: The First Commandment — Exodus 20:3

section: The First Commandment — Exodus 20:3
text: "You shall have no other gods before Me." While this commandment obviously prohibits idolatry, its scope is considerably wider. At the level of divine establishment, it constitutes a national recognition that Jesus Christ controls history. A client nation that acknowledges this reality aligns itself with the source of its protection and blessing. A nation that abandons this recognition removes itself from the framework of divine blessing that sustains national freedom.

section: The Second Commandment — Exodus 20:4–6
text: The Second Commandment — Exodus 20:4–6

section: The Second Commandment — Exodus 20:4–6
text: The second commandment prohibits overt idolatry, defined in Scripture as contact with the demonic (Zechariah 10:2; 1 Corinthians 10:19–21). The distinction between the first and second commandments is the distinction between mental idolatry — substituting any person, system, or ideology for the recognition of God — and overt idolatry, the active practice of demon-influenced religion. Mental idolatry destroys individual freedom; overt idolatry destroys a nation, as demonstrated in the prophetic record (Isaiah 28; Isaiah 36:18–20; Isaiah 37:12–19; Jeremiah 3:6–11; Ezekiel 6:4–6).

section: The Third Commandment — Exodus 20:7
text: The Third Commandment — Exodus 20:7

section: The Third Commandment — Exodus 20:7
text: "You shall not use the name of the Lord your God for shav'" — the Hebrew term (שָׁוְא) means evil, worthlessness, or vanity. The commandment prohibits invoking the name of God as a cover for deception, false testimony, perjury, or manipulation. It is commonly misunderstood as referring only to profanity. While using God's name as a mere expletive does violate this commandment, the primary referent is the use of God's name to sponsor a lie — calling God as witness to a falsehood, or invoking divine authority to coerce a decision. God's name is properly used in worship, prayer, praise, thanksgiving, and doctrinal communication. It is not to be used as a front for theft, manipulation, or coercion.

section: The Fourth Commandment — Exodus 20:8–11
text: The Fourth Commandment — Exodus 20:8–11

section: The Fourth Commandment — Exodus 20:8–11
text: The Sabbath commandment relates human volition to time and establishes an economic principle under the laws of divine establishment: those who work must have adequate rest. The Sabbath mandates a full day of cessation from labor. This was a radical innovation in the ancient world, where no concept of a regular day off existed. The physiological and psychological necessity of a twenty-four-hour rest period was not understood; the Mosaic law mandated it as a matter of divine establishment. The man who has no rest becomes a slave to his labor and loses the capacity to exercise personal freedom. The Sabbath also carries a theological dimension: resting from work is a picture of grace — of receiving benefit without personal exertion — and was designed to point Israel to the grace of God. The faith-rest application of the Sabbath principle, treated elsewhere in the epistle, is distinct from this establishment function.

section: The Fifth Commandment — Exodus 20:12
text: The Fifth Commandment — Exodus 20:12

section: The Fifth Commandment — Exodus 20:12
text: "Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be prolonged in the land which the Lord your God gives you." This commandment establishes the principle that orientation to authority is the foundational pattern for all of life. The parents are the first authority encountered by the individual, and the child's response to parental authority determines the pattern of response to all subsequent authority structures. Orientation to legitimate authority is the basis for long life, stability, and national blessing. Resistance to authority, by contrast, produces a short, unstable, and ultimately destructive existence.

section: The Sixth Commandment — Exodus 20:13
text: The Sixth Commandment — Exodus 20:13

section: The Sixth Commandment — Exodus 20:13
text: "You shall not murder" — the corrected translation. The Hebrew term is רצח (ratsach), which denotes unlawful killing, not killing as such. Killing is divinely authorized in two contexts: the execution of capital punishment under the law, and the killing of enemy combatants in military service on behalf of one's national entity. Both are compatible with divine policy and the laws of divine establishment.

section: The Sixth Commandment — Exodus 20:13
text: Murder, by contrast, is both a sin and the most fundamental violation of human freedom. When a person is murdered, every remaining opportunity to exercise freedom is permanently foreclosed. The divine prohibition of murder therefore protects the most basic condition of all other freedoms: the right to remain alive. God alone holds the prerogative over the timing of human death. Intrusion upon that prerogative through murder is simultaneously a sin, a violation of establishment law, and a presumption upon divine sovereignty. Of the seven most destructive sins identified in Proverbs 6:16–19, only one is an overt act: murder. The remaining six are attitudinal or verbal. This underscores that murder is the singular overt crime at the apex of anti-establishment behavior.

section: The Seventh Commandment — Exodus 20:14
text: The Seventh Commandment — Exodus 20:14

section: The Seventh Commandment — Exodus 20:14
text: "You shall not commit adultery." Adultery, like murder, is simultaneously a sin and an attack on human freedom. It specifically violates the freedom of the right man–right woman relationship — the divinely designed pairing that provides the highest expression of category two love. The seventh commandment is addressed primarily to the man, consistent with the ancient world's recognition that the husband is the guardian of the marriage bond. Adultery distorts and destroys the capacity for genuine love, substituting predatory exploitation for the covenant relationship. The woman as right woman belongs to one right man; she is not the property of multiple partners. The commandment thus protects the institution of marriage as the structural unit in which category two love is properly expressed and sustained.

section: The Eighth Commandment — Exodus 20:15
text: The Eighth Commandment — Exodus 20:15

section: The Eighth Commandment — Exodus 20:15
text: "You shall not steal." The eighth commandment establishes the right of private property under the laws of divine establishment and demands that government protect both the lives and the possessions of those within a national entity. Stealing is simultaneously a sin, a crime, and a fundamental disorientation to life. It represents the failure to recognize that what belongs to another person is categorically off-limits, regardless of circumstances. The believer who has absorbed doctrine into the soul can walk past any object belonging to another person — however valuable — without the slightest impulse to appropriate it. This orientation is not merely a function of legal compliance but of settled respect for the establishment principle that property is an extension of freedom.

section: The Eighth Commandment — Exodus 20:15
text: The eighth commandment also has a macroeconomic application. Confiscatory taxation beyond the scriptural ceiling of ten percent constitutes governmental theft. When a government systematically appropriates legitimate profits and private wealth under ideological cover, it violates the same establishment principle the commandment was designed to protect. The socialist premise that wealth should be redistributed for the greater good is a direct violation of the eighth commandment at the national level.

section: The Ninth Commandment — Exodus 20:16
text: The Ninth Commandment — Exodus 20:16

section: The Ninth Commandment — Exodus 20:16
text: "You shall not answer as a false witness against your neighbor." The ninth commandment protects human freedom through the objectivity of the legal process. The judicial system cannot function without truthful testimony; hearsay and perjury, when admitted as evidence, transform the courtroom from an instrument of justice into an instrument of oppression. The same principle extends beyond the courtroom: gossip and maligning — spreading falsehoods about another person outside a legal context — are verbal violations of this establishment principle. Verbal sins are always sinful, but this verbal sin is additionally anti-establishment because it undermines the social fabric of trust upon which freedom depends. The standard of live-and-let-live cannot be maintained in a society where false testimony — legal or social — goes unchecked.

section: The Tenth Commandment — Exodus 20:17
text: The Tenth Commandment — Exodus 20:17

section: The Tenth Commandment — Exodus 20:17
text: "You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's." The tenth commandment demands restraint of the lust pattern of the old sin nature under the principle of live-and-let-live. Significantly, this commandment was the instrument through which the Apostle Paul came to recognize the true nature of the old sin nature, as he recounts in Romans 7:7: "I would not have known sin except through the law, for I would not have known about coveting if the law had not said, 'You shall not covet.'" Covetousness — epithymia (ἐπιθυμία) — is the craving for what belongs to another, whether property, position, relationships, or status. It is the internal disposition that, if unchecked, drives theft, adultery, and murder. The tenth commandment therefore strikes at the root of all anti-establishment behavior by demanding restraint at the level of desire itself.

section: III. Summary: The Decalogue as the Framework of Human Freedom
text: III. Summary: The Decalogue as the Framework of Human Freedom

section: III. Summary: The Decalogue as the Framework of Human Freedom
text: The Ten Commandments, taken together, constitute a coherent framework for the protection of human freedom across three domains: the relationship between the individual and God (commandments one through four), the relationship between individuals (commandments five through seven and nine through ten), and the relationship of the individual to property (commandments eight and ten). This framework is not confined to Israel under the Mosaic covenant. The underlying establishment principles — that God governs history, that life must be protected, that property is sacred, that testimony must be truthful, that desire must be disciplined — are universal and apply to every national entity in every age.

section: III. Summary: The Decalogue as the Framework of Human Freedom
text: For the Church Age believer, these establishment principles are integrated into the royal family honor code. Compliance with them is not optional moralism but a component of the believer's responsibility within the Protocol Plan of God. Romans 13:1–7 will demonstrate that the specific application of these principles to the believer's relationship with governing authorities flows directly from this foundation. The exegesis of the passage itself will begin in the following session.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five
text: 1. Freedom is grounded in creation, not in political theory. When God imputed human life to the soul, He simultaneously established the capacity for freedom. The soul's functions — volition, mentality, conscience, emotion, self-consciousness — are the faculties through which freedom is exercised. Freedom is therefore a theological datum before it is a political one.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five
text: 2. Freedom operates in two areas governed by different principles. Establishment freedom, grounded in the imputation of human life at birth, belongs to all people and is protected by the laws of divine establishment. Spiritual freedom, grounded in the imputation of God's righteousness at salvation, belongs to the believer alone and is developed through the principles of Bible doctrine and the royal family honor code.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five
text: 3. The Decalogue defines human freedom, not primarily human sin. The Ten Commandments are a comprehensive framework for the protection of freedom across three relational domains: the individual's relationship to God, to other persons, and to property. Where sin is also addressed, it is because certain sins constitute attacks upon freedom.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five
text: 4. The first commandment requires national recognition that Jesus Christ controls history. Idolatry — whether mental (substituting any ideology or person for God) or overt (demon-influenced religion) — destroys the theological basis for national survival. The prophetic record uniformly demonstrates that idolatry leads to national collapse.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five
text: 5. God's name is properly used only in worship, prayer, praise, and doctrinal communication. Using God's name as a cover for lying, manipulation, or coercion violates the third commandment. The most egregious form of this violation is invoking divine authority to compel a decision or sponsor a falsehood.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five
text: 6. The Sabbath establishes an economic principle: those who labor must have adequate rest. A full day of rest is not merely a religious observance but an establishment requirement. The person who has no rest becomes enslaved to his labor and loses the capacity to exercise freedom in other domains of life.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five
text: 7. Murder is the singular overt act at the apex of anti-establishment behavior. Of the seven most destructive sins, only murder is an overt act. It permanently forecloses every remaining freedom of the victim and constitutes a presumption upon the divine prerogative over the timing of death. Military killing and capital punishment are divinely authorized and are not violations of the sixth commandment.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five
text: 8. The right to private property is a divine establishment principle. The eighth commandment demands that government protect private property and prohibits confiscation under any ideological cover. Covetousness — the internal lust for another's possessions — is addressed by the tenth commandment, which strikes at the root of theft, adultery, and social disorder by demanding restraint at the level of desire.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five
text: 9. Truthful testimony is an establishment requirement, not merely a moral preference. The ninth commandment demands objectivity in the legal process by prohibiting false witness. The same principle governs social discourse: gossip and maligning are anti-establishment violations that destroy the trust upon which freedom depends.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Five
text: 10. The believer's obligation to authority structures is not optional. The royal family honor code requires the Church Age believer to recognize and submit to legitimate authority — governmental, parental, legal — as part of the Protocol Plan of God. Romans 13:1–7 applies this foundational establishment doctrine directly to the believer's relationship with governing authorities. The verse-by-verse exegesis of that passage will proceed in the following session.

section: Romans 13:1 — Christian Responsibility to Government; Divine Establishment and Governing Authorities
text: Romans 13:1 — Christian Responsibility to Government; Divine Establishment and Governing Authorities

section: Romans 13:1 — Christian Responsibility to Government; Divine Establishment and Governing Authorities
text: Romans 13:1 “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God.” (ESV)

section: Romans 13:1 — Christian Responsibility to Government; Divine Establishment and Governing Authorities
text: Corrected translation: All human beings, be subordinating yourselves to governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and the existing authorities have been appointed by God.

section: Romans 13:1 — Christian Responsibility to Government; Divine Establishment and Governing Authorities
text: Romans 13 opens the fourth major block of practical doctrine in the epistle. Having established the doctrinal framework of adjustment to the justice of God through chapters 1–11, and having called for the believer's presentation to God as a living sacrifice in 12:1–2, Paul now addresses a triad of civic responsibilities: to government (13:1–7), to others in the human race (13:8–10), and to oneself as a member of the royal family of God (13:11–14). Chapter 386 covers the concluding section of the Doctrine of Divine Establishment as developed across this lecture series, specifically the principle of morality under establishment, and then opens the exegesis of 13:1 with the foundational command of subordination to governing authorities.

section: I. The Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Morality (Points 10–13)
text: I. The Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Morality (Points 10–13)

section: I. The Doctrine of Divine Establishment — Morality (Points 10–13)
text: The Ten Commandments, surveyed in previous sessions, define morality in terms of divine establishment. This section completes the doctrinal framework with points on the nature, scope, and limits of morality before moving to the exegesis of Romans 13:1.

section: Point 10 — Morality Defined within Establishment
text: Point 10 — Morality Defined within Establishment

section: Point 10 — Morality Defined within Establishment
text: Morality is right conduct and excellence in the practice and function of the laws of divine establishment. It is the observation of those laws. Because the laws of divine establishment govern the entire human race — not the Church alone — morality is commanded of believer and unbeliever alike. Sin in any of its forms constitutes an attack on establishment; morality is the ordered response and antidote to that attack.

section: Point 10 — Morality Defined within Establishment
text: Several implications follow directly. First, morality is not Christianity. Whatever is commanded of the unbeliever is not the Christian way of life as such, since the unbeliever cannot fulfill the specifically Christian requirements. Second, morality is not the monopoly of Christianity. Any member of the human race who understands and complies with the standards of divine establishment can function morally — without the filling of the Holy Spirit, without the intake of Bible doctrine, and without a personal relationship with the Lord Jesus Christ. Third, the equation of morality with Christianity is a category error that produces a false standard: the notion that keeping a simplified moral code constitutes the Christian way of life or qualifies one for eternal salvation.

section: Point 11 — The Christian Way of Life Exceeds Morality
text: Point 11 — The Christian Way of Life Exceeds Morality

section: Point 11 — The Christian Way of Life Exceeds Morality
text: The Christian way of life is not morality. It consists of the following:

section: Point 11 — The Christian Way of Life Exceeds Morality
text: (a) The filling of the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 5:18). (b) Maximum Bible doctrine resident in the soul through the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). (c) Positive volition toward doctrine. (d) Maturity adjustment to the justice of God. (e) Functioning under the royal family honor code. (f) Advancing through the maturity barrier to supergrace and ultra-supergrace.

section: Point 11 — The Christian Way of Life Exceeds Morality
text: None of these elements can be accomplished by the unbeliever. The unbeliever is commanded morality; the believer is commanded morality and infinitely more. Morality is the floor, not the ceiling, of the Christian life. To mistake the floor for the ceiling is reversionism.

section: Point 12 — Morality Protects Freedom but Does Not Produce Salvation
text: Point 12 — Morality Protects Freedom but Does Not Produce Salvation

section: Point 12 — Morality Protects Freedom but Does Not Produce Salvation
text: Morality, as an establishment factor, protects human freedom. It does not provide eternal salvation. This distinction is explicitly established in the following passages: Romans 3:20; Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16; Titus 3:5. Morality cannot produce the filling of the Spirit, cannot learn doctrine, and cannot advance the believer to maturity. These are the exclusive province of the Christian way of life.

section: Point 13 — Morality Provides the Environment for the Function of Christianity
text: Point 13 — Morality Provides the Environment for the Function of Christianity

section: Point 13 — Morality Provides the Environment for the Function of Christianity
text: Morality can and does protect human freedom. Believers are protected by the moral fabric of the society in which they live. A morally ordered society provides the environment of freedom required for evangelism, for Bible teaching, and for the correct function of the local church. Immorality, by contrast, produces anarchy — the collapse of authority — and in that collapse the conditions necessary for the believer's spiritual advance are destroyed.

section: Point 13 — Morality Provides the Environment for the Function of Christianity
text: Christian dynamics therefore includes morality but at the same time exceeds morality. Morality is the environment in which Christianity can function; Christianity is not morality. The mature believer is neither anti-establishment nor immoral. Compliance with establishment doctrines and authority is a morality function; compliance with the royal family honor code is a distinctively Christian function. Both are required. Neither replaces the other.

section: Point 13 — Morality Provides the Environment for the Function of Christianity
text: The privatization of industry, the destruction of property rights, and the suppression of human freedom — characteristic of every form of collectivist statism — are concrete expressions of immorality in the establishment sense. Socialism in all its forms is anti-establishment and therefore immoral, because it denies the individual the product of his own labor and substitutes coercive redistribution for freely exercised right to property. The distinction between property rights and human rights is false: all rights are human rights, and property rights are among the most ancient and essential of them.

section: II. Christian Responsibility to Establishment — Three Governing Texts
text: II. Christian Responsibility to Establishment — Three Governing Texts

section: II. Christian Responsibility to Establishment — Three Governing Texts
text: Three passages define the Christian's civic obligations under divine establishment:

section: II. Christian Responsibility to Establishment — Three Governing Texts
text: Matthew 22:21: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." Our Lord here delineates two sets of standards, both designed by God: the laws of divine establishment (civic responsibility) and the royal family honor code (responsibility to God). They are not in conflict; they are complementary obligations operating at different levels.

section: II. Christian Responsibility to Establishment — Three Governing Texts
text: 1 Timothy 2:1–2: Paul directs prayer on behalf of kings and all in authority, "in order that we may lead undisturbed and tranquil lives in all godliness." Tranquil civic life is the precondition for the assembly of believers to receive doctrine. Godliness here refers to spiritual maturity and integrity — the function of the royal family honor code under the daily intake of doctrine.

section: II. Christian Responsibility to Establishment — Three Governing Texts
text: 1 Peter 2:13–14: "Subordinate yourselves for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether to a king as one in authority or to a governor sent by him for the punishment of those who do evil or the recognition of those who do good." The basis of submission is not the personal character of the ruler but the Lord's own sanction of human government as a divine institution.

text: III. Outline of Romans 13

text: Romans 13 develops Christian responsibility along three axes:

section: III. Outline of Romans 13
text: Paragraph 1 (vv. 1–7): Christian responsibility to government.

section: III. Outline of Romans 13
