section: Romans 13:1–2 — Divine Establishment, Delegated Authority, and the Ordinance of God
text: Romans 13 stands as Paul's definitive treatment of divine establishment — the framework of divinely delegated authority by which God sustains the freedom necessary for evangelism and for spiritual advance. Chapter 389 examines the opening two verses of that chapter, with particular attention to verse 2: the two Greek verbs of opposition, antitassō and anthistēmi, and the dative of disadvantage that closes the verse. The exegesis is grounded in the broader structure of the Protocol Plan of God, within which establishment authority is the indispensable bracket enabling both salvation adjustment and maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

section: I. The Protocol Plan of God and the Necessity of Establishment
text: I. The Protocol Plan of God and the Necessity of Establishment

section: I. The Protocol Plan of God and the Necessity of Establishment
text: The plan of God may be expressed as three successive brackets — the X, Y, and Z radicals — each containing specific divine imputations and their corresponding doctrinal content, and each yielding an absolute hope.

section: A. The X Bracket: Salvation Adjustment
text: A. The X Bracket: Salvation Adjustment

section: A. The X Bracket: Salvation Adjustment
text: The first bracket begins with the imputation of human life at birth. Simultaneously, Adam's original sin is imputed to the genetically prepared old sin nature, producing total condemnation and therefore the potentiality of salvation. The pertinent doctrine is the gospel. The result is the first hope: absolute confidence that faith in Christ produces eternal life. Salvation adjustment to the justice of God by faith in Jesus Christ closes this bracket.

section: A. The X Bracket: Salvation Adjustment
text: The laws of divine establishment operate across the entire X bracket. Without the freedom, privacy, and ordered authority that establishment provides, no individual reaches the point of hearing and responding to the gospel. Establishment is therefore not ancillary to the plan of God — it is constitutive of the conditions under which that plan operates in history.

section: B. The Y Bracket: Maturity Adjustment
text: B. The Y Bracket: Maturity Adjustment

section: B. The Y Bracket: Maturity Adjustment
text: The second bracket begins with two judicial imputations: all personal sins imputed to Christ on the cross and judged, and divine righteousness imputed at salvation. The second judicial imputation is the axis of the entire epistle. The pertinent doctrine covers the mechanism of maturity adjustment. The result is the second hope: absolute confidence that daily intake of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) will crack the maturity barrier and produce great blessing from the justice of God in time, to the glory of Christ.

section: B. The Y Bracket: Maturity Adjustment
text: To advance from salvation to maturity — which is the objective of phase two — the laws of divine establishment are again indispensable. Freedom enables the believer to attend the teaching of the Word of God. Privacy of the priesthood enables objective reception of that teaching without social pressure or embarrassment. Authority structures sustain the stable environment in which doctrine can be consistently communicated and received.

section: C. The Z Bracket: Eternal Blessing
text: C. The Z Bracket: Eternal Blessing

section: C. The Z Bracket: Eternal Blessing
text: The third bracket contains the imputation of eternal life and the imputation of blessing in time, yielding the third hope: absolute confidence that at the judgment seat of Christ, following the rapture, the mature believer will receive great reward and blessing in a resurrection body — the ultimate glorification of the Lord Jesus Christ. This is the good of Romans 8:28. All things — X, Y, and Z — work together for this good.

section: C. The Z Bracket: Eternal Blessing
text: None of these three brackets is accessible without establishment. This is why Paul inserts Romans 13 at this precise structural location: without the establishment framework, there is no orientation to life, no protection of the freedom necessary for evangelism, and no sustained environment for doctrinal advance. Establishment doctrine is shared with believer and unbeliever alike; it operates across the entire human race as the precondition for the plan of God working itself out in history.

section: II. Romans 13:1 — The Vocative Address and Delegated Authority
text: II. Romans 13:1 — The Vocative Address and Delegated Authority

section: A. 'All Human Beings' — The Scope of the Address
text: A. 'All Human Beings' — The Scope of the Address

section: A. 'All Human Beings' — The Scope of the Address
text: The address is universal. It encompasses every member of the human race, defined theologically as those to whom God has imputed human life at birth. Human life is not present at any stage before birth — not in the blastocyst, not in the embryo, not in the fetus. Human life is imputed by the justice of God to the divinely prepared soul at the moment of physical birth. Simultaneously, Adam's original sin is imputed to the old sin nature, which is genetically transmitted through the male line. The result is life and spiritual death simultaneously — a condition that constitutes the basis for salvation, because total condemnation is the prerequisite for the imputation of all personal sins to Christ on the cross.

section: A. 'All Human Beings' — The Scope of the Address
text: This simultaneous imputation also establishes the principle of automatic salvation for those who die before reaching accountability — infants, young children, and those with severely diminished mental capacity. Condemnation occurred at the instant of life; but because that condemnation is entirely the result of Adam's one sin, and not of personal sins, all such persons are covered by the judicial imputation of Christ's work on the cross and proceed automatically to heaven.

section: B. 'Support Nature's Selves to Governing Authorities'
text: B. 'Support Nature's Selves to Governing Authorities'

section: B. 'Support Nature's Selves to Governing Authorities'
text: The imperative of verse 1 addresses the entire human race without exception. The governing authorities to which submission is required are those that operate under the legitimate scope of divine establishment. That scope is precisely defined: government exists to defend the lives and property of all citizens equally, to protect willing exchange and restrain unwilling exchange, to penalize fraud and predatory conduct, to invoke common justice under written law, and to maintain the records incidental to those functions. The legitimate purpose of government is to codify and inhibit all destructive actions while leaving all creative productivity free — including charity, security, and prosperity pursued voluntarily and privately.

section: C. 'No Authority Except Delegated by God'
text: C. 'No Authority Except Delegated by God'

section: C. 'No Authority Except Delegated by God'
text: The grounding clause declares that no authority exists except as delegated by God. Those governing authorities that do exist have been established by divine delegation. The principle carries a significant corollary: only those governmental functions that fall within the scope of legitimate establishment authority bear this divine sanction. Socialism — the governmental assumption of functions that belong to individuals, families, and voluntary associations — does not qualify. It is not a form of delegated authority; it is a usurpation of the domain that divine establishment assigns to the individual.

section: C. 'No Authority Except Delegated by God'
text: The human right to life, liberty, and property is not derived from the state but from the Creator. This is among the fundamental principles that the laws of divine establishment declare in this passage. The limited state exists not to grant these rights but to defend them. The larger the state grows beyond that defense function, the more it destroys the very rights it was ordained to protect.

section: III. Romans 13:2 — Two Verbs of Opposition
text: III. Romans 13:2 — Two Verbs of Opposition

section: A. The Inferential Conjunction
text: A. The Inferential Conjunction

section: A. The Inferential Conjunction
text: Verse 2 opens with the conjunction hōste (ὥστε), introducing an independent clause with an inferential force: therefore, in view of everything established in verse 1. The inference moves from the divine origin of all legitimate authority to the consequences of opposing it.

section: B. The First Verb: antitassō
text: B. The First Verb: antitassō

section: B. The First Verb: antitassō
text: The articular present active participle of antitassō (ἀντιτάσσω) governs the first clause. The verb is a military term: to form a battle line against the opposition. It carries the connotation of organized, deliberate resistance — the product of a soul that has ordered its thinking in opposition to delegated authority.

section: B. The First Verb: antitassō
text: The present tense is a descriptive-customary present, denoting habitual action characteristic of the reversionistic believer. The active voice emphasizes the deliberate decision-making of the agent. The middle voice participle that follows shifts the emphasis to the agent's participation in the outcome of that action.

section: B. The First Verb: antitassō
text: The scope of antitassō extends across the entire range of delegated authority: opposition to law enforcement, refusal of military service, non-payment of taxes, failure to fulfill civic duties, and sustained insubordination toward legitimate workplace authority. Any pattern of soul-organized rejection of establishment structures falls under this term.

section: B. The First Verb: antitassō
text: The theological diagnosis is important: the soul of the reversionistic believer has been filled with content that reverses its orientation toward life. When the soul's frame of reference, memory center, vocabulary, categorical storage, and conscience are saturated with anti-establishment thinking, every evaluative faculty produces inverted conclusions. Self-consciousness relates the individual to government and society through distorted categories. Emotion is trained to respond positively to anti-establishment appeals. Volition is persistently negative toward the structures God has ordained. The result is organized, soul-level opposition — which is precisely what antitassō denotes.

section: C. The Second Verb: anthistēmi
text: C. The Second Verb: anthistēmi

section: C. The Second Verb: anthistēmi
text: The perfect active indicative of anthistēmi (ἀνθίστημι) follows. The consummate perfect tense emphasizes completed action with abiding results: not merely a single act of rejection, but a consummated process of opposition whose consequences are now in effect. The perfect distinguishes this from a momentary lapse; it describes a settled state reached by a completed trajectory.

section: C. The Second Verb: anthistēmi
text: The distinction between the two verbs is deliberately maintained by the Holy Spirit. Had the same word of opposition been intended, one verb would have sufficed. The two verbs are differentiated as cause and effect within the same act of rebellion: antitassō is the organized soul-decision in opposition to authority; anthistēmi is the application — the outward, visible, and completed expression of that inward opposition. Wrong thinking produces wrong application with logical consistency. You cannot have wrong thinking and right application; if the premise is inverted, the conclusion is inverted as well.

section: C. The Second Verb: anthistēmi
text: The corrected translation of verse 2a therefore renders the two verbs distinctly: those who resist [antitassō] the authority have opposed [anthistēmi] the ordinance of God.

section: D. The Dative of Disadvantage: diatagē
text: D. The Dative of Disadvantage: diatagē

section: D. The Dative of Disadvantage: diatagē
text: The noun diatagē (διαταγή) appears in the dative singular. It means divine institution, ordinance. The possessive genitive theou (θεοῦ) identifies it specifically as the ordinance of God — the laws of divine establishment as God's authorized system of authority for the human race. The dative here functions both as indirect object and as dative of disadvantage: those who oppose the ordinance do so to their own detriment and to the detriment of the society in which they live.

section: D. The Dative of Disadvantage: diatagē
text: The believer who opposes establishment ordinances is not simply making a political mistake. He is placing himself in direct opposition to the divine institution by which God sustains the freedom necessary for evangelism, for doctrinal advance, and for the completion of the angelic conflict. He is undermining the very structure on which his own salvation and spiritual growth depend.

section: IV. The Separation of Church and State
text: IV. The Separation of Church and State

section: IV. The Separation of Church and State
text: Verse 2's reference to the ordinance of God raises the permanent question of the proper relationship between civic authority and spiritual authority. Romans 13 demands a clear and consistent separation.

section: IV. The Separation of Church and State
text: The authority of the state rests on the laws of divine establishment. The authority of the church rests on the royal family honor code and the spiritual gifts sovereignly bestowed by God the Holy Spirit at salvation. These two lines of authority must never be mingled. Christian duty toward the church is summarized by the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception. Christian duty toward the state is summarized by obedience to civil authority, including military service when required. Civic power is designed for collective temporal peace and prosperity; spiritual power is designed for individual peace and prosperity.

section: IV. The Separation of Church and State
text: Obedience to civil authority — including the payment of taxes — protects the law-abiding citizen from loss of freedom to enemies within and without. Tax revenues properly belong to law enforcement, military establishment, and the maintenance of limited government — not to socialist redistribution or the welfare state. When the executive governs according to the Constitution and according to the laws of divine establishment simultaneously, he is a double blessing to the nation. When he governs according to principles of statism and reversionism simultaneously, he is a double curse.

section: V. The Believer as Paladin of Establishment
text: V. The Believer as Paladin of Establishment

section: V. The Believer as Paladin of Establishment
text: The term paladin — historically, a warrior-champion of the Frankish imperial household under Charlemagne, later adapted as a title for the military governors of Byzantine provincial themes — captures the posture that every doctrinally informed believer should maintain toward the laws of divine establishment. The believer is to be an active champion and bulwark of these principles, not a passive bystander.

section: V. The Believer as Paladin of Establishment
text: This means that doctrinal advance and political orientation move together. The believer with doctrine resident in the soul consistently recognizes establishment authority, defends the individual's right to freedom, privacy, and property, and resists every legislative, judicial, or executive action that expands the state beyond its authorized scope. This is not a political preference; it is the natural outflow of Bible doctrine in the soul.

section: V. The Believer as Paladin of Establishment
text: Conversely, the sincere believer who operates without doctrine in the soul cannot distinguish between establishment principles and their inversion. Sincerity without doctrine produces the enemy of establishment, not its champion, because the soul's evaluative faculties are functioning on emotion rather than on the categorical content of divine truth. Sincerity is not a Christian virtue. Knowledge of doctrine is the Christian virtue. A sincere believer minus doctrine is functionally opposed to the very structures through which Christ's plan advances in history.

section: V. The Believer as Paladin of Establishment
text: The survival of the human race, the conclusion of the angelic conflict, and the perpetuation of freedom for both evangelism and spiritual advance all depend on the maintenance of establishment principles. Divine institution four — nationalism — protects the freedom of the human race and guarantees local evangelism together with missionary effort in wider geographical areas. God is not the author of confusion. Order and authority in the human race are not optional supplements to His plan; they are constitutive of it.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Nine
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Nine

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Nine
text: 1. Every believer should be a paladin for establishment. The laws of divine establishment are not a secondary political concern but the divinely ordained framework within which evangelism occurs, doctrinal advance is sustained, and the angelic conflict moves toward resolution. Opposition to these laws is opposition to God's plan.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Nine
text: 2. Every believer with doctrine resident in the soul is politically a conservative. Conservatism, properly defined, is the recognition of establishment authority and the defense of each individual's right to freedom, privacy, and property. This is the political expression of doctrinal orientation, not a party affiliation. A pseudo-conservative who harbors anti-Semitism or any form of ethnic hostility is not a true conservative.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Nine
text: 3. A true conservative understands and champions the laws of divine establishment against all satanic and apostate attacks of liberalism. Liberalism in this context means any system of thought that expands the state beyond its authorized function of defending life, liberty, and property, and that uses governmental power to confiscate property, intrude on privacy, or engineer social outcomes.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Nine
text: 4. All believers who oppose establishment ordinances receive two categories of divine discipline. First, direct personal discipline from God for reversionism and apostasy, potentially extending to the sin unto death. Second, historical discipline from God as participants in the opposition to authority, conspiracy, and the sponsoring of revolution.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Nine
text: 5. All apostate believers — both reversionistic and liberal — are in opposition to God. They are, in effect, enemies of the God who saved them and provided a perfect plan for their lives, while simultaneously destroying the establishment principles on which that plan operates.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Nine
text: 6. Freedom and property cannot be separated. When the state confiscates or inflates away the value of private property, it has destroyed freedom by another means. The sacredness of private property is inseparable from personal freedom; lose one and you have effectively lost the other.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Nine
text: 7. Opposition to establishment often arises from ignorance of doctrine. The reversionistic believer is ungrateful and unappreciative of the freedom through which he was evangelized and through which he could advance to maturity. He uses freedom to destroy freedom — an inherently self-contradictory position that reflects the inverted soul-life of the reversionist.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Nine
text: 8. God is not the author of confusion; order and authority are necessary for the survival of the human race. The perpetuation of the human race through the laws of divine establishment is the precondition for concluding the angelic conflict. Without establishment, the human stage on which that conflict is being resolved ceases to function.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Nine
text: 9. The two verbs of verse 2 — antitassō and anthistēmi — represent cause and effect within the same act of opposition. Antitassō is the organized soul-decision against establishment authority. Anthistēmi is the completed application of that opposition. Wrong thinking cannot produce right application; if the premise is inverted, the result is inverted with logical consistency.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Eighty-Nine
text: 10. Separation of church and state is necessary for personal freedom. Civic authority and spiritual authority operate on different bases and must never be mingled. The church functions under the royal family honor code; the state functions under the laws of divine establishment. Obedience to each within its proper sphere is required of every believer.

section: Romans 13:2b — Divine Punishment for Anti-Establishment Believers
text: Romans 13:2b — Divine Punishment for Anti-Establishment Believers

section: Romans 13:2b — Divine Punishment for Anti-Establishment Believers
text: Romans 13:2 “Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.” (ESV)

section: Romans 13:2b — Divine Punishment for Anti-Establishment Believers
text: Corrected translation: Therefore those who resist the authority have opposed the ordinance of God; in fact, they who oppose shall receive punishment to themselves.

section: Romans 13:2b — Divine Punishment for Anti-Establishment Believers
text: We are in the middle of Romans 13:2. The opening clause — 'those who resist the authority have opposed the ordinance of God' — was established in the preceding study. The focus of this chapter is the second clause: the nature, categories, and scope of the punishment that accrues to those who oppose divinely-instituted governmental authority. The passage also provides the occasion for a summary of the laws of divine establishment in their relationship to the Protocol Plan of God.

section: I. Summary Principles: Laws of Divine Establishment (Romans 13:1–2a)
text: I. Summary Principles: Laws of Divine Establishment (Romans 13:1–2a)

section: I. Summary Principles: Laws of Divine Establishment (Romans 13:1–2a)
text: Before proceeding to the exegesis of the second half of verse 2, a set of summary principles consolidates what has been established from verses 1 through 2a.

section: I. Summary Principles: Laws of Divine Establishment (Romans 13:1–2a)
text: 1. Governmental authorities are viewed functionally, not personally. Scripture does not evaluate rulers from the standpoint of individual character or moral worthiness. Rulers are viewed as officers of divine institution, holding authority delegated by God. The personality of the office-holder is irrelevant to the obligation of the governed.

section: I. Summary Principles: Laws of Divine Establishment (Romans 13:1–2a)
text: 2. Human government is a permanent divine institution. Its purpose is threefold: to guarantee individual privacy, to protect private property, and to preserve freedom. It also functions as a safeguard against political internationalism — the satanic strategy of consolidating the human race under a single global authority, thereby eliminating the national boundaries that God established at the Tower of Babel.

section: I. Summary Principles: Laws of Divine Establishment (Romans 13:1–2a)
text: 3. Political internationalism in all its forms opposes the divine ordinance of nationalism. Whether expressed through revolutionary movements, international political bodies, or supranational governance structures, political internationalism represents an assault on the divine institution of the nation-state and constitutes participation in the angelic conflict on the wrong side.

section: I. Summary Principles: Laws of Divine Establishment (Romans 13:1–2a)
text: 4. Religious internationalism is equally contrary to the divine ordinance. Ecumenical structures that subordinate doctrinal precision to organizational unity, and that advocate social revolution as a means of solving human problems, operate outside the divine framework and oppose the work of the local church.

section: I. Summary Principles: Laws of Divine Establishment (Romans 13:1–2a)
text: 5. All forms of internationalism expose and embody the satanic conspiracy against national sovereignty. Nationalism, rightly understood, is not tribalism or ethnic superiority. It is the God-ordained framework within which individual freedom, evangelism, and Bible doctrine can function.

section: I. Summary Principles: Laws of Divine Establishment (Romans 13:1–2a)
text: 6. Civil authority, law, and order — as protectors of human freedom — are ordained by God. This is not merely a pragmatic observation but a theological one: civil order is the structural prerequisite for the fulfillment of the Protocol Plan of God in the life of every believer.

section: II. The Protocol Plan of God and the Laws of Divine Establishment
text: II. The Protocol Plan of God and the Laws of Divine Establishment

section: II. The Protocol Plan of God and the Laws of Divine Establishment
text: The laws of divine establishment are not peripheral to the Christian life. They are the structural prerequisite for every phase of the Protocol Plan of God. The plan may be outlined through the pattern of six imputations, each requiring freedom as its operational condition.

section: A. The X-Radical: Salvation
text: A. The X-Radical: Salvation

section: A. The X-Radical: Salvation
text: The plan begins at birth. God imputes human life to the soul at the moment of birth — not at conception, not at any earlier biological stage. Simultaneously, the justice of God imputes Adam's original sin to the newly-formed human being. This double imputation at birth accomplishes two things.

section: A. The X-Radical: Salvation
text: First, it establishes the need for salvation. Every human being born into the world carries the imputation of Adam's sin and therefore stands under the condemnation of divine justice. Second — and this is the grace provision embedded within the judgment — it guarantees that any person who dies before reaching moral accountability goes immediately to heaven. The condemnation has already been satisfied by the imputation itself; no personal sins have been committed; and divine justice, having already acted, has no further claim. This covers all who die in infancy, as well as those whose mental capacity never reaches the threshold of God-consciousness.

section: A. The X-Radical: Salvation
text: For those who survive to accountability, the first potential becomes operative: salvation through faith in Jesus Christ. The pertinent doctrine is the gospel — that Christ died for our sins, that all sin was imputed to Him on the cross and judged, and that the sole issue is belief. The first hope is the absolute confidence — not a wish, but a certainty grounded in a future fact — that the believer possesses eternal life.

section: A. The X-Radical: Salvation
text: The transition point is salvation adjustment to the justice of God through faith in Christ. The Greek phrase dikaiosynē theou (δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ) — the righteousness/justice of God — is the axis around which the entire Epistle to the Romans turns. All blessing flows through divine justice, not through divine sentiment.

section: B. The Y-Radical: Spiritual Growth
text: B. The Y-Radical: Spiritual Growth

section: B. The Y-Radical: Spiritual Growth
text: At the moment of salvation, two judicial imputations occur. First, all personal sins were already imputed to Christ on the cross and judged there — this is judicial imputation number one, the basis of forgiveness. Second, God's own righteousness is imputed to the newly-born-again believer — this is judicial imputation number two, the basis of all subsequent blessing.

section: B. The Y-Radical: Spiritual Growth
text: This establishes the second potential: the potential for great blessing and reward that glorifies God at spiritual maturity. The pertinent doctrine is the daily intake of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP). The second hope is the absolute confidence that through sustained doctrine intake, the believer will crack the maturity barrier and receive supergrace blessing in time.

section: B. The Y-Radical: Spiritual Growth
text: The maturity adjustment to the justice of God is achieved through the daily function of GAP. This phase requires freedom: freedom to assemble, freedom to hear teaching, freedom to apply doctrine without coercion. The laws of divine establishment are therefore not merely civic arrangements. They are the protective framework within which the Y-radical can function.

section: C. The Z-Radical: Eternity
text: C. The Z-Radical: Eternity

section: C. The Z-Radical: Eternity
text: At the end of the believer's earthly life, two further imputations occur: the imputation of eternal life and the imputation of blessing in time as a preview of eternal reward. These form the third potential — blessing and reward in eternity — and the third hope: the absolute confidence that at the judgment seat of Christ, standing in a resurrection body, the mature believer will receive eternal blessing that glorifies God forever.

section: C. The Z-Radical: Eternity
text: This completes the six imputations. The seventh imputation — the imputation of blessing in eternity — is the fulfillment of the entire plan. Every step from the first to the seventh requires freedom: freedom of volition at salvation, freedom to receive doctrine in the Christian life, and freedom from coercion throughout. This is why the laws of divine establishment are integral to the plan of God, not external to it.

text: A. The Transitional Particle: DE

section: A. The Transitional Particle: DE
text: The clause begins with the post-positive conjunctive particle de (δέ), used here not as a simple connective but as a transitional conjunction introducing an explanatory expansion of the preceding statement. It is best rendered in fact, signaling that what follows elaborates and intensifies the preceding clause.

section: B. The Participle: ANTHISTĒMI
text: B. The Participle: ANTHISTĒMI

section: B. The Participle: ANTHISTĒMI
text: The subject is identified by the nominative plural definite article used as a personal pronoun, governing the perfect active participle of anthistēmi (ἀνθίστημι), meaning to oppose, to resist, to stand against. The dramatic perfect tense is a rhetorical use of the intensive perfect, emphasizing the existing state of those described. The force is not merely that they once resisted but that opposition has become their settled condition — it characterizes them. The active voice identifies the agent as the reversionistic believer: the believer who is theologically and politically liberal, who is anti-establishment, who is involved in revolutionary activity. The participle is circumstantial.

section: C. The Main Verb: LAMBANŌ
text: C. The Main Verb: LAMBANŌ

section: C. The Main Verb: LAMBANŌ
text: The main verb is the future middle indicative of lambanō (λαμβάνω), to receive, to take. The nomic future indicates a fact of judgment from God that can be expected under the specified circumstances. The middle voice is a direct middle, referring the results of the action back to the agent with reflexive force — they bring this upon themselves. The indicative mood is declarative, stating a dogmatic fact.

section: D. The Object: KRIMA
text: D. The Object: KRIMA

section: D. The Object: KRIMA
text: The accusative singular direct object is krima (κρίμα), which is better rendered punishment or punitive action than the traditional damnation. The word does not here refer to eternal condemnation or the lake of fire. It refers to divine discipline — corrective and punitive action administered by God in time. The standard English rendering 'damnation' has generated a false impression that this verse teaches the loss of salvation for those who oppose government, which is theologically impossible and contextually unsupported.

section: E. The Dative of Disadvantage: HEAUTOIS
text: E. The Dative of Disadvantage: HEAUTOIS

section: E. The Dative of Disadvantage: HEAUTOIS
text: The phrase rendered 'to themselves' is the dative plural of disadvantage from the reflexive pronoun heautois (ἑαυτοῖς). When the action expressed by the verb is referred back to the subject, the construction is reflexive. The punishment is self-incurred. No external agent imposes it arbitrarily; the anti-establishment believer, by his own choices, generates the conditions under which divine discipline inevitably follows.

section: F. Corrected Translation
text: F. Corrected Translation

section: F. Corrected Translation
text: In fact, they who oppose shall receive punishment to themselves.

section: IV. The Two Categories of Punishment
text: IV. The Two Categories of Punishment

section: IV. The Two Categories of Punishment
text: The punishment described in this verse falls into two categories, individual and collective, which may ultimately converge.

section: A. Individual Divine Discipline
text: A. Individual Divine Discipline

section: A. Individual Divine Discipline
text: The reversionistic believer who is anti-establishment, revolutionary, or theologically liberal receives individual divine discipline in three progressive stages: warning discipline, intensive discipline, and dying discipline (the sin unto death). These correspond to the individual application of the five cycles of discipline as they apply to the single believer rather than to a national entity.

section: A. Individual Divine Discipline
text: The specific categories of anti-establishment activity that fall under this verse include involvement in revolutionary movements; attempts to circumvent taxation by illegal means; refusal of military service on the basis of so-called conscientious objection; participation in unauthorized labor coercion (the strike as distinguished from voluntary collective resignation); and any form of conspiracy, treason, or violent resistance to civil authority.

section: A. Individual Divine Discipline
text: The so-called conscientious objector who refuses military service on religious grounds is, within the framework of this passage, a reversionistic believer who has confused the Mosaic prohibition against homicide with the divinely authorized function of military service. The Mosaic commandment — correctly rendered — prohibits murder, the unlawful taking of human life for personal motives. It does not prohibit killing in the context of national defense, military service, or the administration of capital punishment. These are separately authorized, and in some cases commanded, elsewhere in Scripture.

section: B. Collective National Discipline
text: B. Collective National Discipline

section: B. Collective National Discipline
text: The anti-establishment believer does not suffer in isolation. He is also a participant in the collective divine discipline that falls upon a national entity when its spiritual pivot is insufficient to sustain divine blessing. The principle of the pivot is decisive here.

section: B. Collective National Discipline
text: The pivot consists of mature believers — the remnant according to the election of grace — whose adjustment to the justice of God at the maturity level sustains divine blessing upon the nation. The spin-off consists of reversionistic believers whose negative volition, emotional instability, and anti-establishment activity generates the conditions for national deterioration. When the spin-off becomes disproportionately large relative to the pivot, Jesus Christ, who controls history, administers progressive cycles of national discipline culminating in the fourth and fifth cycles.

section: B. Collective National Discipline
text: The fifth cycle of discipline — complete national destruction — corresponds to the sin unto death at the national level. At this point, individual discipline and collective discipline converge: those believers who are part of the spin-off and who have pursued reversionism to its terminal expression die the sin unto death as the nation itself is destroyed. The pivot of mature believers, however, is preserved — an expression of the principle that divine justice always provides for those in adjustment, even in the midst of historical catastrophe.

section: B. Collective National Discipline
text: If, on the other hand, there is a return to doctrine — if the pivot is enlarged and the spin-off reduced — the nation is preserved and may recover its former greatness. This is the principle underlying the divine blessing of any national entity: not its technology, not its economic system, not the personal virtue of its rulers, but the size and stability of its pivot.

section: V. The Principle of Authority: Submission Without Approval
text: V. The Principle of Authority: Submission Without Approval

section: V. The Principle of Authority: Submission Without Approval
text: The passage establishes a distinction that is critical to the application of this doctrine: the distinction between respect for an office and approval of the person who holds it. The Christian is required to respect the office — to honor the institution of governmental authority as a divine ordinance. He is not required to approve of the officeholder, to agree with his policies, to suppress legitimate critique, or to refrain from lawful opposition.

section: V. The Principle of Authority: Submission Without Approval
text: The Apostle Paul himself provides the definitive illustration. Tried unjustly, condemned under a degenerate emperor, and executed without legitimate cause, Paul did not advocate assassination, did not encourage revolution, did not organize resistance. He accepted the verdict as the Lord's provision — including the grace provision of dying grace and the imputation of martyrdom — and went to his execution without resistance. His submission was not passivity born of fear or resignation but active obedience grounded in doctrine. He understood that the office of Caesar retained its divine authorization regardless of the character of the man who occupied it.

section: V. The Principle of Authority: Submission Without Approval
text: This is the distinction between active obedience — which is commanded — and passive obedience, which implies a kind of inert non-resistance that the text does not in fact mandate. Active obedience means positive engagement with the responsibilities of citizenship: paying taxes, serving in the military, participating in the civic process, holding office where appropriate, and pursuing the rescission of unjust laws through lawful means.

section: VI. Summary Principles: Anti-Establishment Activity and Christian Responsibility
text: VI. Summary Principles: Anti-Establishment Activity and Christian Responsibility

section: VI. Summary Principles: Anti-Establishment Activity and Christian Responsibility
text: 1. The Christian is not authorized to participate in revolutionary movements. Violence as a means of solving political, social, or economic problems is excluded by the doctrine of divine establishment. The Christian's responsibility is to sustain authority structures, not to destroy them.

section: VI. Summary Principles: Anti-Establishment Activity and Christian Responsibility
text: 2. Christian responsibility to the national entity is positive and active. It includes obedience to the laws of the land, payment of taxes — even confiscatory taxes — participation in the military, jury service, voting, and where applicable the holding of public office.

section: VI. Summary Principles: Anti-Establishment Activity and Christian Responsibility
text: 3. Unlawful and unjust laws are to be contested by lawful means. Legislation, litigation, public advocacy, electoral process, and peaceful protest are all authorized. Violence, assassination, treason, and conspiracy are never authorized, regardless of the perceived justice of the cause.

section: VI. Summary Principles: Anti-Establishment Activity and Christian Responsibility
text: 4. The Bible never advocates assassination. The assassination of any political figure, however corrupt or destructive, is without doctrinal authorization. The removal of tyrannical or unjust rulers is a divine prerogative; when God acts through historical catastrophe or the fifth cycle of discipline, the result is far more thorough and just than any human act of violence could achieve.

section: VI. Summary Principles: Anti-Establishment Activity and Christian Responsibility
text: 5. Even in conditions of severe tyranny, peaceful means remain the Christian's instrument. Paul's example is definitive: unjust imprisonment, unjust trial, unjust execution — all absorbed without resistance and without bitterness. The degree of freedom required to sustain the Christian life is the freedom to hear the Word, to assemble, and to evangelize. As long as these remain operative, no level of political injustice authorizes violent resistance.

section: VI. Summary Principles: Anti-Establishment Activity and Christian Responsibility
text: 6. Active obedience, not passive obedience, is the biblical standard. Passive obedience is an inadequate category. It implies a right of non-cooperation — including the right to strike — that Scripture does not support. The individual has the right to resign from employment, including collective resignation. He does not have the right to coerce employers or prevent willing workers from filling vacated positions. The strike, as an instrument of collective economic coercion, is outside the framework of legitimate activity established by this passage.

section: VI. Summary Principles: Anti-Establishment Activity and Christian Responsibility
text: 7. Freedom of religion, evangelism, and doctrine intake define the threshold of legitimate resistance. When a government destroys the freedom to evangelize, to assemble for Bible teaching, and to take in doctrine, the threshold of extreme tyranny has been reached. Even then, the example of Paul and the early church — functioning in conditions of active persecution within the Roman Empire — demonstrates that the presumption remains against violence. The early church did not overthrow Rome; it outlasted it.

section: VI. Summary Principles: Anti-Establishment Activity and Christian Responsibility
text: 8. The same revolution devours its own children. Anti-establishment believers who participate in revolution, conspiracy, tax evasion, or refusal of military service incur both individual divine discipline and participation in the collective judgment of a nation in reversionism. The judgment they bring upon their nation falls upon them as well. The fifth cycle of discipline is not selective; it sweeps away the spin-off along with the structures they sought to destroy.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety
text: 1. KRIMA does not mean eternal damnation in this context. The traditional rendering 'damnation' has generated theological confusion. The word refers to punitive divine discipline administered in time — warning discipline, intensive discipline, and dying discipline — not to the lake of fire. Salvation cannot be lost; the passage addresses divine discipline of believers, not the eternal destiny of unbelievers.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety
text: 2. The reflexive dative HEAUTOIS establishes personal accountability. The anti-establishment believer does not become a victim of arbitrary divine action. He generates the conditions of his own punishment through sustained negative volition and anti-establishment activity. The punishment is self-incurred.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety
text: 3. Individual and collective divine discipline are structurally linked through the pivot. The size of the pivot relative to the spin-off determines whether a nation advances toward recovery or toward the fifth cycle of discipline. The sin unto death of individual reversionistic believers and the national fifth cycle of discipline converge at the same historical moment.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety
text: 4. The laws of divine establishment are the structural prerequisite for the Protocol Plan of God. Every phase of the plan — salvation adjustment, maturity adjustment, and the reception of eternal blessing — requires the freedom that only stable governmental authority can protect. Anti-establishment activity is therefore not merely politically wrong; it is an assault on the conditions under which the plan of God can be fulfilled in human lives.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety
text: 5. Paul's submission to Roman authority in the face of unjust execution is the defining illustration of this passage. His death under Nero was not a failure of justice but a triumph of doctrine. Dying grace, the imputation of martyrdom, and the reward that awaits him at the judgment seat of Christ are the ultimate vindication of active obedience maintained under maximum pressure.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety
text: 6. Technology does not alter moral or political principle. The fundamental relations of human beings — their need for property, freedom, productivity, and accountability — remain constant across all eras of history. No advance in technology requires or justifies a revision of constitutional principle, moral standard, or the laws of divine establishment. The writings of the Apostle Paul have not been superseded by any development in human civilization.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety
text: 7. Nationalism is a divine ordinance; political internationalism is a satanic strategy. The preservation of distinct national entities is the structural means by which God limits the concentration of tyrannical power and maintains the conditions for freedom. Any movement — political, economic, or religious — that works to dissolve national sovereignty in favor of centralized global governance participates in the satanic conspiracy against the laws of divine establishment.

Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One

section: Romans 13:3 — Divine Establishment, Authority, and the Restraint of Evil
text: Romans 13:3 — Divine Establishment, Authority, and the Restraint of Evil

section: Romans 13:3 — Divine Establishment, Authority, and the Restraint of Evil
text: Romans 13:3 “For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval.” (ESV)

section: Romans 13:3 — Divine Establishment, Authority, and the Restraint of Evil
text: Corrected translation: For the governing authorities are not a cause of fear for moral function, but for evil function. Do you desire not to fear the authority? Practice good function, and you will have approval from it.

section: Romans 13:3 — Divine Establishment, Authority, and the Restraint of Evil
text: Romans 13:3 continues the exposition of divine institution number four — nationalism — and the purpose of governmental authority within the laws of divine establishment. Having established in verses 1–2 that all authority is delegated by God and that resistance to legitimate authority is resistance to God's ordinance, Paul now turns to the function of that authority: to protect freedom, privacy, and property, and to restrain evil through the legitimate application of punitive force. This chapter covers the exegesis of the first half of verse 3, together with a systematic treatment of the doctrine of capital punishment as the enforcement mechanism of the laws of divine establishment.

section: I. Exegesis of Romans 13:3a — The Governing Authorities and Moral Function
text: I. Exegesis of Romans 13:3a — The Governing Authorities and Moral Function

section: The Conjunction Gar and the Predicate of Authority
text: The Conjunction Gar and the Predicate of Authority

section: The Conjunction Gar and the Predicate of Authority
text: The verse opens with the explanatory post-positive conjunctive particle γαρ (*gar*), correctly translated "for." It introduces the ground or reason for the principle stated in verses 1–2: that authority is not to be resisted because it serves a divinely ordained protective function.

section: The Conjunction Gar and the Predicate of Authority
text: The nominative plural subject is from the noun archōn (ἄρχων), governing authority or official of state. In Greek civic usage, archōn designated one of the rulers of Athens; the term became generalized to mean any holder of delegated governmental power. The nominative plural with the definite article here functions generically, denoting the class of individuals entrusted with the responsibility and power to enforce the principles of freedom, privacy, and property within the national entity.

section: The Verb Eimi with the Negative Ou
text: The Verb Eimi with the Negative Ou

section: The Verb Eimi with the Negative Ou
text: The present active indicative of eimi (εἰμί) with the negative ou (οὔ) establishes a present of duration: the principle of establishment begun in the past continues into the present. The active voice places the production of this action — or more precisely the negation of a particular action — squarely on the governing authorities themselves. Legitimate governmental authority does not function as a source of terror.

section: The Predicate Nominative Phobos
text: The Predicate Nominative Phobos

section: The Predicate Nominative Phobos
text: The predicate nominative is the singular of phobos (φόβος), the noun from which the English word phobia derives. In this context phobos denotes fear of punishment — specifically, punitive action by the state for crime, conspiracy, revolution, or the violent overthrow of legitimate government. The predicate nominative construction asserts what the governing authorities are not: a cause of fear, a source of terror.

section: The Predicate Nominative Phobos
text: This assertion must be understood in its proper context. Under the laws of divine establishment — where governmental authority exists to protect freedom, privacy, and property — law-abiding citizens have no reason to fear the authorities. The state is not an instrument of terror directed at those who function within establishment principles. The contrast is with totalitarian systems, under which governmental authority becomes a source of terror regardless of the conduct of the individual.

section: II. Good Function and Evil Function — Agathos and Kakos
text: II. Good Function and Evil Function — Agathos and Kakos

section: The Dative of Advantage: Agathos Ergon
text: The Dative of Advantage: Agathos Ergon

section: The Dative of Advantage: Agathos Ergon
text: The phrase "good works" represents the dative of advantage from the adjective agathos (ἀγαθός) combined with ergon (ἔργον). Agathos denotes intrinsic goodness or inner worth — the same term encountered in Romans 8:28. Here it carries the connotation of moral function in the sense defined by the laws of divine establishment: the protection of and respect for freedom, privacy, and property. It does not mean religious observance or social benevolence in a general sense.

section: The Dative of Advantage: Agathos Ergon
text: Ergon (ἔργον) refers to deeds or function that exhibit consistent moral character — here specifically the exercise of free will, ambition, and initiative within the framework of freedom, privacy, and property. The generic use of the definite article with agathos encompasses not only personal moral conduct but the productive function of free enterprise: the courage to start a business, meet a payroll, produce a product, and compete openly in the marketplace.

section: The Dative of Advantage: Agathos Ergon
text: Good function, then, is observance of the laws of divine establishment. It means not violating the freedom of others (which would include homicide), not violating the privacy of others (which would include blackmail and coercion), and not violating the property of others (which would include theft). Moral function in this passage is not the imposition of equality or the redistribution of resources — it is the exercise of individual capacity within the boundaries that preserve everyone else's freedom, privacy, and property.

section: The Adversative Conjunction Alla and the Dative of Disadvantage: Kakos
text: The Adversative Conjunction Alla and the Dative of Disadvantage: Kakos

section: The Adversative Conjunction Alla and the Dative of Disadvantage: Kakos
text: The adversative conjunction alla (ἀλλά) introduces the contrast. The dative of disadvantage follows from kakos (κακός), which in this context denotes crime — the violation of freedom, privacy, or property. Evil function encompasses crime (murder, blackmail, theft), revolution, conspiracy for the violent overthrow of government, assassination as a political instrument, and any system of social organization that systematically deprives the individual of freedom, privacy, and property under the pretext of the common good.

section: The Adversative Conjunction Alla and the Dative of Disadvantage: Kakos
text: The corrected translation of Romans 13:3a reads: "For the governing authorities are not a cause of fear for moral function, but for evil function." This is the foundational statement of the purpose of government under the laws of divine establishment: to be a terror to evil function, not to good function.

section: III. The Doctrine of Restraint — Fear, Respect, and the Old Sin Nature
text: III. The Doctrine of Restraint — Fear, Respect, and the Old Sin Nature

section: Two Mechanisms of Restraint
text: Two Mechanisms of Restraint

section: Two Mechanisms of Restraint
text: Within any national entity, the old sin nature must be restrained if freedom, privacy, and property are to be maintained for the population as a whole. The laws of divine establishment provide two mechanisms of restraint.

section: Two Mechanisms of Restraint
text: The first and more basic mechanism is fear — fear of punishment, fear of reprisal, fear of incarceration, fear of the loss of life. This mechanism operates on old sin natures that are oriented toward criminal function and that do not respond to reason, persuasion, or social pressure. Fear of punitive consequences is not an indication of advanced moral development; it is the floor-level mechanism that prevents the breakdown of civil order.

section: Two Mechanisms of Restraint
text: The second mechanism is respect — respect for authority, respect for the rights of others, respect for the law as an institution, and ultimately respect for God as the delegating source of all legitimate authority. Respect operates on old sin natures that have been oriented to establishment principles through the intake of Bible doctrine, through sound upbringing, or through civic formation. A society in which respect predominates as the restraining mechanism is a more advanced and more stable society than one in which fear alone provides the restraint.

section: Two Mechanisms of Restraint
text: Both mechanisms are necessary and legitimate. The laws of divine establishment do not assume that all members of a national entity will be believers or spiritually mature. They provide a framework within which both the fearful and the respectful can coexist in an ordered society, each restrained by the mechanism appropriate to their orientation.

section: The Criminal Mind and Disorientation to the Laws of Divine Establishment
text: The Criminal Mind and Disorientation to the Laws of Divine Establishment

section: The Criminal Mind and Disorientation to the Laws of Divine Establishment
text: A criminal mind, in the context of establishment doctrine, is a mind disoriented to the laws of divine establishment. It is not defined by the commission of specific acts but by an orientation that recognizes no authority unless compelled by the threat of violence or punishment. Such an orientation is incompatible with the function of freedom, privacy, and property in a national entity. The criminal mind cannot be corrected by social engineering, psychological programming, or material redistribution. The only legitimate paths of correction are, first, the fear of adequate punishment sufficient to restrain the old sin nature, and second, the reception of Bible doctrine resident in the soul, which alone can produce genuine reorientation to establishment principles.

section: IV. Capital Punishment as the Enforcement Mechanism of Divine Establishment
text: IV. Capital Punishment as the Enforcement Mechanism of Divine Establishment

section: IV. Capital Punishment as the Enforcement Mechanism of Divine Establishment
text: The term "fear" in the predicate nominative of verse 3 — φόβος (*phobos*) — refers specifically to fear of punishment administered by the state. This leads directly to the doctrine of capital punishment, which will be treated in full in the exegesis of verse 4. The following conclusions from the current passage establish the doctrinal framework.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One
text: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One
text: 1. Phobos as fear of punishment: The predicate nominative φόβος (*phobos*) in Romans 13:3 refers to fear of punishment by the state for crime, conspiracy, revolution, or the violent overthrow of legitimate government. Governing authorities under establishment principles are a terror to evil function, not to moral function.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One
text: 2. Capital punishment and the laws of divine establishment: The Bible and the laws of divine establishment require that punishment for anti-establishment violence include death. The sword of state — introduced explicitly in verse 4 — is the instrument by which the national entity enforces this principle. Key texts are Genesis 9:6 and Romans 13:4.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One
text: 3. Restraint of society requires law enforcement: Society contains a range of old sin natures, some restrained by respect and others restrained only by fear. Legitimate government must be capable of activating both mechanisms. Law enforcement without punitive teeth — without the credible threat of serious punishment — cannot sustain the conditions necessary for freedom, privacy, and property.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One
text: 4. Fear is the only effective restraint on certain expressions of the old sin nature: Criminal function, conspiracy, revolution, and anarchy can only be suppressed when the cost of such activity — in terms of punishment — exceeds whatever advantage the criminal mind perceives in pursuing it. Reasoning, negotiation, and social programs cannot substitute for this calculus.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One
text: 5. Capital punishment is mandated by Scripture as the means of controlling criminal, revolutionary, and anarchical violence: This principle is grounded in Genesis 9:6 and will be elaborated in the exegesis of Romans 13:4. The sword delegated to governing authority is not ornamental; it represents the legitimate exercise of lethal force in the service of establishment order.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One
text: 6. Capital punishment is the highest power in human government: No governmental function exceeds in significance the power to administer death as the terminal punishment for the most severe violations of freedom, privacy, and property. This power, properly exercised within due process, is the capstone of establishment authority.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One
text: 7. Only with capital punishment can government guarantee freedom, privacy, and property: Without the ultimate sanction, the protections afforded by the laws of divine establishment are unenforceable at the margin. The guarantees of freedom, privacy, and property presuppose that the state possesses and is willing to exercise the full range of punitive authority.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One
text: 8. Legislation and law enforcement are useless without punitive teeth: Statutes that carry no credible punishment, or courts that systematically decline to impose serious penalties, provide no effective restraint on the criminal mind. The bite — capital punishment for the most severe offenses — is what gives law its deterrent force.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One
text: 9. Fear of capital punishment is a basic principle in the orderly function of the laws of divine establishment: This fear is not pathological; it is the rational response of the old sin nature to the credible threat of lethal punishment. It is the mechanism by which establishment order is maintained among those whose orientation does not yet include genuine respect for authority.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One
text: 10. Capital punishment is administered by legitimate judicial authority: Whether in a monarchy, republic, or oligarchy, capital punishment falls within the competence of legitimately constituted government — local, regional, or national — provided that the sword is directed toward evil function and not toward the suppression of moral function. The form of government is secondary; the criterion is the proper direction of punitive authority.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One
text: 11. Restraint in society rests on fear and respect as complementary mechanisms: Fear restrains those oriented to criminal function; respect restrains those oriented to establishment principles. A stable national entity requires both. Spiritual advance — the intake of Bible doctrine and maturity adjustment to the justice of God — progressively shifts the believer from fear-based restraint to respect-based restraint, but neither mechanism is illegitimate.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Three Hundred Ninety-One
text: 12. Good function in Romans 13:3 refers to the exercise of freedom, privacy, and property under the laws of divine establishment: The term ἀγαθός (*agathos*) in this context does not denote religious piety or philanthropic sentiment but the morally sound function of the individual within the framework of establishment: productive work, competitive exchange, voluntary cooperation, and respect for the rights of others.

section: Glossary
text: ἄρχων archōn — ruler, governing authority

section: Glossary
text: Nominative masculine singular noun. In Attic usage, one of the nine or twelve chief magistrates of Athens. In the New Testament, generalized to denote any holder of delegated governmental authority. In Romans 13:3, used in the nominative plural to designate the class of legitimate state officials.

section: Glossary
text: phobos

section: Glossary
text: φόβος phobos — fear, terror, cause of fear

section: Glossary
text: Nominative masculine singular noun. Root of the English words phobia and phobic. In Romans 13:3, functions as predicate nominative: the governing authorities are not a phobos — not a cause of fear — for those engaged in moral function. In the doctrinal context of this passage, phobos specifically denotes fear of punitive action by the state for criminal, revolutionary, or anarchical conduct.

section: Glossary
text: agathos

section: Glossary
text: ἀγαθός agathos — good, intrinsically good, morally sound

section: Glossary
text: Adjective of the second declension. Denotes intrinsic goodness or inner worth, as distinguished from kalos (outward excellence). In Romans 13:3, used in the dative of advantage with ergon to describe the function that governing authorities are not designed to restrain: the productive, law-abiding exercise of freedom, privacy, and property under the laws of divine establishment. Previously encountered in Romans 8:28.

section: Glossary
text: ergon

section: Glossary
text: ἔργον ergon — work, deed, function, occupation

section: Glossary
text: Neuter noun, second declension. Refers to deeds or actions that exhibit consistent moral character, or to a person's work or occupation. In Romans 13:3, combined with agathos to describe moral function in the establishment sense: productive activity that operates within and upholds the framework of freedom, privacy, and property.

section: Glossary

text: κακός kakos — evil, bad, criminal function

section: Glossary
text: Adjective of the second declension. Denotes that which is bad or evil in character or effect. In the establishment context of Romans 13:3, kakos encompasses crime (the violation of freedom, privacy, or property), conspiracy, revolution, the violent overthrow of legitimate government, and any system that systematically deprives individuals of their establishment rights.

section: Glossary

section: Glossary
text: ἀλλά alla — but, on the contrary

section: Glossary
text: Strong adversative conjunction. Sets up a direct antithesis between the two datives in Romans 13:3: good function (agathos ergon) versus evil function (kakos ergon). Signals that the relationship of governing authority to each category is opposite in kind.

section: Glossary
text: gar

section: Glossary
text: γαρ gar — for, because

section: Glossary
text: Post-positive explanatory conjunction. Introduces the ground or reason for a preceding statement. In Romans 13:3, gar connects the principle that governing authorities are not a cause of fear for moral function with the foregoing instruction to subordinate oneself to those authorities: the reason one is to subordinate oneself is precisely because legitimate authority protects rather than threatens the person engaged in moral function.

section: Glossary
text: Laws of Divine Establishment

section: Glossary
text: The God-ordained structural principles governing human society in the post-Fall age, applicable to all humanity regardless of spiritual status. The four divine institutions are: volition (individual free will), marriage, family, and nationalism (the national entity with its governmental authority). The three core establishment rights are freedom, privacy, and property. These rights are inseparable: the loss of any one entails the loss of the others.
